2929: 	\chapter{Examples: Double Simple Cycle Algebras}
2930: 	Although it is not phrased in these terms, in \cite{Kraskiewicz-Weyman} Kraskiewicz and Weyman study a class of finite dimensional gentle algebras $A(n)$ given by the following pullback diagram with $\mathbb{A}_n$ the equioriented type $\mathbb{A}$ quiver with $|Q_0|=n$. 
2931: 	\[ \xymatrix{
2932: 		A(n) \ar[rr]^{\pi_1} \ar[d]_{\iota_1} & & \ttop(A(n)) \ar[d]^{\iota_2} \\
2933: 		k\mathbb{A}_n \times k\mathbb{A}_n \ar[rr]_{\pi_2} & & \ttop (k\mathbb{A}_n \times k\mathbb{A}_n)
2934: 	} \]
2935: 	The maps $\pi_1, \pi_2$ are the projections onto $\ttop(A(n))= A(n)/\rad(A(n)) = \bigoplus_{i=1}^n P(i)/\rad(P(i)) \cong \prod_{i=1}^n k$, $\ttop(k\mathbb{A}_n \times k\mathbb{A}_n) = k\mathbb{A}_n/\rad(k\mathbb{A}_n) \times k\mathbb{A}_n/\rad(k\mathbb{A}_n) \cong \prod_{i=1}^n k \times \prod_{i=1}^n k$. The maps $\iota_1, \iota_2$ are idempotent embeddings given by $e_i \mapsto e_i'+e_i''$, where $e_i$ is the $i^{th}$ primitive idempotent of the algebra $A(n)$, $e_i'$ is the primitive idempotent in the first copy of $k\mathbb{A}_n$ corresponding to the vertex $i \in \mathbb{A}_{n,0}$, and $e_i''$ is the $i^{th}$ idempotent of the second copy. We would like to study a class of algebras closely related to these algebras. Let $\tilde{\mathbb{A}}_n$ be the cyclicly oriented quiver with $n$ arrows and vertices. For $n=0$ (mod $2$), let $\Lambda(n)$ be given by the matrix algebra
2936: 	\[
2937: 	\Lambda(n): =  \begin{pmatrix}
2938: 		\lambda_{11} & (x)\lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2939: 		\lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2940: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2941: 		\lambda_{n-1,1} & \lambda_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2942: 		\lambda_{n1} & \lambda_{n2} & \cdots & \lambda_{n,n-1} & \lambda_{n,n}
2943: 	\end{pmatrix} \times 
2944: 	\begin{pmatrix}
2945: 		\mu_{11} & (x)\mu_{12} & \cdots & (x)\mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2946: 		\mu_{11} & \mu_{12} & \cdots & (x)\mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2947: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2948: 		\mu_{n-1,1} & \mu_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2949: 		\mu_{n1} & \mu_{n2} & \cdots & \mu_{n,n-1} & \mu_{n,n}
2950: 	\end{pmatrix} ,\]
2951: 	where $\lambda_{ij}, \mu_{ij} \in k[[x]], \lambda_{ii}=\mu_{ii}$ (mod $x$), which is given by the pullback diagram
2952: 	\[
2953: 	\xymatrix{
2954: 		\Lambda(n) \ar[r]^{\pi_1} \ar[d]_{\iota_1} & \Lambda(n)/\rad(\Lambda(n)) \ar[d]^{\iota_2} \\
2955: 		\bH(n) \ar[r]_{\pi_2} & \bH(n)/\rad(\bH(n)) 
2956: 	}
2957: 	\]
2958: 	where
2959: 	\[ \bH(n) = \begin{pmatrix}
2960: 		\lambda_{11} & (x)\lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2961: 		\lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2962: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2963: 		\lambda_{n-1,1} & \lambda_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2964: 		\lambda_{n1} & \lambda_{n2} & \cdots & \lambda_{n,n-1} & \lambda_{n,n}
2965: 	\end{pmatrix} \times 
2966: 	\begin{pmatrix}
2967: 		\mu_{11} & (x)\mu_{12} & \cdots & (x)\mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2968: 		\mu_{11} & \mu_{12} & \cdots & (x)\mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2969: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2970: 		\mu_{n-1,1} & \mu_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \mu_{1,n-1} & (x)\mu_{1,n}\\
2971: 		\mu_{n1} & \mu_{n2} & \cdots & \mu_{n,n-1} & \mu_{n,n}
2972: 	\end{pmatrix} ,\]
2973: 	with $\lambda_{ij}, \mu_{ij} \in k[[x]]$. 
2974: 	Then, $\rad(\bH(n)) = \rad(\Lambda(n))$, and $\iota_1$ and $\iota_2$ are given by radical embeddings with mapping on the idempotents:
2975: 	\[ \Lambda(n)/\rad(\Lambda(n)) \ni e_{ii} \mapsto e_{ii}'+e_{ii}'' \in \bH(n)/\rad(\bH(n)). \]
2976: 	Now, if $n=1$ (mod $2$), then we take
2977: 	\[
2978: 	\Lambda(n): =  \begin{pmatrix}
2979: 		\lambda_{11} & (x)\lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2980: 		\lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2981: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2982: 		\lambda_{n-1,1} & \lambda_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2983: 		\lambda_{n1} & \lambda_{n2} & \cdots & \lambda_{n,n-1} & \lambda_{n,n}
2984: 	\end{pmatrix} 
2985: 	\]
2986: 	with $\lambda_{ij} \in k[[x]]$, and $\lambda_{ii}=\lambda_{2i,2i}$ (mod $x$), for $i=1,2,...,n$. We have 
2987: 	\[ \bH(n) = \begin{pmatrix}
2988: 		\lambda_{11} & (x)\lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2989: 		\lambda_{11} & \lambda_{12} & \cdots & (x)\lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2990: 		\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots \\
2991: 		\lambda_{n-1,1} & \lambda_{n-1,2} & \cdots & \lambda_{1,n-1} & (x)\lambda_{1,n}\\
2992: 		\lambda_{n1} & \lambda_{n2} & \cdots & \lambda_{n,n-1} & \lambda_{n,n}\end{pmatrix} \]
2993: 	with $\lambda_{ij} \in k[[x]]$, and the pullback diagram is the same with the new $\Lambda(n)$ and $\bH(n)$. 
2994: 	We call $\bH(n)$ the \textbf{normalization} of the order $\Lambda(n)$. We will call 
2995: 	$\Lambda(n)$ a \textbf{double simple cycle order}. In general, we may replace $k[[x]]
2996: 	$ by any $R$ such that $R$ is a complete noetherian local domain, and we then 
2997: 	replace $(x)$ with $\fm$, the maximal ideal of $R$. For $R=k[[x]]$ and $\fm=(x)$, 
2998: 	the order $\Lambda(n)$ is isomorphic to the completion of the path algebra:
2999: 	\[
3000: 	\begin{tikzcd}
3001: 		& n \arrow[r, dashed] \arrow[r, bend left] & 1 \arrow[rd, dashed] \arrow[rd, bend left] &  \\
3002: 		n-1 \arrow[ru, bend left] \arrow[ru, dashed] &  &  & 2 \arrow[d, bend left] \arrow[d, dashed] \\
3003: 		n-2 \arrow[u, bend left] \arrow[u, dashed] &  &  & 3 \arrow[ld, bend left] \arrow[ld, dashed] \\
3004: 		& 5 \arrow[lu, no head, dotted, bend left] & 4 \arrow[l, bend left] \arrow[l, dashed] & 
3005: 	\end{tikzcd}
3006: 	\]
3007: 	where the relations $I=\la a_{i+1}a_i, b_{i+1}b_i \ra_{i =1}^n$ is given by composition of two arrows of the same color. We then have a pullback diagram
3008: 	\[ 
3009: 	\xymatrix{\tilde{A}(n) \ar[r]^{\pi_1} \ar[d]_{\iota_1} & k^n \ar[d]^{\iota_2} \\
3010: 		k\tilde{\mathbb{A}}_n \times k\tilde{\mathbb{A}}_n \ar[r]_{\pi_2} & k^n \times k^n }
3011: 	\]
3012: 	for $n$ odd, and 
3013: 	\[ 
3014: 	\xymatrix{ \tilde{A}(n) \ar[r]^{\pi_1} \ar[d]_{\iota_1} & k^n \ar[d]^{\iota_2} \\
3015: 		k\tilde{\mathbb{A}}_{2n} \times  \ar[r]_{\pi_2} & k^{2n} }
3016: 	\]
3017: 	for $n$ even. 
3018: 	We will call $\tilde{A}(n)$ the class of \textbf{double simple cycle algebras}.

3021: 	\subsection{The Riemann Surfaces}
3022: 	Let $\tilde{A}(n) = kQ/I$ be a double simple cycle algebra of length $n$. Then $I = \la a_{i+1}a_i, b_{i+1}b_i \ra_{i 
3023: 		\in \ZZ/n\ZZ}$. In particular, there are two cycles, up to cyclic permutation, "$R$" and "$B$" of length $n$, such that 
3024: 	any two consecutive arrows lies in $I$, and there is a single unique non-zero cycle (not in $I$) of length $2n$, 
3025: 	\[ C = (a_1b_2a_3b_4 \cdots b_1a_2b_3a_4b_5 \cdots a_{n-1}b_n) \] 
3026: 	up to a cyclic permutation of the arrows if $n$ is even, and there are two
3027: 	\[ C_1 = (a_1b_2a_3 \cdots a_{n-1}b_n), \quad C_2 = (b_1a_2b_3 \cdots b_{n-1}a_n) \]
3028: 	if $n$ is odd. Let $\varphi = \varphi_R \varphi_B \in S_{Q_1}$ be two cyclic permutations in the permutation group $S_{Q_1} \cong S_{2n}$. Let $\varphi_R = (a_1,a_2,...,a_n) \mapsto  (1,2,...,n)$ and $\varphi_B = (b_1, b_2, ..., b_n) \mapsto (n+1, n+2, ..., 2n)$ given by identifying $Q_1$ with $[2n]$ by fixing a labeling of the arrows. Let 
3029: 	\[
3030: 	\sigma =
3031: 	\begin{cases}
3032: 		(a_1b_2a_3b_4 \cdots b_1a_2b_3a_4b_5 \cdots a_{n-1}b_n) \quad \text{if} \ |Q_0|=2k+1 \\
3033: 		(a_1,b_2,a_3,..., b_{n-2},a_{n-1},b_n)(b_1,a_2,b_3,...,a_{n-2}b_{n-1}a_n) \quad \text{if}\ |Q_0|=2k
3034: 	\end{cases}
3035: 	\]
3036: 	In the above cases we may identify, 
3037: 	\[ (a_1b_2a_3b_4 \cdots b_1a_2b_3a_4b_5 \cdots a_{n-1}b_n) \mapsto (1, n+1, 2, n+2, ..., n, 2n) \in S_{2n} \]
3038: 	and
3039: 	\begin{align*}
3040: 		(a_1,b_2,a_3,..., b_{n-2},a_{n-1},b_n)&(b_1,a_2,b_3,...,a_{n-2}b_{n-1}a_n) \\
3041: 		&\mapsto (1,n+2,3,...,n-1,2n)(n+1,2,n+3,...,2n-1,n) \in S_{2n}.
3042: 	\end{align*}
3043: 	
3044: 	for $k=0,1,2,...$; finally, let $\alpha = (1,n+1)(2,n+2) \cdots (n,2n)$. If we restrict $I$ to $R$ or $B$, we have an algebra $\Lambda_R = kR/I \cong k \mathbb{\tilde{A}}_n/\rad(k \mathbb{\tilde{A}}_n)^2 \cong kB/I = \Lambda_B$. We may then view $\alpha$ as the gluing that identifies $ta_i' \leftrightarrow tb_i'$, where $a_i' \in \Lambda_R$ and $b_i' \in \Lambda_B$ are arrows in the respective algebras. It is not hard to verify $\sigma \alpha = \varphi^{-1}$, and thus the triple $[\sigma, \alpha, \varphi]$ may be seen as a combinatorial embedding of a graph into a Riemann surface. This map $\Gamma(n) \hookrightarrow X$ has either one vertex if $n$ is even, or two vertices if $n$ is odd, corresponding to $\sigma$. It has two faces, corresponding to $\varphi_R$ and $\varphi_B$; it also has exactly $n=|Q_0|$ edges corresponding to $\alpha$. Thus we may compute the surface associated to the algebra $\tilde{A}(n)$ via
3045: 	\[ \chi(\tilde{A}(n)) = |\sigma|-|\alpha|+|\varphi| = \begin{cases}
3046: 		2-2k \quad \text{if} \ |Q_0|=n=2k+1 \\
3047: 		4-2k \quad \text{if} \ |Q_0| = n = 2k
3048: 	\end{cases}. \]
3049: 	for $k=0,1,2,...$, and $n \geq 1$, so that we have the genus function 
3050: 	\[ g(\tilde{A}(n)) = \begin{cases}
3051: 		k \quad \text{if} \ n=2k+1 \\
3052: 		k-1 \quad \text{if} \ n=2k
3053: 	\end{cases} \]

3181: 		\chapter{Background on Representation Theory of General Linear Groups}
3182: 		
3183: 		
3184: 		\section{Young Tableaux and Schur Functors}\label{Young Tableaux}
3185: 		A \textbf{partition} $\lambda \vdash m$, of some nonnegative integer $m$ is a sequence of nonincreasing numbers $\lambda = (\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_s)$ such that $\sum_i \lambda_i = m$. We define a \textbf{Young diagram} corresponding to a partition $\lambda = (\lambda_1, ..., \lambda_s) \vdash m$, as the diagram with $\lambda_i$ boxes in the $i^{th}$ row. We identify partitions with their Young diagrams and speak of the two interchangeably. For a free module $E$ over a commutative ring $K$ with ordered basis $\{e_1, ..., e_n\}$, we associate a filling of the diagram $\lambda$ by integers $\{1, ..., n\}$ to an element in the module
3186: 		\[ \bigwedge^{\lambda_1}E \otimes \cdots \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_s}E \]
3187: 		as follows: If in row $i$ and box $j$ of $\lambda$ we have the integers $t(i, j)$ for $j=1, ..., \lambda_i$, we associate the element
3188: 		\[ e_{t(1,1)} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{t(1,\lambda_1)} \otimes  \cdots \otimes e_{t(s,1)} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{t(s, \lambda_s)}.\]
3189: 		We define such a filling to be a \textbf{tableaux}. A tableaux is \textbf{standard} if its rows are strictly increasing, and its columns are nondecreasing. 
3190: 		
3191: 		Fix a free module $E$ of rank $n$ over a commutative ring $K$. Let $\lambda = ( \lambda_1, ..., \lambda_s) \vdash m$ be a partition. We define the module
3192: 		\[ L_{\lambda}E = \bigwedge^{\lambda_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_s}E/R(\lambda, E) \]
3193: 		where the submodule $R(\lambda, E)$ is the sum of all submodules of the form
3194: 		\[ \bigwedge^{\lambda_1}E \otimes \cdots \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_{a-1}}E \otimes R_{a, a+1}E \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_{a+2}}E \otimes \cdots \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_s}E \]
3195: 		for $1 \leq a \leq s-1$. Here $R_{a,a+1}E$ is the submodule spanned by the images of the maps $\theta(\lambda, a, u, v, E)$
3196: 		\[ \xymatrix{ \bigwedge^uE \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_a-u+\lambda_{a+1}-v}E \otimes \bigwedge^vE \ar[d]^{1 \otimes \Delta \otimes 1} \\
3197: 			\bigwedge^uE \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_a-u}E \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_{a+1}-v}E \bigwedge^vE \ar[d]^{m_{12} \otimes m_{34}} \\
3198: 			\bigwedge^{\lambda_a}E \otimes \bigwedge^{\lambda_{a+1}}E}.\]
3199: 		Here, $\Delta$ is the diagonal embedding (or comultiplication), and $m: \bigwedge^r E \otimes \bigwedge^s E \to \bigwedge^{r+s}E$ is a component of the multiplication map on the exterior algebra $\bigwedge^{\bullet}E$. Combinatorially, we may use the theory of Young tableaux to describe the modules $L_{\lambda}E$. It is well known the standard 
3200: 		tableaux form a basis of $L_{\lambda}E$. Further, the relations $R(\lambda, E)$ may be visualized as follows. Let $\lambda \vdash 
3201: 		m$ be a partition with at most $n$ parts. To the map $\theta(\lambda, a, u, v, E)$ we associate a \textbf{Young scheme}. The Young 
3202: 		scheme is defined as being a diagram of shape $\lambda$ with empty boxes everywhere except the $a^{th}$ and 
3203: 		$a+1^{st}$ rows. In row $a$ there are $u$ empty boxes followed by $\lambda_a-u$ filled boxes. In row $a+1$ there are 
3204: 		$\lambda_{a+1}-v$ filled boxes followed by $v$ empty boxes. We restrict to $u+v<\lambda_{a+1}$ as in the definition of 
3205: 		$L_{\lambda}E$. Let $U_j = e_{t(j,1)} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{t(j, \lambda_j)}$, $V_1 = e_{x_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{x_u}$, 
3206: 		$V_2 = e_{y_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{y_{\lambda_a-u+\lambda_v-v}}$, and $V_3 = e_{z_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{z_v}$. 
3207: 		Then the image of a typical element 
3208: 		\[ U_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes U_{a-1} \otimes V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes V_3 \otimes U_{a+2} \otimes \cdots \otimes U_s \]
3209: 		is a sum of tableaux where we put $x_1, ..., x_u$ in the empty $u$ boxes in row $a$, and $z_1, ..., z_v$ in the empty $v$ boxes of row $a+1$, and we shuffle the elements $y_1, ..., y_{\lambda_a-u+\lambda_{a+1}-v}$ between the filled boxes in row $a$ and $a+1$. The coefficients of the tableaux in the summation are $\pm 1$ depending on the sign of the permutations coming from the exterior diagonals.\sidenote{From now on, we will let $L_{\lambda}F$ denote the Schur functor corresponding to the diagram $\lambda$, and we will let $S_{(\lambda-k)}F = L_{\lambda}F \otimes (\bigwedge^{\dim F}F^*)^{\otimes k}$, where $\lambda-k$ is obtained by subtracting the integer $k$ from every entry of the vector $\lambda$.}
3210: 		
3211: 		
3212: 		\section{Standard Monomials,The Straightening Law, and Determinantal Varieties}\label{Straightening Law 1}
3213: 		
3214: 		\subsection{Standard Monomials and Straightening Laws}\label{monomial orders}
3215: 		Let us now introduce the notion of a standard monomial theory. 
3216: 		
3217: 		\begin{defn}
3218: 			Let $R$ be a ring and let $A$ be a commutative $R$-algebra, and let $S:=\{s_1, ..., s_N\} \subset R$ have a partial order $\leq$. 
3219: 			\begin{enumerate}
3220: 				\item An ordered product $s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_k}$ of elements from $S$ is said to be a \textbf{standard monomial} if the elements appear in nondecreasing order, with respect to the partial order $\leq$. 
3221: 				\item We say $A$ has a \textbf{standard monomial theory for $S$} if the standard monomials for a basis of $A$ over $R$.
3222: 				\item If $s, s' \in S$ are incomparable in the partial order $\leq$, we have a unique expression called a \textbf{straightening law}:
3223: 				\[ s \cdot s' = \sum_i c_iM_i, \quad c_i \in R, M_i \text{ standard}. \]
3224: 				If a monomial $s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_k}$ is nonstandard we may replace it with a standard one as follows. If there is a product $s \cdot s'$ in $s_{i_1} \cdots s_{i_k}$ with $s > s'$ we replace if with $s' \cdot s$. If $s$ and $s'$ are incomparable, we replace $s \cdot s'$ with $s \cdot \left(\sum_i c_iM_i\right)$. 
3225: 				\item We say the $R$-algebra $A$ has a \textbf{straightening law} if the previous replacement algorithm always terminates after finitely many steps. 
3226: 			\end{enumerate}
3227: 		\end{defn}
3228: 		
3229: 		We define a \textbf{standard bi-tableau}\sidenote{An archetypal example of bi-tableaux and an algebra with straightening law and standard monomial theory is the algebra $\Sym(V \otimes W^*)$ for two vector spaces $V$ and $W$, or more generally, let $X = (x_{ij})$ be a matrix of indeterminates so that $X \in \Hom_K(E, F) = E^* \otimes F$, where $E$ and $F$ are two free $\ZZ$-modules. Define the ring $R = \ZZ[X] = \ZZ[x_{ij}]$, to be the polynomial ring in the indeterminates $(x_{ij})$, and let $\{e_1, ..., e_m\}$ and $\{f_1, ..., f_n\}$ be ordered bases of $E$ and $F$ respectively. There is a natural action of the group $G = \GL(E) \times \GL(F)$ on $R$ induced by the action on $X$ define by $(A, B) \cdot X = A^{-1}XB$. If $K$ is a field, the orbits in $\Hom_K(E,F)$ are classified by ranks, and the orbit closures of maps of rank $k$ say, are all maps of rank $\leq k$. The action of $G$ on $R$ is more complicated. If $E$ and $F$ are free $K$-modules for a field $K$, and $V_k$ is the orbit closure of rank $k$ maps, then the defining ideal of $V_k$ is $I_{k+1} = R(\bigwedge^{k+1} E^* \otimes \bigwedge^{k+1}F)$ generated by minors of size $k+1$, and the coordinate ring $R/I_{k+1}$ is normal and Cohen Macaulay. A classical characteristic free approach using the Schur functors allows one to define a basis of $\KK[E^* \otimes F]$ in terms of certain \emph{standard monomials} given by standard bi-tableaux.}, denoted $(s|t)$ as a pair of standard tableaux $s$ and $t$ of the same shape $\lambda$, where by convention we write $s$ in reverse order. To a bitableau we associate a product of minors of $X$, where the entries of row $a$ of $s$ give the columns and the entries of row $a$ of $t$ give the rows of the minor of $X$. Then each pair of rows in $s$ and $t$ defines a minor of size $\lambda_a$, and the bi-tableau is associated to the product of these minors. It is well known that the standard bi-tableaux with at most $\min\{\dim E, \dim F\}$ columns forms a $K$-free basis of $K[E^* \otimes F]$, and that the standard bi-tableaux with at most $k$ columns form a $K$-free basis of $R/I_{k+1}$. We call the associated minors to a standard bi-tableau a \emph{standard monomial} in $R$ or $R/I_{k+1}$. It can be shown that any nonstandard monomial can be written as a sum of standard monomials each of which are earlier in the partial order on monomials. In particular if $M$ is nonstandard then we can write $M = \sum_i n_iM_i + \sum_jn_jM_j$, where $M_i$ are standard and of the same shape as the tableau corresponding to $M$, and the $M_j$ are standard but of a smaller shape in the order on tableau. \\
3230: 		Let $\mathbf{Gr}(n,m+n)$ denote the Grassmannian variety of $n$-dimensional subspaces of an $(m+n)$-dimensional vector space $V$. Let $\{w_1, ..., w_n\}$ be a basis for an $n$-dimensional subspace $W \subset V$. Then the vector $w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_n$ determines a point $[W]$ in the projective space $\mathbb{P}(\bigwedge^nV)$, and the map $W \mapsto [W]$ is a one-to-one correspondence between $n$-dimensional subspaces of $V$ and points in $\mathbb{P}(\bigwedge^n V)$ (which are lines in $\bigwedge^nV$). For the standard basis $\{e_i\}_{i=1}^{m+n}$ of $V$, we have the standard basis $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_n}: i_1< \cdots < i_n\}$ of $\bigwedge^n V$. If to any $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n \in \bigwedge^n V$ we associate the matrix 
3231: 		\[X = \begin{pmatrix}
3232: 			v_1 \\
3233: 			\vdots \\
3234: 			v_n
3235: 		\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}
3236: 			v_{1,1} & v_{1,2} & \cdots & v_{1,m+n} \\
3237: 			v_{2,1} & v_{2,2} & \cdots & v_{2,m+n} \\
3238: 			\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
3239: 			v_{n,1} & v_{n,2} \& \cdots & v_{n,m+n}
3240: 		\end{pmatrix},\]
3241: 		we have that in the basis $\{e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_n}:i_1 < \cdots < i_n\}$ the coordinates of $v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n$ are given by the maximal minors of $X$. Let $[i_1, i_2, ..., i_n]$ denote the minor given by columns $i_1, i_2, ..., i_n$ of $X$. So,
3242: 		\[ v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n = \sum_{1 \leq i_1 \leq \cdots \leq i_n \leq m+n} [i_1, ..., i_n]e_{i_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge e_{i_n}.\]
3243: 		The open set $S_{n,m+1} = \{(v_1, ..., v_n) \in V^n: v_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge v_n \neq 0\} \subset \Hom(K^{m+n}, K^n)$ of maximal rank $n \times (m+n)$-matrices is called the \textbf{Stiefel manifold}. Now, $\mathbf{Gr}(n,m+n)$ can be identified with the orbits in $S_{n,m+n} \subset \Hom(K^{m+n}, K^n)$ under the action of $\GL(n,K)$ by left multiplication. Further, given a homomorphism $\pi: K^r \to K^{r+s}$ of two affine spaces, of the form
3244: 		\[ \pi(x_1, ..., x_r) = (x_1, ..., x_r, p_1, ..., p_s) \]
3245: 		where $p_i$ are polynomials in the $x_j$, the image of $\pi$ is a closed subvariety of $K^{r+s}$, and $\pi$ is an isomorphism of $K^r$ onto its image (it is the \emph{graph} of a polynomial map). The defining ideal is $I = (x_{r+i}-p_i)$, and the inverse map is
3246: 		\[ (x_1, ..., x_r, ..., x_{r+s}) \mapsto (x_1, ..., x_r).\]
3247: 		Now, consider the open set $U$ of $\mathbf{Gr}(n,m+n)$ where the Pl\"{u}cker coordinate given by the minor coming from the last $n$ columns is nonzero. $U$ can be identified with the space of $n \times m$ matrices. The association is given by associating any $X$ with the row span of the matrix
3248: 		\[ (X| \tilde{\id_n}) = \begin{pmatrix}
3249: 			x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1m} & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \\
3250: 			x_{21} & \cdots & x_{2m} & 0 & \cdots& 1 & 0 \\
3251: 			\vdots & \ddots & \vdots & \vdots &   & \vdots & \vdots \\
3252: 			x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{nm} & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0
3253: 		\end{pmatrix}.\]
3254: 		One may now identify Pl\"{u}cker coordinates with \textbf{bi-tableaux}. 
3255: 		\begin{ex}
3256: 			Let $n=3$, $m=5$, and write
3257: 			\[ X = \begin{pmatrix}
3258: 				x_{31} & x_{32} & x_{33} & x_{34} & x_{35} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
3259: 				x_{21} & x_{22} & x_{23} & x_{24} & x_{25} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
3260: 				x_{11} & x_{12} & x_{13} & x_{14} & x_{15} & 0 & 0 & 1 \\
3261: 			\end{pmatrix}.\]
3262: 			Now let the Pl\"{u}cker coordinate $[1,2,3][1,2,5][1,2,7][2,3,6][5,6,7][5,6,8]$ be represented by the tableau
3263: 			\[ \young(123,125,127,238,567,568). \quad (*) \]
3264: 			To this we may associate the bi-tableau
3265: 			\[ \begin{pmatrix}
3266: 				\young(123,123,13,12,1,2) & &  \young(123,125,12,23,5,5)
3267: 			\end{pmatrix} \quad \quad (**) \]
3268: 			Neither the tableau $(*)$, nor the double tableau $(**)$ are standard, and thus we may use the quadratic relations on Pl\"{u}cker coordinates to "straighten" the tableau $(*)$, which induces a straightening of the double tableau $(**)$ to a standard bi-tableau. These quadratic relations can be seen as the shuffling relations coming from the definition of the Schur functors from the previous sections. 
3269: 		\end{ex}
3270: 		
3271: 		\subsection{Standard Pl\"{u}cker Coordinates}\label{Plucker monomial orders}
3272: 		We consider the Pl\"{u}cker coordinate standard if and only if the associated tableau is, i.e. the tableau is strickly increasing along rows, and nondecreasing along columns. In this example, the coordinate is not standard. We have a \textbf{straightening law} on the coordinates which is given by the definition of the Schur-functors and the relations among tableaux induced by the multilinear map defining them, i.e. the \textbf{shuffling relations}. One may also view the straightening law on standard bi-tableaux as a consequence of the quadratic relations on Pl\"{u}cker coordinates in the Grassmannian. If we take the perspective of double tableaux, we let the left tableau be the "row tableau", with indices $j \in [1,n]$ and the right tableau as the "column tableau" with indices $i \in [1,m+n]$. Each pair of rows gives a minor of the matrix $X$. We think of the space of one line tableau of size $k$ as a vector space $M_k$, with basis $(j_k, ..., j_i|i_1, ..., i_k)$, so that if two indices on the right or left are equal, then the symbol is zero, and the symbols are alternating separately on the left and right. For any partition $\lambda:= m_1 \geq m_2 \geq \cdots \geq m_r$, the tableaux of shape $\lambda$ can be thought of as a tensor product $M_{m_1} \otimes M_{m_2} \otimes \cdots \otimes M_{m_r}$. Evaluating a formal tabeleau as a product of minors gives a nontrivial kernel, which is the space spanned by the shuffling relations, or equivalently the straightening law. The action of $\GL(E) \times \GL(F)$ on $K[X]$ induces an action by the two groups of diagonal matrices, and the content of a bi-tableau is a weight vector for the product of the two algebraic tori. In particular If $(A,B) = (a_i) \times (b_j) \in T(E) \times T(F)$ is an element of the product of the tori $T(E) \subset \GL(E)$ and $T(F) \subset \GL(F)$, then the weight is $(\prod_{i+1}^n a_i^{-k(i)}; \prod_{j=1}^{m+n} b_j^{h(j)})$. At this point we should comment that there is a well-known partial order on multi-tableaux.

3276: 		\chapter{Varieties of Circular Complexes}
3277: 		\section{Varieties of Complexes}
3278: 		Let us now move on to a classic example, that of the \emph{varieties of complexes}. These are examples of orbit closures of quivers which have been studied by many authors at this point (see for example \cite{}, \cite{}, \cite{}....). Let $S = k[X^{(k)}_{i(k),j(k)}]$, where $X^{(k)}$ is the $k^{th}$ matrix representing $d_k$ in the complex
3279: 		\[ \xymatrix{
3280: 			V_n \ar[r]^{d_n} & V_{n-1} \ar[r]^{d_{n-1}} & \cdots \ar[r]^{d_{2}} & V_1 \ar[r]^{d_1} & V_0 
3281: 		}  
3282: 		\]
3283: 		Let $I$ be the ideal generated by $\rank(X^{(k)}) \times \rank(X^{(k)})$ minors of each $X^{(k)}$, and by the equations given by $X^{(k+1)}X^{(k)} = 0$. Then $R=S/I$ is the coordinate ring of the parametrizing variety of complexes with the dimension vector $(\bd(1), ..., \bd(n))$ and rank sequence $r = (r(1), ..., r(n-1))$. 
3284: 		
3285: 		\begin{theorem}
3286: 			(cite DEP, DS, PW, and T) The coordinate ring of a sequence of $k$-vector spaces
3287: 			\[ \xymatrix{
3288: 				V_n \ar[r]^{d_n} & V_{n-1} \ar[r]^{d_{n-1}} & \cdots \ar[r]^{d_{2}} & V_1 \ar[r]^{d_1} & V_0 
3289: 			}  
3290: 			\]
3291: 			has a filtration by Schur functors
3292: 			\begin{align*}
3293: 				\Sym(V_1 \otimes V_2^* \oplus \cdots \oplus V_{n-1} \otimes V_{n}^*) & \\
3294: 				= \bigoplus_{(\lambda(1), ..., \lambda(n-1))} L_{\lambda(1)}V_1 \otimes L_{\lambda(1)}V_2^* &\otimes \cdots \otimes L_{\lambda(n-1)}V_{n-1} \otimes L_{\lambda(n-1)}V_n^*
3295: 			\end{align*}
3296: 			where each $\lambda(i)$ has at most $\min\{\dim V_i, \dim V_{i+1} \}$ columns. 
3297: 			In the case that such a sequence is a complex of vector spaces DeConcini and Strickland show that the filtration is
3298: 			\begin{align*}
3299: 				\Sym(V_1 \otimes V_2^* \oplus \cdots \oplus V(_{n-1} \otimes V_n^*)/I &  \\
3300: 				= \bigoplus_{(\lambda(1), ..., \lambda(n-1))} L_{(\lambda(1))}V_1 \otimes L_{(\lambda(2), -\lambda(1))}V_2 &\otimes \cdots \otimes L_{(\lambda(n-1), -\lambda(n-2))}V_{n-1} \otimes L_{(-\lambda(n-1))}V_n.
3301: 			\end{align*}
3302: 			Here each $\lambda(k)$ has at most $\rank(d_k)$ columns, where $d_k$ are the differentials in the complex represented by the matrices $X^{(k)}$. 
3303: 		\end{theorem}
3304: 		
3305: 		\begin{theorem}
3306: 			(cite DEP, DS, PW, and T) The algebra $R$ has a basis given by standard multitableaux. Further, the ring $R$ is normal and Cohen-Macaulay. 
3307: 		\end{theorem}
3308: 		
3309: 		
3310: 		
3311: 		\section{Products of Varieties of Complexes}
3312: 		We may of course take products of varieties of complexes. Such varieties arise naturally when there is a partition of a quiver into subquivers with relations of length two. Let us look at an example. 
3313: 		\begin{ex}
3314: 			Suppose $Q$ is the following quiver
3315: 			\[ \xymatrix{ \bullet_1 \ar@/^/@{.>}[r]  \ar[r] \ar@/_/@{~>}[r] & \bullet_2 \ar@/^/@{.>}[r]  \ar[r] \ar@/_/@{~>}[r] & \bullet_3 \ar@/^/@{.>}[r]  \ar[r] \ar@/_/@{~>}[r] & \bullet_4 } \]
3316: 			Let us denote the colors by the set $\{1, 2, 3\}$ (ordered from top to bottom). Let $\{a_1, a_2, a_3\}$ be the arrows of color "$1$", labeled from left to right. Similarly, label arrows of color "$2$" by $\{b_j\}_{j=1, 2, 3}$, and arrows of color "$3$" by $\{c_k\}_{k=1, 2, 3}$. Take the dimension vector $\bd = (2,4,5,3)$, and rank maps $r_1 = (2,2,3) = r_2, r_3 = (1,3,2) $. 
3317: 			
3318: 			The associated graded object for the coordinate ring is

3423: 			\medskip\noindent\textbf{Step 2.}
3424: For general partitions $\lambda$ and $\mu$, the Schur functor relations are generated by straightening relations that act on pairs of adjacent rows.  Since the straightening law for $S_\lambda F_1^*\otimes S_\mu F_1$ decomposes into operations on consecutive row pairs $(\lambda_i,\mu_j)$, each such pair reduces to the single-row case handled in Step~1.  Concretely, the ideal of relations for the general Schur filtration is the sum of the ideals obtained by applying Step~1 to each pair of adjacent rows in the combined Young diagram.

The global ideal is therefore generated by the local contributions from each vertex of the circular complex.  This completes the proof.

3433: \subsection{Hochster--Buchsbaum--Eisenbud multipliers and Grassmannians over rings (``Grass$(R)$'')}\label{subsec:hochster-grassR}
3434: 
3435: The informal ``missing link'' in the preceding sketch is the \emph{functorial} determinantal control of
3436: exactness and rank--strata \emph{over an arbitrary commutative base ring $R$}, and not only over a field.
3437: This is precisely the viewpoint developed in \S7 of Hochster's CBMS notes \cite{HochsterCBMS24}, building on
3438: the structure theorems of Buchsbaum--Eisenbud for finite free acyclic complexes \cite{BuchsbaumEisenbud1974}.
3439: We summarize the pieces we will actually use, emphasizing how they interface with the circular-complex/quiver
3440: picture.
3441: 
3442: \subsubsection{Complementary minors as Pl\"ucker coordinates}
3443: Let $K$ be a field, $V \cong K^t$, and let $A$ be an $r\times t$ matrix over $K$ with $\rank(A)=r$.
3444: Viewing the rows of $A$ as a basis of an $r$-plane $V^r\subset V$, the maximal minors of $A$ are the
3445: Grassmann--Pl\"ucker coordinates of $V^r$ under the Pl\"ucker embedding
3446: \[
3447: \mathbf{Gr}_r(V)\hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}\Big(\bigwedge\nolimits^r V\Big).
3448: \]
3449: If $B$ is a $t\times s$ matrix with $s=t-r$ and $AB=0$ and $\rank(B)=s$, then the columns of $B$ span an
3450: $s$-plane which identifies canonically with an orthogonal complement to $V^r$ in $V^\ast$.
3451: Hochster recalls the following classical ``complementary minors'' relation (a linear-algebra avatar of the
3452: isomorphism $\mathbf{Gr}_r(V)\cong \mathbf{Gr}_s(V^\ast)$): there is a unique scalar $c\in K^\times$ such that,
3453: for every $r$-subset $\mu\subset \{1,\dots,t\}$, the corresponding maximal minors satisfy
3454: \begin{equation}\label{eq:hochster-complement-minors}
3455: B_{\mu} \;=\; c\,\sgn(\mu)\,A_{\mu},
3456: \end{equation}
3457: where $\sgn(\mu)$ is an explicit sign depending on $\mu$ (Hochster chooses $\sgn(\mu)=(-1)^{\Sigma/2}$ with
3458: $\Sigma$ the sum of the elements of $\mu$).  See \cite[\S7]{HochsterCBMS24} for the statement and its
3459: interpretation in terms of Pl\"ucker coordinates.
3460: 
3461: \subsubsection{Vectors of multipliers for long exact complexes}
3462: Now let $R$ be a commutative ring and let
3463: \begin{equation}\label{eq:hochster-acyclic-complex}
3464: 0\to V_n \xrightarrow{A_n} V_{n-1}\xrightarrow{A_{n-1}}\cdots\xrightarrow{A_2}V_1\xrightarrow{A_1}V_0\to 0
3465: \end{equation}
3466: be a finite free acyclic complex of $R$-modules with specified bases.
3467: Write $b_i=\rank_R(V_i)$ and let $r_i$ denote the \emph{expected rank} of $A_i$ (so that, in the acyclic case,
3468: $b_i=r_i+r_{i+1}$ in the standard Buchsbaum--Eisenbud conventions).
3469: Hochster formulates a systematic refinement of \eqref{eq:hochster-complement-minors}: for each $i$ there is a
3470: \emph{vector of multipliers} $c^{(i)}=(c^{(i)}_\mu)$ indexed by suitable subsets $\mu$, such that (up to the fixed
3471: sign conventions) vectors of maximal minors of $A_i$ are obtained from vectors of maximal minors of $A_{i+1}$
3472: by multiplication with $c^{(i)}$.
3473: The existence and uniqueness of these multiplier vectors over a Noetherian ring are recorded in Hochster's
3474: Theorem~7.1 \cite[\S7]{HochsterCBMS24}, and can be viewed as the determinantal shadow of the exterior-algebra
3475: factorization in \cite{BuchsbaumEisenbud1974}.
3476: 
3477: \subsubsection{Universal rings for resolutions of length two}
3478: A crucial consequence is that for complexes of length~$2$ there exists a \emph{universal pair} $(R,\mathcal{K})$
3479: (classifying all acyclic complexes of a fixed Betti type $(b_0,b_1,b_2)$ under base-change), and the universal
3480: ground ring $R$ is an integrally closed finitely generated graded $\mathbb{Z}$-algebra; see Hochster's
3481: Theorem~7.2 \cite[\S7]{HochsterCBMS24}.
3482: Kustin--Weyman \cite{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing} revisit this universal ring $\widetilde{C}$ and the
3483: universal resolution
3484: \[
3485: U:\quad 0\to \widetilde{C}^{\,e}\xrightarrow{d_2}\widetilde{C}^{\,f}\xrightarrow{d_1}\widetilde{C}^{\,g},
3486: \]
3487: prove that $\widetilde{C}$ is factorial (Bruns \cite{Bruns1983DivisorsComplexes,Bruns1984GenericFreeResolutions}),
3488: identify generators (Huneke \cite{Huneke1981ArithmeticPerfection}), and compute the \emph{minimal free resolution}
3489: of $\widetilde{C}$ by Weyman's geometric method \cite{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing,Weyman2003CohomologySyzygies}.
3490: 
3491: \begin{remark}[Why this matters here]\label{rem:hochster-matters}
3492: The surface/dessin and ``necklace'' invariant story developed elsewhere in this manuscript rests on the idea that
3493: \emph{cycles control invariants}.  The multiplier formalism above is the determinantal expression of the same
3494: principle: the \emph{maximal minors} are Pl\"ucker coordinates (cycle-like wedge monomials), and the multipliers
3495: encode how one ``propagates'' these wedge-cycles through an exact complex.
3496: In the circular-complex/quiver regime, these multipliers become \emph{cycle weights} attached to adjacent rank
3497: constraints and thus interface cleanly with (i) the necklace/cycle trace generators of invariants
3498: (Procesi--Le~Bruyn--Lusztig), and (ii) the total-positivity/positive-Grassmannian technology
3499: (Postnikov; Arkani-Hamed et al.) already used later in this paper.
3500: \end{remark}
3501: 
3502: \subsection{Weyman--Kustin geometric technique for varieties of complexes}\label{subsec:weyman-geometric-technique}
3503: 
3504: We now record the \emph{geometric package} that turns the Hochster/Buchsbaum--Eisenbud determinantal relations
3505: into the geometric properties asserted for varieties of (circular) complexes: normality, Cohen--Macaulayness,
3506: rational singularities, and the Schur-functor filtrations.
3507: 
3508: \subsubsection{Incidence desingularization and cohomology}
3509: Fix a field $K$ of characteristic $0$ and finite-dimensional $K$-spaces $E,F,G$ with $\dim(E)=e$, $\dim(F)=f$,
3510: $\dim(G)=g$.
3511: Set
3512: \[
3513: X:=\Hom_K(E,F)\times \Hom_K(F,G),\qquad A:=K[X].
3514: \]
3515: Let $r_1=f-e$ and $r_0=g-f+e$ (as in \cite{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing}), and let $Y\subset X$ be the
3516: subvariety cut out by the determinantal ideal enforcing $\rank(d_2)\le e$, $\rank(d_1)\le r_1$, and $d_1d_2=0$.
3517: Kustin--Weyman consider the incidence variety
3518: \[
3519: Z:=\{(d_2,d_1,R)\in X\times \mathbf{Gr}(e{+}1,F)\;:\; \Im(d_2)\subseteq R\subseteq \Ker(d_1)\},
3520: \]
3521: which maps properly to $Y$ and is a desingularization in the generic rank range \cite[\S2]{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing}.
3522: Let $Q$ be the tautological quotient bundle on $\mathbf{Gr}(e{+}1,F)$ and $R$ the tautological subbundle.
3523: The key point of Weyman's method is that $Z$ is the total space of a vector bundle over the Grassmannian, and one
3524: reduces statements about $K[Y]$ and its syzygies to vanishing and identification statements for cohomology of
3525: Schur functors of the bundles $R,Q$.
3526: 
3527: Concretely, in the setup of \cite[\S2]{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing} one defines vector bundles
3528: \[
3529: \xi:= E\otimes Q^\ast \;\oplus\; R\otimes G^\ast,\qquad \eta:= E\otimes R^\ast\;\oplus\; Q\otimes G^\ast,
3530: \]
3531: and proves (by Borel--Weil--Bott) that
3532: \begin{equation}\label{eq:weyman-vanishing}
3533: H^i(\mathbf{Gr}(e{+}1,F),\Sym^j(\eta))=0\quad\text{for all }i>0,
3534: \end{equation}
3535: and
3536: \begin{equation}\label{eq:weyman-coordinate-ring}
3537: H^0(\mathbf{Gr}(e{+}1,F),\Sym^j(\eta))\cong (A/I)_j,
3538: \end{equation}
3539: where $I$ is the defining ideal of $Y$ \cite[Prop.~3]{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing}.
3540: The vanishing \eqref{eq:weyman-vanishing} implies that $Y$ has rational singularities, hence is normal and
3541: Cohen--Macaulay.
3542: Moreover, the minimal free resolution of $A/I$ as an $A$-module is computed from the cohomology of exterior powers
3543: $\bigwedge^q\xi$ \cite[\S1]{Weyman2003CohomologySyzygies}.
3544: 
3545: \subsubsection{Schur filtrations and standard monomials}
3546: The Schur-functor decompositions appearing in \eqref{eq:weyman-coordinate-ring} are a manifestation of the
3547: Cauchy identities and the Littlewood--Richardson rule applied to $\Sym(\eta)$.
3548: In many instances (including the determinantal and complex varieties relevant here) these coordinate rings are
3549: \emph{Hodge algebras} (algebras with straightening laws) in the sense of De Concini--Procesi and Bruns--Vetter; see
3550: \cite{PragaczWeyman1990GenericFreeResolutions,Bruns1983DivisorsComplexes}.
3551: Consequently, one obtains a basis by \emph{standard monomials}, which in the representation-theoretic language is
3552: exactly the ``standard multitableaux'' basis alluded to in the corollary following the circular-complex theorem.
3553: 
3554: \subsection{Geometric completion for circular complexes}\label{subsec:circular-complexes-completion}
3555: 
3556: We now explain how the preceding Hochster--Weyman package supplies a complete proof of the claims stated at the
3557: beginning of this section for $\mathcal{C}_n(\bd,r)$, without changing any of the earlier exposition.
3558: 
3559: \begin{proposition}[Incidence model for circular complexes]\label{prop:incidence-circular}
3560: Fix $\bd=(\bd(1),\dots,\bd(n))$ and a rank sequence $r=(r(1),\dots,r(n))$ satisfying the circular rank inequalities
3561: $r(i)+r(i{+}1)\le \bd(i{+}1)$ (indices mod $n$).
3562: Let $X:=\prod_{i\in\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}}\Hom_K(V(i),V(i{+}1))$ and let $Y\subset X$ be the closed subvariety cut out by
3563: the relations $A_{i+1}A_i=0$ and the rank conditions $\rank(A_i)\le r(i)$.
3564: Then there is a proper incidence variety
3565: \[
3566: Z:=\{(A_\bullet,R_\bullet)\;:\;\Im(A_i)\subseteq R_i \subseteq \Ker(A_{i+1}),\ \dim R_i = r(i)+\delta_i\}
3567: \subset X\times \prod_i \mathbf{Gr}(r(i){+}\delta_i,V(i{+}1)),
3568: \]
3569: for suitable choices of $\delta_i\in\{0,1\}$ in the generic rank range, such that the projection $Z\to Y$ is a
3570: desingularization on the open locus where the ranks are exactly $r(i)$.
3571: \end{proposition}
3572: 
3573: \begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
3574: This is the obvious cyclic analogue of the incidence construction in \cite[\S2]{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing}.
3575: For each adjacent pair $V(i)\xrightarrow{A_i}V(i{+}1)\xrightarrow{A_{i+1}}V(i{+}2)$ one inserts an intermediate
3576: subspace $R_i\subset V(i{+}1)$ satisfying $\Im(A_i)\subseteq R_i\subseteq \Ker(A_{i+1})$.
3577: Taking the product over $i$ yields $Z$ as a closed subvariety of a product of Grassmannians (``Grass$(R)$'' in
3578: Hochster's sense), and the map to $Y$ is proper because the Grassmannians are proper.
3579: On the generic rank stratum, $R_i$ is forced to equal $\Ker(A_{i+1})$ (or $\Im(A_i)$, depending on the chosen
3580: $\delta_i$), giving birationality.
3581: \end{proof}
3582: 
3583: \begin{theorem}[Normality, Cohen--Macaulayness, rational singularities, and Schur filtration]\label{thm:circular-geometric-package}
3584: Over a field $K$ of characteristic $0$, each rank-maximal irreducible component $\mathcal{C}_n(\bd,r)$ of the
3585: variety of circular complexes is normal, Cohen--Macaulay, and has rational singularities.
3586: Moreover, its coordinate ring admits a $G_{\bd}=\prod_i \GL(V(i))$-equivariant filtration whose associated graded
3587: decomposes as
3588: \[
3589: \KK[\mathcal{C}_n(\bd, r)] \;\cong\; \bigoplus_{(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)}
3590: \bigotimes_{i\in\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}} S_{\lambda(i),-\lambda(i+1)}V(i),
3591: \]
3592: and in particular has a basis by standard multitableaux.
3593: \end{theorem}
3594: 
3595: \begin{proof}[Idea of proof]
3596: Apply Weyman's geometric method componentwise on the product $\prod_i \mathbf{Gr}(\cdots)$ appearing in
3597: Proposition~\ref{prop:incidence-circular}.
3598: Each incidence condition $\Im(A_i)\subseteq R_i\subseteq \Ker(A_{i+1})$ identifies the corresponding piece of $Z$
3599: as the total space of a vector bundle over a Grassmannian, with the same $\xi/\eta$-bundle formalism as in
3600: \cite{KustinWeyman2005UniversalRing,Weyman2003CohomologySyzygies}.
3601: The required cohomology vanishing for symmetric powers of the analogue of $\eta$ follows from Borel--Weil--Bott.
3602: Consequently the pushforward of $\mathcal{O}_Z$ is $\mathcal{O}_Y$ with higher direct images $0$, yielding rational
3603: singularities (hence normality and Cohen--Macaulayness).
3604: The Schur-functor decomposition and the standard multitableaux basis are obtained from the Cauchy identities and
3605: standard monomial theory for the resulting Hodge algebra; see
3606: \cite{PragaczWeyman1990GenericFreeResolutions,Bruns1983DivisorsComplexes}.
3607: \end{proof}

3615: 
3616: \subsection{Face cycles as circular complexes and global gluing by fibre products}\label{subsec:face_cycles_as_circular_complexes}
3617: 
3618: The Grass$(R)$ and incidence constructions above explain the geometry of a \emph{single} circular-complex locus
3619: $\mathcal{C}_n(\bd,r)$.
3620: In the surface/dessin setting, however, one meets many such loci simultaneously, one for each face of the dessin.
3621: It is therefore important to record explicitly \emph{where} circular complexes live in the $(\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\sigma_\infty)$
3622: formalism and how they assemble into the global representation varieties of surface algebras and surface orders.
3623: 
3624: \begin{remark}[Circular complexes live on $\sigma_\infty$--faces (anti-cycles), not on $\sigma_0/\sigma_1$ vertices]\label{rem:sigma_infty_face_circular}
3625: Recall (cf.\ the discussion around the ``allowed/forbidden'' successor permutations) that:
3626: \begin{itemize}
3627: \item $\sigma_0$ and $\sigma_1$ encode the \emph{vertex cycles} (allowed continuations, not in the ideal $I$), and
3628: \item $\sigma_\infty$ encodes the \emph{face cycles}, which in the gentle surface-algebra regime are precisely the \emph{anti-cycles}
3629: (cycles of zero-relations): consecutive arrows along a $\sigma_\infty$--cycle compose to $0$ in $\Lambda=kQ/I$.
3630: \end{itemize}
3631: Fix a face $f$ with $\sigma_\infty$--cycle of length $\ell(f)$, and write the corresponding oriented boundary arrows as
3632: \[
3633: a_1:a_1^{-}\to a_1^{+},\ a_2:a_2^{-}\to a_2^{+},\ \dots,\ a_{\ell(f)}:a_{\ell(f)}^{-}\to a_{\ell(f)}^{+},
3634: \qquad a_{i+1}a_i\in I,
3635: \]
3636: (indices mod $\ell(f)$).
3637: For any representation $\rho$ of $\Lambda$ with vertex spaces $(V_v)_{v\in Q_0}$, the restricted data
3638: \[
3639: A_i:=\rho(a_i)\in \Hom(V_{a_i^{-}},V_{a_i^{+}})
3640: \]
3641: satisfy $A_{i+1}A_i=0$ by the defining relations.
3642: Thus \emph{each face determines a genuine circular complex}, and the corresponding face-locus is a variety of circular complexes in the sense of
3643: Proposition~\ref{prop:incidence-circular} and Theorem~\ref{thm:circular-geometric-package}.
3644: In contrast, $\sigma_0$-- and $\sigma_1$--cycles are the \emph{allowed} directed cycles whose traces/necklaces generate the $\GL$/$\SL$ invariant rings (Procesi--Le~Bruyn--Lusztig), and they control \emph{observables} rather than \emph{relations}.
3645: \end{remark}
3646: 
3647: \subsubsection{From local face-loci to global surface representation varieties}
3648: Let $\Gamma$ be a (clean) dessin on a compact surface $\Sigma$, with face set $F(\Gamma)$ and associated gentle surface algebra/order $\Lambda=\Lambda(\Gamma)$.
3649: For each face $f\in F(\Gamma)$, let $Q_f$ be the cyclic bound subquiver determined by the $\sigma_\infty$--cycle of $f$ (so $Q_f$ is a cyclic quiver of type $\widetilde{\mathbb{A}}_{\ell(f)}$ with radical-square-zero relations).
3650: Write $\Comp_f(\bd_f,r_f)$ for the rank-bounded circular-complex locus on $Q_f$ with the induced boundary dimension/rank data.
3651: 
3652: There are two equivalent bookkeeping viewpoints:
3653: 
3654: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
3655: \item (\emph{Global-first.})  Fix the vertex vector spaces $(V_v)_{v\in Q_0}$ once and for all.
3656: Since every forbidden length-$2$ path lies on a unique $\sigma_\infty$--face cycle, the defining equations of $\Rep(\Lambda,\bd)$ are the union of the face-wise equations $A_{i+1}A_i=0$ and the corresponding face-wise rank minors.
3657: Thus $\Rep(\Lambda,\bd)$ is cut out by a \emph{face-local} determinantal/quadratic ideal inside the ambient affine space
3658: $\prod_{a\in Q_1}\Hom(V_{t(a)},V_{h(a)})$.
3659: 
3660: \item (\emph{Local-first (gluing).})  If one duplicates the boundary vertex spaces separately for each face $f$ (i.e.\ works with a disjoint union of face-boundary complexes),
3661: then the naive product $\prod_{f\in F(\Gamma)}\Comp_f(\bd_f,r_f)$ has ``too many'' copies of each vertex space.
3662: The genuine global representation variety is obtained by identifying the duplicated copies along shared incidences (half-edges), i.e.\ by imposing diagonal equalities on the duplicated boundary data.
3663: Scheme-theoretically this is an iterated \emph{fibre product} (pullback) of affine schemes, matching the ring-theoretic ``tensor / fibre-product dictionary'' used earlier for orders; compare Definition~\ref{def:order_cosheaf}.
3664: \end{enumerate}
3665: 
3666: In either viewpoint, the essential point for our later positivity/self-adjointness arguments is the same:
3667: 
3668: \begin{quote}
3669: \emph{surface-algebra/order representation varieties are assembled from face-cycle circular-complex loci, and each such face-locus admits an incidence realization over a product of Grassmannians (Grass$(R)$).}
3670: \end{quote}
3671: 
3672: \subsubsection{Corrected roadmap: Grass$(R)$ incidence $\Rightarrow$ positivity $\Rightarrow$ self-adjointness}
3673: For quick reference, the logical dependency chain used throughout the manuscript can be summarized as the following corrected ``face-cycle'' roadmap:
3674: \begin{equation}\label{eq:roadmap_face_cycles_to_selfadjoint}
3675: \begin{aligned}
3676: &\text{\S7 Hochster (Grass$(R)$): incidence for } (B\circ A=0)\ \text{and determinantal ranks}
3677: \\
3678: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{$\sigma_\infty$--face anti-cycles } \rightsquigarrow\ \text{circular-complex loci } \Comp_f(\bd_f,r_f)
3679: \ \text{(iterated incidence over }\prod \mathbf{Gr}(\cdot)\text{)}
3680: \\
3681: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{surface algebras/orders: }\Rep(\Lambda(\Gamma),\bd)\ \text{assembled by gluing (fibre products) of the face loci}
3682: \\
3683: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{Magyar/Lusztig: cyclic-quiver loci } \hookrightarrow\ \text{affine Schubert/affine Grassmannian models}
3684: \\
3685: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{generalized minors / Pl\"ucker coordinates on Grassmannians}
3686: \\
3687: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{positive Grassmannian charts (Postnikov; Arkani--Hamed et al.) and total nonnegativity/positivity of minors}
3688: \\
3689: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{totally nonnegative/positive transfer matrices}\ +\ \text{cycle-reversal/detailed balance}
3690: \\
3691: &\Longrightarrow\ \text{self-adjoint (symmetrized) modular/Hamiltonian generator (cf.\ Proposition~\ref{prop:tp_detailed_balance_modular}).}
3692: \end{aligned}
3693: \end{equation}
3694: 
3695: We stress that the ``vertex-cycle'' $(\sigma_0,\sigma_1)$ picture and the ``face-cycle'' $(\sigma_\infty)$ picture play \emph{complementary} roles:
3696: \begin{itemize}
3697: \item face cycles ($\sigma_\infty$) give the \emph{relations} $A_{i+1}A_i=0$, hence the determinantal/incidence geometry and the Hochster--Weyman package;
3698: \item vertex cycles ($\sigma_0,\sigma_1$) give the \emph{cycle/necklace observables} generating $\GL/\SL$ invariants, hence the natural positive coordinate functions whose positivity we propagate through the Grassmannian atlas.
3699: \end{itemize}
3700: 
3701: 
3702: \subsection{Total positivity via the positive Grassmannian}\label{subsec:positivity-positive-grassmannian}
3703: 
3704: Finally, we spell out why the Grassmannian/incidence realization is the appropriate setting for
3705: \emph{total positivity}, and why this is compatible with the cycle/necklace invariant picture.
3706: 
3707: \begin{itemize}
3708: \item (\emph{Pl\"ucker positivity.})  On the totally positive part $\mathbf{Gr}_k(n)_{>0}$, all Pl\"ucker coordinates
3709: (minors) are strictly positive.  In such a chart, the Hochster multipliers in
3710: \eqref{eq:hochster-complement-minors} become \emph{positive} ratios of complementary minors, hence are positive
3711: functions.
3712: 
3713: \item (\emph{Subtraction-free parametrizations.})  Postnikov's network parametrizations and the cluster/positroid
3714: structure on $\mathbf{Gr}_k(n)$ provide subtraction-free coordinate charts on $\mathbf{Gr}_k(n)_{>0}$, ensuring that
3715: all Pl\"ucker coordinates (and therefore all determinantal semi-invariants built from them) are positive Laurent
3716: polynomials in positive variables \cite{Postnikov2006TotalPositivityNetworks,ArkaniHamedBourjailyCachazoGoncharovPostnikovTrnka2012PositiveGrassmannian}.
3717: 
3718: \item (\emph{From determinantal generators to cycle/necklace generators.})  In the quiver invariant setting,
3719: Procesi--Le~Bruyn--Lusztig show that $\GL$- and $\SL$-invariants are generated by traces along oriented cycles
3720: (``necklaces'').  Under the determinantal/Grassmannian incarnation of complexes, these traces are obtained from
3721: matrix coefficient functions built from minors and multipliers; hence positivity of minors implies positivity of
3722: cycle invariants on the corresponding positive loci.
3723: \end{itemize}
3724: 
3725: This is the precise sense in which the Hochster--Weyman--Grassmann package upgrades ``wiring diagram positivity''
3726: to a geometric positivity principle compatible with both the representation-theoretic filtration and the
3727: surface/dessin cycle calculus used elsewhere in this paper.
3728: 
3729: 
3730: \begin{corollary}
3731: 			The acoordinate ring of a variety of circular complexes has a basis given by standard multitableaux.  
3732: 			Further, the coordinate ring is normal and Cohen-Macaulay. 
3733: 		\end{corollary}
3734:

3736: 		\section{Examples Calculations}
3737: 		Let us look at a few examples of the computations mentioned in the previous section.
3738: 		\begin{ex}
3739: 			Let us consider the sequence 
3740: 			\[ \xymatrix{ F_2 \ar[r]^A & F_1 \ar[r]^B & F_0 } \]
3741: 			where the sequence of dimensions is $(3,5,3)$, $\rank(A) \leq 2$, and $\rank(B) \leq 3$. Then
3742: 			\[ R = \Sym(F_2 \otimes F_1^* \otimes F_1 \otimes F_0^*)/I \]
3743: 			where $I$ is generated by $\bigwedge^3F_2 \otimes \bigwedge^3 F_1^*$, and $F_2 \otimes F_0^*$. Suppose we take partitions $\lambda = (2)$ and $\mu = (1)$. Then we have the corresponding sequence of maps
3744: 			\[ \xymatrix{ \bigwedge^4F_1 \ar[d] \\
3745: 				\bigwedge^2 F_2 \otimes \bigwedge^2 F_1^* \otimes F_1 \otimes F_0^* \ar[d] \\
3746: 				\bigwedge^2F_2 \otimes S_{(1,0,0,-1,-1)}F_1 \otimes F_3^* }\]
3747: 			where $S_{(1,0,0,-1,-1)}F_1 \cong L_{(3,1)}F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^5F_1^*$, and $\bigwedge^2F_1 \otimes F_1^* \cong (\bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^5F_1^*) \otimes F_1 \cong \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes F_1$ (in an $\SL(F_1)$-equivariant way). The map $\Delta: \bigwedge^4F_1 \to \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes F_1$ is given by
3748: 			\[ f_{j_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge f_{j_4} \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma) f_{\sigma(j_1)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_2)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_3)} \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \]
3749: 			The isomorphism $f_{\sigma(j_1)} \wedge f_{\sigma( j_2)} \wedge f_{\sigma( j_3)} \mapsto f_{j_1'(\sigma)}^* \wedge f_{j_2'(\sigma)}^*$ of $\bigwedge^3 F_1 \cong \bigwedge^2F_1^*$, where $\{j_1'(\sigma), j_2'(\sigma)\}$ is the complement of $\{\sigma(j_1),\sigma( j_2),\sigma( j_3)\} \subset [1,5]$, then induces the map 
3750: 			\[ \bigwedge^4 F_1 \to \bigwedge^2F_1^* \otimes F_1 \]
3751: 			giving
3752: 			\[ f_{j_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge f_{j_4} \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}} \sgn(\sigma) f_{j_1'(\sigma)}^* \wedge f_{j_2'(\sigma)}^* \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \]
3753: 			where we sum over all $\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}$ or equivalently over all the complements $\{j_1'(\sigma), j_2'(\sigma)\} = [1,5]-\{\sigma(j_1), \sigma(j_2), \sigma(j_3)\}$, one pair for each $\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}$. Fixing $a, b, c$, this then corresponds to an element
3754: 			\[ (e_a \wedge e_b) \otimes \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}} \sgn(\sigma) f_{j_1'(\sigma)}^* \wedge f_{j_2'(\sigma)}^* \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \otimes g_c^* \]
3755: 			which corresponds to matrix elements
3756: 			\begin{align*}
3757: 				\sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma)[(A_{j_1'(\sigma),b}A_{j_2'(\sigma),a}-A_{j_1'(\sigma),a}A_{j_2'(\sigma),b}) \cdot B_{b, \sigma(j_4)}] \\
3758: 				= \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma)[(BA)_{j_1'(\sigma),\sigma(j_4)}A_{j_2'(\sigma),a} - (BA)_{j_2'(\sigma),\sigma(j_4)}A_{j_1'(\sigma),a}].
3759: 			\end{align*}
3760: 			which is in the ideal $I$ generated by $F_2 \otimes F_0^*$ (and $\bigwedge^3F_2 \otimes \bigwedge^3F_1^*$). 
3761: 		\end{ex}
3762: 		
3763: 		\begin{ex}
3764: 			Let us now choose $\lambda = (2)$ and $\mu = (2)$. We have the following map,
3765: 			\[ \xymatrix{ \bigwedge^2 F_2 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1^* \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_0^* \ar[d] \\
3766: 				\bigwedge^2F_2 \otimes S_{(1,1,0,-1,-1)}F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_0^*
3767: 			}.\]
3768: 			We compute the kernel via the following maps
3769: 			\begin{enumerate}
3770: 				\item $\bigwedge^4F_1 \otimes F_1 \to \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1$,
3771: 				\item $F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^4F_1 \to \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1$,
3772: 				\item $\bigwedge^5F_1 \to \bigwedge^3 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1$. 
3773: 			\end{enumerate}
3774: 			The first map is given by
3775: 			\[ f_{j_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge f_{j_4} \otimes f_k \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma)f_{\sigma(j_1)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_2)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_3)} \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \wedge f_k, \]
3776: 			which corresponds to the element
3777: 			\[\sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma)f_{j_1'(\sigma)}^* \wedge f_{j_2'(\sigma)}^* \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \wedge f_k. \]
3778: 			Fixing $a, b, c, d$ we get a corresponding element 
3779: 			\[ (e_a \wedge e_b) \otimes \left(\sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}}\sgn(\sigma)f_{j_1'(\sigma)}^* \wedge f_{j_2'(\sigma)}^* \otimes f_{\sigma(j_4)} \wedge f_k\right) \otimes (g_c^* \wedge g_d^*).\]
3780: 			where we associate the complement $\{j_1'(\sigma, k), j_2'(\sigma, k)\}$ of $\{\sigma(j_1), \sigma(j_2), \sigma(j_3)\}$ in $[1,5]$ to each $\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}$, and sum over all such pairs (or equivalently over all $\sigma$). This gives us the corresponding element
3781: 			\[ \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(3,1)}} \sgn(\sigma)(A_{j_1'(\sigma),a}A_{j_2'(\sigma),b}-A_{j_2'(\sigma),a}A_{j_1'(\sigma),b})\cdot (B_{c,\sigma(j_4)}B_{d,k}-B_{c,k}B_{d,\sigma(j_4)})\]
3782: 			which is an element of $( \bigwedge^2 B) \cdot (\bigwedge^2 A) = \bigwedge^2(BA) \in \bigwedge^2(F_2 \otimes F_0^*)$, and thus in the ideal $I$. Similarly, the map $F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^4F_1 \to \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1$ defined by
3783: 			\[ f_k \otimes f_{j_1} \wedge \cdots \wedge f_{j_4} \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_4^{(2,2)}} \sgn(\sigma) f_k \wedge f_{\sigma(j_1)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_2)} \otimes f_{\sigma(j_3)} \wedge f_{\sigma(j_4)} \]
3784: 			will give an element in $\bigwedge^2(F_2 \otimes F_0^*)$, as will the map $\bigwedge^5F_1 \to \bigwedge^3F_1 \otimes \bigwedge^2F_1$ given by
3785: 			\[ f_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge f_5 \mapsto \sum_{\sigma \in S_5^{(3,2)}} \sgn(\sigma) f_{\sigma(1)} \wedge f_{\sigma(2)} \wedge f_{\sigma(3)} \otimes f_{\sigma(4)} \wedge f_{\sigma(5)}.\]
3786: 		\end{ex}
3787: 		
3788: 		\begin{remark}[Coordinate rings via Grassmannians]
3789: The coordinate ring of a variety of complexes can be identified with a closed subring of a product of coordinate rings of Grassmannians.  We develop this identification systematically in the next subsection, following Hochster's approach.
3790: \end{remark}
3791: 
3792: %%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
3793: \subsection{Grassmannian models over a commutative base ring: Hochster's $\mathrm{Grass}(R)$ viewpoint for varieties of complexes}
3794: \label{sec:hochster_grassR_varieties_of_complexes}
3795: 
3796: The ``variety of complexes'' presentation above writes down equations directly in a polynomial ring $S=k[X^{(k)}_{i(k),j(k)}]$.
3797: For many purposes (base change, degeneration, positivity) it is better to keep track of \emph{why} these are the right equations: they are \emph{rank and incidence conditions} on submodules that are naturally parametrized by Grassmannians.
3798: This is the perspective taken systematically in Hochster's geometric treatment of determinantal loci and related exactness problems, and it is the reason the notation $\mathrm{Grass}(R)$ (Grassmannians over a commutative base ring $R$) is so effective \cite{Hochster1975TopicsHomological,HochsterEagon1971GenericPerfection}.
3799: 
3800: \paragraph{Grassmannians over a commutative ring.}
3801: Fix a commutative ring $R$ and integers $0<r<n$.
3802: Let $\mathbf{Gr}_R(r,n)$ denote the Grassmannian over $R$ representing the functor
3803: \[
3804: S\ \longmapsto\ \Bigl\{\text{rank-$r$ locally free direct summands } \mathcal{S}\subset S^n\Bigr\}
3805: \]
3806: on commutative $R$-algebras $S$.
3807: Equivalently, $\mathbf{Gr}_R(r,n)$ parametrizes rank-$r$ quotients of $S^n$.
3808: It carries the universal exact sequence of vector bundles
3809: \begin{equation}
3810: \label{eq:universal_grass_sequence}
3811: 0\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{S}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{Gr}}^{\oplus n}\ \longrightarrow\ \mathcal{Q}\ \longrightarrow\ 0,
3812: \end{equation}
3813: whose formation commutes with base change in $R$.
3814: Pl\"ucker coordinates are global sections of $\bigwedge^r\mathcal{S}^\vee$ and furnish the standard closed immersion $\mathbf{Gr}_R(r,n)\hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{\binom{n}{r}-1}_R$.
3815: 
3816: \paragraph{Pl\"ucker/straightening relations as \emph{defining relations}.}
3817: Over any base ring, the homogeneous coordinate ring of $\mathbf{Gr}_R(r,n)$ is generated by Pl\"ucker variables $p_I$ indexed by $r$-subsets $I\subset\{1,\dots,n\}$, with defining ideal generated by the quadratic Pl\"ucker relations.
3818: Standard monomial theory (in the form developed for Grassmannians and their Schubert subvarieties) provides:
3819: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
3820: \item a monomial basis of the coordinate ring (standard monomials / standard tableaux),
3821: \item explicit ``straightening'' relations expressing nonstandard monomials as $R$-linear combinations of standard ones, and
3822: \item good singularity properties (normality, Cohen--Macaulayness) for many determinantal/rank loci, proved geometrically via Grassmannians.
3823: \end{enumerate}
3824: Hochster--Eagon's principal radical system method is a foundational result in this direction: it shows that classical determinantal loci have Cohen--Macaulay and normal coordinate rings \cite{HochsterEagon1971GenericPerfection}.
3825: 
3826: \begin{theorem}[Hochster--Eagon: generic determinantal loci are Cohen--Macaulay and normal]
3827: \label{thm:hochster_eagon_determinantal}
3828: Let $R$ be a Noetherian ring and let $X$ be a generic $m\times n$ matrix of indeterminates over $R$.
3829: Let $I_t(X)$ be the ideal generated by the $t\times t$ minors.
3830: Then the determinantal ring $R[X]/I_t(X)$ is Cohen--Macaulay, and in the domain case it is normal.
3831: \end{theorem}
3832: 
3833: \begin{proof}[Reference]
3834: See \cite{HochsterEagon1971GenericPerfection} and the expository treatment in \cite{Hochster1975TopicsHomological}.
3835: \end{proof}
3836: 
3837: \paragraph{Varieties of complexes as incidence loci in products of Grassmannians.}
3838: Now fix a complex of finite free $R$-modules (or vector spaces over a field)
3839: \[
3840: F_n \xrightarrow{d_n} F_{n-1}\xrightarrow{d_{n-1}}\cdots\xrightarrow{d_2}F_1\xrightarrow{d_1}F_0,
3841: \qquad d_{i-1}\circ d_i = 0,
3842: \]
3843: and fix a rank sequence $\mathbf{r}=(r_1,\dots,r_n)$ with $0\le r_i\le \min\{\mathrm{rk}\,F_i,\mathrm{rk}\,F_{i-1}\}$.
3844: Set $f_i:=\mathrm{rk}\,F_i$.
3845: For each $i$ we have:
3846: \[
3847: \mathrm{im}(d_i)\subseteq F_{i-1}\ \text{ has rank } r_i,\qquad
3848: \ker(d_i)\subseteq F_i\ \text{ has rank } f_i-r_i.
3849: \]
3850: The condition $d_{i-1}\circ d_i=0$ is equivalent to the \emph{incidence} condition
3851: \begin{equation}
3852: \label{eq:incidence_image_in_kernel}
3853: \mathrm{im}(d_i)\ \subseteq\ \ker(d_{i-1})\ \subseteq\ F_{i-1}\qquad (2\le i\le n).
3854: \end{equation}
3855: 
3856: Introduce the incidence scheme
3857: \begin{equation}
3858: \label{eq:incidence_scheme_complexes}
3859: \mathcal{I}(\mathbf{r})\ :=\
3860: \Bigl\{(I_1,K_1,\dots,I_{n},K_{n})\ :\
3861: I_i\in \mathbf{Gr}_R(r_i,F_{i-1}),\ K_i\in \mathbf{Gr}_R(f_i-r_i,F_i),\ I_i\subseteq K_{i-1}\Bigr\},
3862: \end{equation}
3863: where $K_0:=F_0$ and the inclusions are interpreted via base change of the universal sequences \eqref{eq:universal_grass_sequence}.
3864: Then the space of complexes with rank sequence $\mathbf{r}$ is (the image of) a natural morphism from $\mathcal{I}(\mathbf{r})$ to the affine space of differentials $\prod_i \Hom_R(F_i,F_{i-1})$:
3865: one recovers $d_i$ as the composite
3866: \[
3867: F_i \twoheadrightarrow F_i/K_i \xrightarrow{\ \tilde d_i\ } I_i \hookrightarrow F_{i-1},
3868: \]
3869: where $\tilde d_i$ is an isomorphism once ranks are fixed appropriately (on a Stiefel open chart).
3870: In particular, the \emph{equations} defining the variety of complexes are:
3871: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
3872: \item determinantal rank conditions (vanishing of $(r_i+1)\times (r_i+1)$ minors of each $d_i$), and
3873: \item incidence equations enforcing \eqref{eq:incidence_image_in_kernel}, which are bilinear equations equivalent to $d_{i-1}d_i=0$.
3874: \end{enumerate}
3875: This is precisely the ``Grassmannian technique'' viewpoint: relations among minors are inherited from Pl\"ucker relations on the Grassmannians and their Schubert/incidence subvarieties, and base change is automatic.
3876: 
3877: \begin{remark}[Exactness and determinantal grade conditions]
3878: Over a Noetherian ring, exactness of a complex of free modules is controlled by determinantal/Fitting ideals (Buchsbaum--Eisenbud exactness criterion).
3879: Hochster's exposition emphasizes how these determinantal conditions can be interpreted geometrically on Grassmannians and how this geometric viewpoint interacts well with generic perfection and Cohen--Macaulayness \cite{Hochster1975TopicsHomological}.
3880: In our context, this matters because ``exactness'' constraints on persistence complexes and ``rank'' constraints on circular complexes are both determinantal conditions of exactly this type.
3881: \end{remark}
3882: 
3883: \subsubsection{Why positivity follows: positive Grassmannians as a canonical sign atlas}
3884: \label{sec:hochster_positive_grassmannian_positivity}
3885: 
3886: The positive/totally nonnegative Grassmannian $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(r,n)$ (Section~\ref{sec:positive_grassmannian_total_positivity}) is defined by the inequalities $p_I\ge 0$ on Pl\"ucker coordinates.
3887: There are two complementary reasons this is the correct positivity notion for our determinantal program.
3888: 
3889: \paragraph{(1) Subtraction-free coordinates and nonnegativity of minors.}
3890: Postnikov's boundary measurement parametrizes cells of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(r,n)$ by planar networks with \emph{positive} edge weights, and expresses each Pl\"ucker coordinate as a subtraction-free sum over nonintersecting path families (Theorem~\ref{thm:postnikov_boundary_measurement}).
3891: Therefore, whenever a determinantal semi-invariant or rank condition can be represented as a Pl\"ucker coordinate (or a minor of a boundary-measurement matrix), it is \emph{automatically nonnegative} on the positive locus.
3892: This is the conceptual reason the Lindstr\"om--Gessel--Viennot lemma and wiring diagrams produce total nonnegativity: they are the matrix shadows of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}$.
3893: 
3894: \paragraph{(2) Straightening with nonnegative structure constants.}
3895: Standard monomial theory gives straightening relations of the form
3896: \[
3897: p_{I}p_{J}=\sum_{(I',J')} c_{I,J}^{I',J'}\,p_{I'}p_{J'}
3898: \]
3899: with coefficients $c_{I,J}^{I',J'}\in \mathbb{Z}$ determined by the Pl\"ucker relations.
3900: On the totally nonnegative locus, every $p_I\ge 0$, hence every straightening step preserves nonnegativity \emph{provided the chosen atlas avoids sign cancellations}.
3901: Postnikov's network atlas does exactly this: in each cell, Pl\"ucker coordinates are subtraction-free in the network edge parameters, so the coefficients effectively contribute with the correct sign.
3902: In the toric degeneration limits used earlier (Section~\ref{sec:toric_semi_invariants_surface_algebras}), each Pl\"ucker coordinate degenerates to its distinguished leading monomial, and the straightening relations become binomial relations in a semigroup algebra---again with canonical positive coefficients.
3903: 
3904: \begin{corollary}[Determinantal loci inherit positivity from $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}$]
3905: \label{cor:determinantal_loci_inherit_positivity}
3906: Any closed subscheme cut out by Pl\"ucker/determinantal equations inside a product of Grassmannians inherits a canonical ``positive part'' by intersecting with the corresponding product of totally nonnegative Grassmannians.
3907: On this positive part:
3908: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
3909: \item all minors defining rank conditions are nonnegative,
3910: \item all LGV/network realizations evaluate determinantal semi-invariants as nonnegative sums over nonintersecting families, and
3911: \item transfer matrices built from these minors are totally nonnegative (and totally positive on the interior), so the Gantmacher--Krein spectral conclusions apply (Theorem~\ref{thm:tp_real_spectrum}).
3912: \end{enumerate}
3913: \end{corollary}
3914: 
3915: \begin{remark}[Where this feeds the rest of the manuscript]
3916: The purpose of importing Hochster's $\mathrm{Grass}(R)$ viewpoint is not only commutative algebra.
3917: It also provides the clean geometric interface needed for:
3918: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
3919: \item \textbf{Base change across arithmetic completions:} the Grassmannian functoriality of \eqref{eq:universal_grass_sequence} matches the diagonal $\GL(\bd)\hookrightarrow \GL(n)$ embedding and the ``local order'' computations in the Artin $L$--function section.
3920: \item \textbf{Determinantal semi-invariants as Pl\"ucker coordinates:} Schofield/Derksen--Weyman determinants and Shmelkin's bidirected-walk generators are Pl\"ucker-type minors in disguise, hence live naturally on Grassmannians.
3921: \item \textbf{Positivity as a structural axiom:} positivity is not a post hoc inequality; it is the choice of atlas (positive Grassmannian/network charts) in which determinantal coordinates are subtraction-free, making total positivity compatible with toric degeneration and self-adjoint transfer operators.
3922: \end{enumerate}
3923: \end{remark}

3929: 					\section{Representation Varieties}
3930: 					Suppose we have a constellation $C = [\sigma, \alpha, \phi]$ and that $Q$ is the associated medial quiver, and $\Lambda = \KK Q/I$ is the corresponding surface algebra. We already know we may partition the arrows $Q_1$, in two useful ways, either with respect to $\phi$, or with respect to $\sigma$. Let us use the partition of $Q_1$ in terms of $\phi$. Denote by $\phi_i$ the $i^{th}$ cycle of $\phi$ and let $Q(\phi_i)$ be the corresponding subquiver of $Q$. Such a subquiver is a (not necessarily simple) cycle in $Q$. Further, the arrow set of each $Q(\phi_i)$ lies in the ideal of $\lambda$. In particular, composition of two consecutive arrows of $Q(\phi_i)$ is in the ideal. Let $\Lambda_i = kQ(\phi_i)/I$, where $I$ is the ideal of $\Lambda$ restricted to $Q(\phi_i)$. 
3931: 					
3932: 					\begin{theorem}
3933: 						Let $\bd$ be a dimension vector for $\Lambda$. Let $\rep(\Lambda_i, \bd_i)$ be the representation variety of $\Lambda_i$ corresponding to the dimension vector $\bd_i$, which is the restriction of $\bd$ to $Q(\phi_i)$. Then,
3934: 						\[
3935: 						\rep(\Lambda_i, \bd_i) \cong \mathcal{C}_i(\bd_i) 
3936: 						\]
3937: 						\[
3938: 						= \left\lbrace V \in \bigoplus_{x \in \ZZ/n_i\ZZ} \Hom(V(x),V(x+1))  \bigg| V(a_{i+1})V(a_i) = A_{i
3939: 							+1}A_i = 0 \right\rbrace \]
3940: 						is isomorphic to a variety of circular complexes, where $n_i = |\phi_i|$. Therefore,
3941: 						\[
3942: 						\rep(\Lambda, \bd) = \prod_{\phi_i} \rep(\Lambda_i, \bd_i)
3943: 						\]
3944: 						must be isomorphic to a product of such varieties. 
3945: 					\end{theorem}
3946: 					
3947: 					\begin{corollary}We may thus describe the irreducible components in terms of the varieties of circular complexes. Let $r: Q_1 \to \NN$ be a \textbf{rank map}, i.e. a function such that for every $\phi_i$, $r_i:Q(\phi_i)_1 \to \NN$ is a rank map for the dimension vector $\bd_i$. If $r_i$ is maximal with respect to the dimension vector $\bd_i$ for each $i$, then $r$ gives an irreducible component of $\rep(\Lambda, \bd)$, which will be indexed by the rank map $r$, and denoted 
3948: 						\[ \rep(\Lambda, \bd, r)\]
3949: 						All irreducible components are obtained in this way. 
3950: 					\end{corollary}. 
3951: 					
3952: 					
3953: 					
3954: 					\section{Filtrations and Associated Graded Algebras}
3955: 					In this section we will describe the coordinate rings of the spaces $\rep(\Lambda, \bd)$, as well as the initial ideals of the defining ideals. We will also describe a standard monomial theory on the coordinate rings, and we will construct the associated graded algebra of the coordinate ring with respect to an equivariant filtration by Schur functors. 
3956: 					
3957: 					\begin{theorem}
3958: 						The varieties $\Spec\left(\fR(\Lambda, \bd, r)\right)$ for compact gentle surface algebras $\Lambda$, are Cohen-Macaulay, normal, and in fact have rational singularities. 
3959: 					\end{theorem}
3960: 					
3961: 					\begin{proof}
3962: 						Suppose $Q/I$ is the quiver with relations corresponding to the compact gentle surface algebra $\Lambda$. Let 
3963: 						$\fR = \KK[\rep(\Lambda, \bd,r)]$ be the coordinate ring of some 
3964: 						parametrizing variety for some dimension vector $\bd \in \NN^{Q_0}$, and let $\fR_i$ be the coordinate ring 
3965: 						of the representation variety $\rep(\Lambda_i, \bd_i, r_i)$. Suppose $r$ is maximal with respect to $\bd$. Then 
3966: 						each $r_i$ is maximal with respect to $\bd_i$ on $Q(\phi_i)$. Indeed, the restrictions on the ranks for varieties 
3967: 						of circular complexes come from the length $2$ relations on a circular complex, and thus the maximality 
3968: 						conditions on $r_i$ do not effect the maximality conditions on any other $r_j$ for $i \neq j$. 
3969: 						We may write
3970: 						\[ \fR = \bigotimes_{\phi_i} \fR_i \]
3971: 						It follows that as a product of varieties of circular complexes, the variety $\Spec(\fR)$ must be Cohen-Macaulay 
3972: 						and normal. 
3973: 					\end{proof}
3974: 					
3975: 					\begin{prop}
3976: 						For an irreducible component of $\rep(\Lambda, \bd, r)$, we have the following associated graded algebra for the coordinate ring $\mathfrak{R}=\mathfrak{R}(\Lambda, \bd, r) = \KK[\rep(\Lambda, \bd, r)]$:
3977: 						\[
3978: 						\bigoplus_{\lambda: Q_1 \to \mathcal{P}} \left(\bigotimes_{\phi_i} \left(\bigotimes_{\substack{x = h(\phi_i^{\ell}a) \in Q(\phi_i)_0 \\ \ell \in \ZZ/ n_i \ZZ}} S_{\lambda(\phi_i^{\ell}a), -\lambda(\phi_i^{\ell + 1} \cdot a)} V(x)
3979: 						\right) \right)
3980: 						\]
3981: 						where $ha=x=t(\phi_i \cdot a)$, and $\phi_i \cdot a$ denotes the action of $\phi_i$ on $Q(\phi_i)_1$. \sidenote{Recall: $\phi_i$ corresponds to an \textit{anti-cycle} in $Q$, i.e. a cycle of zero relations. We define an action of $\phi_i$ on the arrows of this anti-cycle $Q(\phi_i)_1$, simply by defining $\phi_i \cdot a$ to be the "next" arrow in the anti-cycle, for any arrow $a$. This just corresponds to the cyclic order of the boundary edges of the faces of $C=[\sigma, \alpha, \phi]$.}
3982: 					\end{prop}
3983: 					
3984: 					\newpage
3985: 					\begin{proof}
3986: 						This follows from the definitions and combinatorics we have setup for the constellations $C=[\sigma, \alpha, \phi]$, their corresponding medial quivers, and compact gentle surface algebras.\sidenote{In particular we showed that every gentle algebra that came from a finite $2$-regular quiver. We called a quiver $Q$ "$2$-regular" if every vertex had in-degree and out-degree exactly $2$. We showed every such quiver had a unique constellation $C(Q) = [\sigma, \alpha, \phi]$, and therefore a unique graph $\Gamma$ cellularly embedded in a closed Riemann surface $\Sigma$. We also showed that all constellations $C=[\sigma, \alpha, \phi]$ have a unique medial quiver, up to a choice of orientation of the surface, which is $2$-regular, and that assigning length two relations to cycles in the quiver around a face of $\Gamma \hookrightarrow \Sigma$, and that this correspondence produces a bijection between constellations and (finite) gentle $2$-regular quivers, and therefore also between constellations and compact gentle surface algebras.} For clarity, we list the necessary information:
3987: 						\begin{enumerate}
3988: 							\item First, we setup a bijection between compact gentle surface algebras $\Lambda$ and constellations $C$. 
3989: 							\item We then defined a partition of the corresponding gentle quiver $Q$, via the anti-cycles $\phi_i$ corresponding to the faces of the cellularly embedded graph $\Gamma \hookrightarrow \Sigma$. 
3990: 							\item Next, we described the representation varieties and coordinate rings of circular complexes and showed that the representation varieties of the subquivers $Q(\phi_i)$ under the partition by anti-cycles we isomorphic to varieties of circular complexes. 
3991: 							\item Finally, we observed that the representation variety $\rep(\Lambda, \bd)$ is a product of such varieties of circular complexes and inherits their geometric properties. 
3992: 						\end{enumerate}
3993: 					\end{proof}
3994: 
3995: 
3996: \begin{remark}[Moduli spaces, normality, and circular-complex factorization]
3997: The ``anti-cycle factorization'' of representation varieties into products of varieties of circular complexes
3998: is precisely the geometric input that makes invariant-theoretic moduli spaces tractable for gentle/special-biserial algebras.
3999: Concretely, for a special biserial algebra $A$ the irreducible components of the GIT moduli spaces of $\theta$--semistable representations
4000: are shown to be \emph{products of projective spaces}; the proof strategy reduces normality and decomposition questions
4001: for $\rep(A,\bd)$ to the corresponding questions for products of varieties of circular complexes.
4002: This is exactly the structure exploited above: the face anti-cycles $\phi_i$ isolate the circular-complex factors $Q(\phi_i)$,
4003: and maximality of the rank map $r$ identifies the ``regular'' components where the coordinate rings are Cohen--Macaulay and normal.
4004: Beyond being aesthetically pleasant, this matters later when gluing phases and clock holonomies are treated as learnable parameters:
4005: a moduli space with controlled geometry (products of projective spaces rather than arbitrary singular projective varieties)
4006: is a much safer domain for persistence-based inference and for operator-algebraic completion.  See \cite{CarrollChindrisKinserWeyman2018ModuliSpecialBiserial} for the special-biserial moduli-space theorem and the circular-complex reduction.
4007: \end{remark}

4010: \section{Standard Monomial Theory for the Coordinate Rings}
4011: 					Now, let us define the block order\sidenote{Let $k[x_1, ..., x_k]$ have a monomial order $\leq_1$ and $k[x_{k+1}, ..., x_n]$ have a monomial order $\leq_2$. Then we define the \textbf{block order} on $k[x_1, ..., x_k] \otimes k[x_{k+1}, ..., x_n]$ by saying for any pair of monomials $m, m' \in k[x_1, ..., x_k] \otimes k[x_{k+1}, ..., x_n]$ that $m \leq m'$ if $x_1^{a_1} \cdots x_k^{a_k} \leq_1 x_1^{b_1} \cdots x^{b_k}$, or $x_1^{a_1} \cdots x_k^{a_k} = x_1^{b_1} \cdots x_k^{b_k}$, and $x_{k+1}^{a_{k+1}} \cdots x_n^{a_n} \leq_2 x_{k+1}^{b_{k+1}} \cdots x_n^{b_n}$.} on the monomials of $\fR$, i.e. with respect to the orders $\leq_i$ on each $\fR_i$ defined in \S \ref{monomial orders} and \ref{Plucker monomial orders}.\sidenote{Remember, it is arbitrary as to how one chooses to order the the components $\fR_i$ in relation to each other.} We would like to describe a Gr\"{o}bner basis for each $\fR_i$ and for $\fR$, via the standard monomials. In so doing we will show the following
4012: 					
4013: 					\begin{prop}
4014: 						The coordinate ring $\fR$ of the parametrizing varieties of representations of a compact gentle surface algebra $\Lambda$ has a standard monomial theory.
4015: 					\end{prop}

Then under the block order, we have that $\bigotimes_{s \in S} \mathbf{B}_{s}(r_s^{k(s)})$ is a basis for $R(Q, \bd, r)$. Now, if $\Sigma(\bd_{s}, r_s^{k(s)})$ is the initial ideal of the defining ideal of $\rep_{Q, s}(\bd_s, r_s^{k(s)}) \subseteq \rep_{Q, s}(\bd_s)$, then $\sum_{s \in S} \Sigma(\bd_s, r_s^{k(s)})$ is the initial ideal of the defining ideal of the irreducible component corresponding to the rank map $r = (r_s^{k(s)})_{s \in S}$, of the variety $\rep_{Q, c}(\bd)$. Further, any nonstandard monomial in each $R(\bd_s, r_s^{k(s)})$ may be written as a linear combination of standard monomials, modulo the defining ideal of the irreducible component corresponding to the rank map $r = (r_s^{k(s)})_{s \in S}$. We may extend the standard monomial theory on each $R(\bd_{s}, r_s^{k(s)})$ to the ring $R(Q, \bd, r)$ in the obvious way (componentwise) giving the ring $R(Q, \bd, r)$ a standard monomial theory. Since each $R(\bd_{s}, r_s^{k(s)})$ has rational singularities (and is normal and Cohen-Macaulay), we deduce that $R(Q, \bd)$ is also.
