5236: \section{Hom-controlled push-down along Galois coverings (Zwara--Riedtmann)}
5237: \label{sec:homcontrolled_pushdown_proofs}
5238: 
5239: \subsection{Setup: coverings of bound quivers and the push-down functor}
5240: Let $k$ be algebraically closed. Let $(\widetilde Q,\widetilde I)\to(Q,I)$ be a (connected) \emph{Galois covering}
5241: of bound quivers with deck group $G$ (in the sense of Riedtmann's covering theory for locally bounded categories).
5242: Write $\widetilde\Lambda := k\widetilde Q/\widetilde I$ and $\Lambda := kQ/I$.
5243: Assume $\widetilde\Lambda$ is \emph{locally bounded} and \emph{locally finite} so that the categories of finitely
5244: presented representations $\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda)$ and $\rep(\Lambda)$ are Krull--Schmidt and Hom-finite.
5245: 
5246: There is a canonical \emph{push-down} (a.k.a.\ covering) functor
5247: \[
5248: F_\lambda:\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda)\longrightarrow \rep(\Lambda),
5249: \]
5250: defined on objects by \emph{orbit-summing along fibers}:
5251: for a vertex $x\in Q_0$, choose a lift $\tilde x\in\widetilde Q_0$ and set
5252: \[
5253: (F_\lambda M)(x)\ :=\ \bigoplus_{g\in G} M(g\tilde x),
5254: \qquad
5255: (F_\lambda M)(a)\ :=\ \bigoplus_{g\in G} M(g\tilde a),
5256: \]
5257: where $\tilde a$ is a chosen lift of $a$. One checks independence of choices by the $G$-equivariance of the covering.
5258: 
5259: \subsection{Zwara's ``Hom-control'' identity for coverings}
5260: The key mechanism is that $F_\lambda$ is exact and controls Homs by a \emph{direct-sum decomposition} over the deck group.
5261: 
5262: \begin{theorem}[Hom-controlled decomposition for a Galois push-down]
5263: \label{thm:homcontrolled_galois}
5264: Let $F_\lambda:\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda)\to\rep(\Lambda)$ be the push-down of a Galois covering with deck group $G$.
5265: For any $M,N\in\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda)$ there is a natural isomorphism
5266: \[
5267: \Hom_\Lambda(F_\lambda M,\;F_\lambda N)\ \cong\ \bigoplus_{g\in G}\Hom_{\widetilde\Lambda}(M,\;{}^{g}N),
5268: \]
5269: where ${}^{g}N$ denotes the $G$-translate (pullback along the deck transformation $g$).
5270: In particular,
5271: \[
5272: \dim_k\Hom_\Lambda(F_\lambda M,F_\lambda N)\ =\ \sum_{g\in G}\dim_k\Hom_{\widetilde\Lambda}(M,{}^{g}N),
5273: \]
5274: so $F_\lambda$ is Hom-controlled in the strong sense: the Hom-dimension is determined by finitely many
5275: translated Hom-dimensions on the cover.
5276: \end{theorem}
5277: 
5278: \begin{proof}
5279: Write $x\in Q_0$ and fix lifts $\tilde x\in\widetilde Q_0$.
5280: By definition $(F_\lambda M)(x)=\bigoplus_{g\in G}M(g\tilde x)$ and similarly for $N$.
5281: A $\Lambda$-morphism $\varphi:F_\lambda M\to F_\lambda N$ is a collection of linear maps
5282: $\varphi_x:(F_\lambda M)(x)\to(F_\lambda N)(x)$ commuting with all arrow maps.
5283: Writing $\varphi_x$ in block form with respect to the direct-sum decompositions along $G$,
5284: we can project to the $(1,g)$-block
5285: \[
5286: \varphi_{x}^{(g)}:\ M(\tilde x)\longrightarrow N(g\tilde x).
5287: \]
5288: Naturality with respect to arrows forces these blocks to form a morphism of $\widetilde\Lambda$-representations
5289: $M\to {}^{g}N$. Conversely, given a family $(f_g:M\to {}^{g}N)_{g\in G}$, define $\varphi_x$ by putting the
5290: $(h,hg)$-block equal to $({}^{h}f_g)_{x}:M(h\tilde x)\to N(hg\tilde x)$; the $G$-equivariance of the covering
5291: ensures this is well-defined and yields a $\Lambda$-morphism.
5292: These constructions are inverse to each other and are compatible with composition, giving the stated isomorphism.
5293: \end{proof}
5294: 
5295: \subsection{Geometric consequence: smoothness on module schemes}
5296: Let $\rep(\Lambda,\mathbf d)$ denote the representation variety of dimension vector $\mathbf d$ (and similarly on the cover).
5297: Zwara's theory shows that Hom-control implies smoothness of the induced morphisms on module schemes and rank schemes.
5298: 
5299: \begin{corollary}[Smoothness along covering images]
5300: \label{cor:smooth_covering}
5301: Fix dimension data so that $F_\lambda$ maps $\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda,\tilde{\mathbf d})$ into $\rep(\Lambda,\mathbf d)$.
5302: Then the induced morphism of schemes (on the corresponding strata)
5303: \[
5304: f_{\mathbf d}:\rep^+(\widetilde\Lambda,\tilde{\mathbf d})\longrightarrow \rep(\Lambda,\mathbf d)
5305: \]
5306: is smooth. In particular, for any $M$ on the cover, the étale-local singularity type of the orbit closure
5307: $\overline{\mathcal O_{F_\lambda M}}$ in $\rep(\Lambda,\mathbf d)$ agrees with that of
5308: $\overline{\mathcal O_M}$ in $\rep(\widetilde\Lambda,\tilde{\mathbf d})$ up to a smooth factor.
5309: \end{corollary}
5310: 
5311: \begin{proof}
5312: The tangent space at a representation can be identified with derivations modulo inner derivations,
5313: and the obstruction space is governed by $\Ext^1$. The decomposition of Theorem~\ref{thm:homcontrolled_galois}
5314: shows that the linear maps controlling first-order deformations split into a direct sum over $G$,
5315: hence the differential of $f_{\mathbf d}$ is surjective (formally smooth). Finite-type hypotheses then imply smoothness.
5316: This is precisely the covering-specialized instance of Zwara's smoothness theorem for Hom-controlled functors.
5317: \end{proof}
5318: 
5319: \section{Auslander--Reiten components and TikZ illustrations}
5320: \label{sec:ar_tikz}
5321: 
5322: This section provides \emph{explicit} translation-quiver pictures for the AR component types that occur in
5323: gentle/surface settings: (i) string components with local meshes (diamonds), (ii) homogeneous tubes for bands,
5324: and (iii) components containing projectives/injectives (preprojective/preinjective).
5325: 
5326: \subsection{String components: a 9-vertex mesh (hook/cohook diamond)}
5327: In a gentle algebra, irreducible maps between string modules are generated by the elementary operations
5328: of adding/removing a hook or a cohook at either end of the defining string.
5329: When both ends allow both moves, the local AR mesh consists of 9 indecomposables.
5330:

5332: 	\centering

5334: 		% 9 vertices in left-to-right diamond (45° rotation)

5336: 		\node (x) at (-2.4, 0) {$X$};
5337:

5339: 		\node (hl) at (-1.2, 1.2) {$H_LX$};
5340: 		\node (cl) at (-1.2, -1.2) {$C_LX$};
5341:

5434: \section{Self-injective algebras: stable AR translation and the Nakayama functor}
5435: \label{sec:selfinjective_tau}
5436: 
5437: Let $\Lambda$ be a finite-dimensional self-injective algebra. Write $\nu$ for the Nakayama functor
5438: $\nu := D\Hom_\Lambda(-,\Lambda)$ and $\Omega$ for the syzygy functor on the stable category $\underline{\mathrm{mod}}\,\Lambda$.
5439: 
5440: \begin{theorem}[Stable AR translation for self-injective algebras]
5441: \label{thm:tau_selfinjective}
5442: In the stable category $\underline{\mathrm{mod}}\,\Lambda$ of a self-injective algebra, the Auslander--Reiten translation satisfies
5443: \[
5444: \tau \ \cong\ \Omega^2\circ \nu.
5445: \]
5446: If $\Lambda$ is moreover symmetric (so $\nu\cong \mathrm{Id}$), then $\tau \cong \Omega^2$.
5447: \end{theorem}
5448: 
5449: \begin{proof}
5450: For any finite-dimensional algebra, $\tau \cong D\Tr$ on nonprojective modules, where $\Tr$ is the transpose.
5451: For self-injective $\Lambda$, the stable category is Frobenius and $\Omega$ is an autoequivalence.
5452: One identifies $D\Tr$ with $\Omega^2\nu$ by comparing the standard projective presentation
5453: $P_1\to P_0\to M\to 0$ and its dual, using that injectives coincide with projectives and that $\nu$ accounts for the
5454: twist between left and right projectives in the duality. Concretely, the AR sequence ending in $M$ is obtained from a
5455: minimal projective resolution of $M$ by splicing, and the middle term identifies with $\Omega^{-1}\nu^{-1}\Omega M$,
5456: yielding $\tau\simeq \Omega^2\nu$. Symmetry implies $\nu\simeq \mathrm{Id}$, giving $\tau\simeq\Omega^2$.
5457: \end{proof}

5474: 					\section{Zelevinsky's Total Positivity and Wiring Diagrams}
5475: \label{sec:zelevinsky_total_positivity}
5476: 
5477: This section provides a \emph{positivity technology} that we will reuse in several later places:
5478: \begin{itemize}
5479: \item in the QFT discussion (Wick rotation/transfer matrices), where positivity of Euclidean evolution underlies positivity of energy,
5480: \item in the renormalization-as-channel viewpoint, where we want certificates that coarse-grained transfer maps have controlled spectra, and
5481: \item in the Hilbert--Pólya/GRH program, where the analytic difficulty is to extract a \emph{self-adjoint} generator from arithmetic/geometric input without hidden tuning.
5482: \end{itemize}
5483: The relevant mathematics is the theory of \emph{total positivity} and its combinatorial parametrization by \emph{wiring diagrams} (planar networks), developed in depth by
5484: Berenstein--Fomin--Zelevinsky and Fomin--Zelevinsky \cite{BFZ1996TotallyPositive,FominZelevinsky2000TotalPositivity}, building on classical work of Gantmacher--Krein and Karlin \cite{Karlin1968TotalPositivity,Pinkus1996TotallyPositive}.
5485: 
5486: \subsection{Totally nonnegative and totally positive matrices}
5487: 
5488: \begin{definition}[Total nonnegativity and total positivity]
5489: A real matrix $A\in M_n(\R)$ is \emph{totally nonnegative} (TN) if every minor of $A$ is $\ge 0$.
5490: It is \emph{totally positive} (all minors strictly positive) if every minor of $A$ is $>0$.
5491: We write $A\in GL_n^{\ge 0}$ (resp.\ $GL_n^{>0}$) if $A$ is invertible and totally nonnegative (resp.\ totally positive).
5492: \end{definition}
5493: 
5494: Total positivity is much stronger than entrywise positivity.
5495: For example, a totally positive matrix is automatically invertible, and the inverse has a controlled sign pattern (checkerboard up to a positive diagonal scaling) \cite[Ch.\ 1--2]{Pinkus1996TotallyPositive}.
5496: Two structural properties make total positivity / total nonnegativity useful as a \emph{certificate} in physics-style constructions:
5497: 
5498: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
5499: \item \textbf{Spectral reality and simplicity.}
5500: Totally positive matrices are \emph{oscillatory} in the Gantmacher--Krein sense, which forces all eigenvalues to be real, positive, and simple.
5501: \item \textbf{Variation-diminishing (stability).}
5502: TN matrices are variation-diminishing: multiplying by a TN matrix cannot increase the number of sign changes of a vector, a discrete analogue of monotonicity/causality constraints.
5503: \end{enumerate}
5504: 
5505: We isolate the spectral statement we will use.
5506: 
5507: \begin{theorem}[Gantmacher--Krein: totally positive $\Rightarrow$ real, simple, positive spectrum]
5508: \label{thm:tp_real_spectrum}
5509: If $A\in GL_n^{>0}$ is totally positive, then $A$ is diagonalizable over $\R$ with eigenvalues
5510: \[
5511: \lambda_1>\lambda_2>\cdots>\lambda_n>0.
5512: \]
5513: Moreover, the eigenvectors have strictly controlled sign-variation (the $k$th eigenvector has exactly $k-1$ sign changes).
5514: \end{theorem}
5515: 
5516: \begin{proof}[Proof sketch / reference]
5517: A totally positive matrix is an \emph{oscillatory matrix}: it is TN and some power has all minors strictly positive.
5518: The classical Gantmacher--Krein oscillation theorem then implies that the spectrum is real, positive, and simple, with the stated nodal/sign-variation properties of eigenvectors.
5519: A modern reference is \cite[Thm.\ 2.5 and surrounding discussion]{Pinkus1996TotallyPositive}.
5520: \end{proof}
5521: 
5522: \subsection{Planar networks and the Lindstr\"om--Gessel--Viennot lemma}
5523: 
5524: Total nonnegativity admits a concrete combinatorial realization via planar directed networks.
5525: 
5526: \begin{definition}[Weighted planar network and its weight matrix]
5527: Fix $n$ sources $s_1,\dots,s_n$ and $n$ sinks $t_1,\dots,t_n$ arranged on the boundary of a planar disk in that cyclic order.
5528: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a finite directed acyclic planar graph embedded in the disk, with all sources on one side and all sinks on the opposite side.
5529: Assign a nonnegative weight $w(e)\ge 0$ to each directed edge $e$.
5530: For a directed path $P=e_1\cdots e_m$, define its weight $w(P)=\prod_{r=1}^m w(e_r)$.
5531: The \emph{weight matrix} $A(\mathcal{N})\in M_n(\R)$ is
5532: \[
5533: A(\mathcal{N})_{ij}:=\sum_{P:s_i\rightsquigarrow t_j} w(P),
5534: \]
5535: the sum of weights of all directed paths from $s_i$ to $t_j$ (finite because the network is acyclic).
5536: \end{definition}
5537: 
5538: \begin{theorem}[Lindstr\"om--Gessel--Viennot (LGV)]
5539: \label{thm:LGV}
5540: For any subsets $I,J\subset\{1,\dots,n\}$ with $|I|=|J|=k$, the minor
5541: $\det A(\mathcal{N})_{I,J}$ equals the sum of weights of all families of $k$ pairwise vertex-disjoint directed paths connecting $\{s_i\}_{i\in I}$ to $\{t_j\}_{j\in J}$, with the appropriate sign determined by the induced matching.
5542: In particular, if all edge weights are nonnegative then every minor of $A(\mathcal{N})$ is nonnegative, hence $A(\mathcal{N})$ is TN.
5543: \end{theorem}
5544: 
5545: \begin{proof}[Proof sketch / reference]
5546: Expand the determinant by permutations.
5547: A sign-reversing involution cancels collections of paths with intersections, leaving only vertex-disjoint families.
5548: See \cite{GesselViennot1985Nonintersecting,Lindstrom1973Paths} for proofs.
5549: \end{proof}
5550: 
5551: \begin{corollary}[Wiring/network $\Rightarrow$ total nonnegativity]
5552: \label{cor:wiring_TN}
5553: If $\mathcal{N}$ is a weighted planar network with nonnegative edge weights, then its weight matrix $A(\mathcal{N})$ is totally nonnegative.
5554: If in addition every relevant nonintersecting family exists and all edge weights are \emph{strictly} positive, then $A(\mathcal{N})$ is totally positive.
5555: \end{corollary}
5556: 
5557: 
5558: \subsection{Positive Grassmannians and positive geometry: Postnikov and Arkani--Hamed et al.}
5559: \label{sec:positive_grassmannian_total_positivity}
5560: 
5561: The wiring-diagram technology above can be phrased more invariantly in the language of \emph{positive Grassmannians} and \emph{boundary measurement maps}.
5562: This matters for two reasons:
5563: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
5564: \item it supplies a conceptual explanation of why planar networks parametrize totally nonnegative objects (and why different network moves preserve positivity), and
5565: \item it provides a bridge to the modern ``positive geometry'' viewpoint in mathematical physics, where positivity is not merely a technical lemma but a \emph{structural axiom}.
5566: \end{enumerate}
5567: 
5568: \paragraph{Totally nonnegative Grassmannian.}
5569: For $0<k<n$, the \emph{totally nonnegative Grassmannian} $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$ is the subset of the real Grassmannian $\mathbf{Gr}(k,n)$ consisting of $k$-planes whose Pl\"ucker coordinates can be chosen to be all nonnegative (and not all zero).
5570: Equivalently, $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$ is the closure of the locus where all Pl\"ucker coordinates are strictly positive.
5571: 
5572: \begin{theorem}[Postnikov: boundary measurements parametrize cells of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$]
5573: \label{thm:postnikov_boundary_measurement}
5574: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a planar directed network embedded in a disk with $n$ labeled boundary vertices, with positive edge weights.
5575: Postnikov's \emph{boundary measurement map} assigns to $\mathcal{N}$ a point in $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$ (for an appropriate $k$ determined by the source/sink data) whose Pl\"ucker coordinates are given by weighted sums of collections of nonintersecting directed paths in $\mathcal{N}$.
5576: Moreover, every cell of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$ admits such a parametrization by a planar network, and network moves (square moves, reductions) correspond to changing coordinates within the same cell decomposition.
5577: \end{theorem}
5578: 
5579: \begin{proof}[Reference]
5580: This is the main structural output of Postnikov's work connecting planar networks, total positivity, and Grassmannian stratifications; see \cite{Postnikov2006TotalPositivityNetworks}.
5581: \end{proof}
5582: 
5583: \begin{remark}[Relation to LGV and total nonnegativity]
5584: The LGV lemma (Theorem~\ref{thm:LGV}) is the ``matrix'' shadow of the boundary measurement story:
5585: minors of a path matrix are sums of nonintersecting families, hence nonnegative.
5586: Postnikov upgrades this from matrices to \emph{Pl\"ucker coordinates} and supplies a cell stratification and coordinate atlas on the positive locus.
5587: Thus, in this manuscript, whenever we realize a transfer matrix or a semi-invariant minor by a planar network,
5588: we are implicitly working in a chart on a positive Grassmannian cell.
5589: \end{remark}
5590: 
5591: \paragraph{Positive geometry in scattering amplitudes (Arkani--Hamed et al.).}
5592: The positive Grassmannian reappears in mathematical physics through the identification of on-shell diagrams with cells of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$ and the emergence of canonical differential forms with logarithmic singularities on boundaries.
5593: In particular, Arkani--Hamed and collaborators build a dictionary between:
5594: \begin{center}
5595: on-shell diagrams $\leftrightarrow$ plabic graphs $\leftrightarrow$ positive Grassmannian cells,
5596: \end{center}
5597: and propose ``positive geometries'' (including the \emph{amplituhedron}) whose canonical forms encode amplitudes \cite{ArkaniHamedBourjailyCachazoGoncharovPostnikovTrnka2012PositiveGrassmannian,ArkaniHamedTrnka2013Amplituhedron,ArkaniHamedHodgesTrnka2014PositiveAmplitudes}.
5598: For our purposes, the relevance is methodological: it is an independent, physics-driven validation that \emph{positivity constraints organize large determinantal computations} and that different combinatorial presentations (networks, plabic graphs, wiring diagrams) are equivalent positivity atlases.
5599: 
5600: \paragraph{Mirzakhani, moduli, and positivity of geometric measures.}
5601: On the moduli-space side, Mirzakhani's work on Weil--Petersson volumes and the growth of simple closed geodesics produces \emph{positive} volume polynomials/recursions and canonical ergodic measures on moduli spaces of hyperbolic surfaces \cite{MirzakhaniModuli}.
5602: In the present framework, this motivates two complementary uses of positivity:
5603: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
5604: \item \textbf{Measure selection (ergodic input).} A canonical positive measure (e.g.\ Weil--Petersson) provides a natural stationary distribution for coarse-grained dynamics on cycle/lamination data, feeding directly into detailed-balance/self-adjointness arguments.
5605: \item \textbf{Positivity of coordinates.} In decorated Teichm\"uller/cluster coordinate systems (lambda-length type coordinates), many naturally occurring functions on moduli are subtraction-free and hence positive on the positive locus; this is the moduli-space analogue of ``positive network coordinates'' on Grassmannians.
5606: \end{enumerate}
5607: We will not attempt to reprove these deep geometric positivity statements here; we use them as a guide for choosing \emph{canonical} positive structures rather than ad hoc sign conventions.
5608: 
5609: 
5610: \begin{remark}[Why ``wiring diagrams'' show up]
5611: A \emph{wiring diagram} is a particularly rigid planar network: it is an arrangement of $n$ monotone ``wires'' with crossings, encoding a reduced word in the symmetric group.
5612: The LGV lemma applies verbatim to wiring diagrams, and (because wiring diagrams are built by concatenating simple crossings) it meshes perfectly with factorization results in reductive groups.
5613: \end{remark}
5614: 
5615: \subsection{Zelevinsky-style parametrization by wiring diagrams (factorization in $GL_n^{>0}$)}
5616: 
5617: One way to \emph{construct} totally positive matrices is to factor them into elementary ``Jacobi'' matrices with positive parameters.
5618: Let $E_{ij}$ denote the standard matrix unit.
5619: For $t>0$ define the elementary upper- and lower-bidiagonal matrices
5620: \[
5621: x_i(t):=I+tE_{i,i+1},\qquad y_i(t):=I+tE_{i+1,i},\qquad 1\le i\le n-1,
5622: \]
5623: and let $D=\mathrm{diag}(d_1,\dots,d_n)$ with all $d_i>0$.
5624: Products of these matrices are automatically totally nonnegative/totally positive, and Zelevinsky-type results show that (up to mild choices) \emph{every} totally positive matrix arises this way.
5625: 
5626: \begin{theorem}[Berenstein--Fomin--Zelevinsky: wiring-diagram factorization]
5627: \label{thm:BFZ_factorization}
5628: Fix a reduced word $\mathbf{i}=(i_1,\dots,i_N)$ for the long permutation $w_0\in S_n$.
5629: Then the map
5630: \[
5631: (t_1,\dots,t_N; d_1,\dots,d_n)\ \longmapsto\
5632: x_{i_1}(t_1)\cdots x_{i_N}(t_N)\,D\, y_{i_N}(t_N)\cdots y_{i_1}(t_1)
5633: \]
5634: parametrizes an open dense subset of $GL_n^{>0}$, and the reduced word $\mathbf{i}$ can be drawn as a wiring diagram whose crossings carry the parameters $t_r$.
5635: \end{theorem}
5636: 
5637: \begin{proof}[Reference]
5638: This is one of the standard parametrizations of the totally positive part of a reductive group (here $GL_n$), expressed in terms of reduced words and generalized minors.
5639: See \cite{BFZ1996TotallyPositive,FominZelevinsky2000TotalPositivity}.
5640: \end{proof}
5641: 
5642: \begin{remark}[Network interpretation]
5643: Each elementary factor $x_i(t)$ or $y_i(t)$ is the weight matrix of a tiny planar ``crossing gadget'' with a single tunable edge of weight $t$.
5644: Concatenating gadgets corresponds to matrix multiplication, hence the entire product in Theorem~\ref{thm:BFZ_factorization} is the weight matrix of an explicit wiring diagram network.
5645: Thus, by Corollary~\ref{cor:wiring_TN}, total positivity of these products is a direct LGV consequence.
5646: \end{remark}
5647: 
5648: \subsection{Total positivity as a positive-energy / self-adjointness certificate (Wick-rotated transfer matrices)}
5649: \label{sec:tp_positive_energy_certificate}
5650: 
5651: In Euclidean (Wick-rotated) lattice QFT, one often works with a \emph{transfer matrix} $T$ rather than a unitary.
5652: The formal relation is $T=\exp(-aH)$ for lattice spacing $a>0$.
5653: To conclude that $H$ is self-adjoint and bounded below, one typically imposes Osterwalder--Schrader reflection positivity.
5654: Total positivity gives a more combinatorial (and, in discrete settings, sometimes easier to verify) sufficient condition.
5655: 
5656: \begin{theorem}[Symmetric totally positive transfer matrix $\Rightarrow$ self-adjoint Hamiltonian with positive energy]
5657: \label{thm:tp_positive_energy}
5658: Let $T\in M_n(\R)$ be \emph{symmetric} and totally positive.
5659: Then:
5660: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
5661: \item $T$ has real, positive, simple eigenvalues $\lambda_1>\cdots>\lambda_n>0$;
5662: \item for any $a>0$, the matrix
5663: \[
5664: H:=-\frac{1}{a}\log T
5665: \]
5666: is real symmetric (hence self-adjoint) with eigenvalues $E_k=-(1/a)\log\lambda_k\in\R$;
5667: \item after rescaling $T$ by its top eigenvalue (equivalently shifting $H$ by a scalar), one may assume $\lambda_1=1$, in which case $E_k\ge 0$ for all $k$ (positivity of energy).
5668: \end{enumerate}
5669: \end{theorem}
5670: 
5671: \begin{proof}
5672: (a) By Theorem~\ref{thm:tp_real_spectrum}, $T$ has real, positive, simple eigenvalues.
5673: (b) Because $T$ is symmetric, there exists an orthogonal matrix $U$ with $T=U\,\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\,U^\top$.
5674: Define $\log T:=U\,\mathrm{diag}(\log\lambda_1,\dots,\log\lambda_n)\,U^\top$; this is real symmetric.
5675: Then $H=-(1/a)\log T$ is real symmetric with eigenvalues $E_k$ as stated.
5676: (c) Replace $T$ by $\widetilde T:=\lambda_1^{-1}T$.
5677: Then $\widetilde T=\exp(-a\widetilde H)$ where $\widetilde H=H-(1/a)\log\lambda_1\,I$ is a scalar shift of $H$.
5678: Now $0<\widetilde\lambda_k\le 1$, hence $-\log\widetilde\lambda_k\ge 0$ and $\widetilde H\ge 0$.
5679: \end{proof}
5680: 
5681: \paragraph{Worked example: a $2\times 2$ totally positive transfer matrix.}
5682: 
5683: To make the theorem concrete, consider the simplest case: a symmetric $2\times 2$ totally positive matrix
5684: \[
5685: T = \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ b & c \end{pmatrix},
5686: \quad a,b,c > 0, \quad \det(T)=ac-b^2>0.
5687: \]
5688: For total positivity, we need all minors positive: $a>0$, $c>0$, $\det(T)>0$, which hold by assumption.
5689: 
5690: The eigenvalues are
5691: \[
5692: \lambda_\pm = \frac{(a+c) \pm \sqrt{(a+c)^2-4(ac-b^2)}}{2} = \frac{(a+c) \pm \sqrt{(a-c)^2+4b^2}}{2}.
5693: \]
5694: Both are real and positive (since $a,c,b>0$), and $\lambda_1>\lambda_2>0$ by the spectral ordering.
5695: 
5696: Now define $H=-\frac{1}{a}\log T$ (using Euclidean time step $a>0$).
5697: Diagonalizing $T=U\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)U^\top$ with an orthogonal $U$, we get
5698: \[
5699: H = U\,\mathrm{diag}\left(-\frac{1}{a}\log\lambda_1, -\frac{1}{a}\log\lambda_2\right)U^\top.
5700: \]
5701: This is manifestly real symmetric. Its eigenvalues are
5702: \[
5703: E_1=-\frac{1}{a}\log\lambda_1, \quad E_2=-\frac{1}{a}\log\lambda_2.
5704: \]
5705: If we rescale $T \to \widetilde T:=\lambda_1^{-1}T$ so that $\widetilde\lambda_1=1$, then $\widetilde E_1=0$ and $\widetilde E_2=-\frac{1}{a}\log(\lambda_2/\lambda_1)\ge 0$ (since $0<\lambda_2\le\lambda_1$).
5706: Thus the shifted Hamiltonian has nonnegative spectrum—positive energy, as desired.
5707: 
5708: This example shows explicitly how total positivity of $T$ (enforced via planar-network construction) leads to the required self-adjointness and spectral positivity without any appeal to Osterwalder--Schrader positivity or other limiting procedures.
5709: 
5710: \subsection{Density-operator phrasing: totally positive transfer matrices as states and modular Hamiltonians}
5711: 
5712: If $T$ is symmetric and positive definite, then after normalization it is literally a density operator.
5713: Define
5714: \[
5715: \rho:=\frac{T}{\Tr(T)}.
5716: \]
5717: Then $\rho\succeq 0$, $\rho=\rho^\top$ and $\Tr(\rho)=1$, so $\rho$ is a finite-dimensional (real) density matrix.
5718: Its modular Hamiltonian is
5719: \[
5720: K:=-\log\rho = -\log T + \log\Tr(T)\,I.
5721: \]
5722: Thus Theorem~\ref{thm:tp_positive_energy} can be reread as:
5723: \begin{quote}
5724: \emph{if a one-step Euclidean evolution operator is symmetric totally positive, then its normalized version is a bona fide density operator whose modular Hamiltonian is self-adjoint and nonnegative (after a scalar shift).}
5725: \end{quote}
5726: 
5727: \begin{remark}[How this is used later]
5728: In the Hilbert--Pólya/GRH chapter we extract candidate generators from \emph{channels} (CPTP maps) rather than from a single matrix.
5729: A common finite-dimensional reduction is to look at the channel's action on a commutative subalgebra (a coarse-grained classical shadow) or to restrict to a basis in which the channel becomes reversible.
5730: In such reductions, wiring-diagram/total-positivity conditions give a concrete, checkable route to self-adjoint modular generators.
5731: \end{remark}
5732: 
5733: \paragraph{Capstone: The architecture of total positivity in the Hilbert--Pólya program.}
5734: 
5735: We now summarize the complete picture that this chapter has built.
5736: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
5737: \item \textbf{Combinatorial layer (Zelevinsky).}
5738: Wiring diagrams and planar networks provide a concrete, parameter-counting realization of totally positive matrices.
5739: By the Berenstein--Fomin--Zelevinsky factorization theorem, every totally positive $n\times n$ matrix factors as a product of elementary bidiagonal matrices with nonnegative parameters, and this factorization structure is encoded in a wiring diagram.
5740: \item \textbf{Algebraic layer (Postnikov; positive Grassmannians).}
5741: The positive Grassmannian and its boundary measurement maps supply an invariant geometric language for positivity: wiring diagrams are coordinate charts on cells of $\mathbf{Gr}_{\ge 0}(k,n)$, and different network moves correspond to different coordinate patches on the same cell.
5742: This ties positivity to the underlying moduli geometry.
5743: \item \textbf{Spectral layer (Gantmacher--Krein).}
5744: Totally positive matrices have \emph{real, positive, and simple eigenvalues}.
5745: This is the crucial certificate: in any transfer-matrix or channel-based construction, total positivity automatically ensures the spectrum is real and bounded.
5746: \item \textbf{Self-adjointness and energy (Wick rotation).}
5747: When a symmetric totally positive transfer matrix $T$ is Wick-rotated via $H=-\frac{1}{a}\log T$, the resulting Hamiltonian is self-adjoint and, after a scalar shift, has nonnegative eigenvalues (positive energy).
5748: This is exactly what the Hilbert--Pólya construction requires: a self-adjoint generator whose spectrum is real and controlled.
5749: \end{enumerate}
5750: 
5751: The synthesis is this:
5752: \begin{quote}
5753: \emph{A clock/shift operator built by gluing totally positive transfer matrices (via wiring-diagram concatenation) automatically yields a self-adjoint Hamiltonian with real spectrum and positive energy.
5754: The wiring diagram is the certificate of positivity; the Gantmacher--Krein theorem is the certificate of reality; the logarithm is the bridge to self-adjointness.
5755: This mechanism is the core of the Hilbert--Pólya proposal for GRH developed in the final chapters:
5756: we will construct candidate generators of time evolution from surface orders and arithmetic data, demand that they are (or factor through) totally positive transfer matrices, and thereby obtain self-adjoint operators whose spectrum encodes the Riemann zeros.}
5757: \end{quote}
5758: 
5759: This is the ``icing in the middle of the cake''—a complete, self-contained layer that makes rigorous and checkable the claim that discrete/combinatorial/arithmetic input can yield a self-adjoint spectral problem with controlled reality and positivity properties.
5760:

\chapter{Wick Rotation and the Positivity of Energy in QFT} · lines 5767–5839
5767: \chapter{Wick Rotation and the Positivity of Energy in QFT}
5768: \label{ch:wick_rotation_positive_energy}
5769: 
5770: \section*{Bridge from total positivity}
5771: 
5772: The total positivity machinery developed in the preceding chapter provides the \emph{algebraic certificate} that certain transfer matrices have controlled spectra and self-adjoint logarithms.
5773: We now translate that machinery into the \emph{physical language} of Wick rotation and positive energy—the form needed for the Hilbert--Pólya operator construction.
5774: The key insight is simple: a symmetric totally positive transfer matrix $T$, when analytically continued to imaginary Euclidean time via $H:=i\log T$ (or equivalently $H=-\frac{1}{a}\log T$), automatically yields a self-adjoint Hamiltonian whose spectrum is real and, after normalization, nonnegative.
5775: This chapter makes the connection explicit and develops the quantum-field-theoretic context in which these transfer matrices arise naturally.
5776: 
5777: \section*{}
5778: 
5779: The basic analytic tension in QFT (and in any proposal that tries to build QFT-like dynamics from discrete/combinatorial input) is:
5780: 
5781: \begin{quote}
5782: \emph{Lorentzian time evolution wants a self-adjoint Hamiltonian $H$ (so that $U(t)=e^{-itH}$ is unitary), while Euclidean constructions and coarse-grained dynamics naturally produce \emph{positive} transfer operators $T$ (or channels) instead.}
5783: \end{quote}
5784: 
5785: A standard bridge between the two is \textbf{Wick rotation}:
5786: \[
5787: t\mapsto -i\tau,\qquad U(t)=e^{-itH}\ \leadsto\ e^{-\tau H}.
5788: \]
5789: On a lattice, $\tau$ is discretized and one works with a one-step transfer matrix $T$ that formally satisfies $T=e^{-aH}$ for time step $a>0$.
5790: The question is then: \emph{when is $H:=-(1/a)\log T$ actually self-adjoint and bounded below?}
5791: 
5792: \section{Euclidean transfer matrices and positivity}
5793: 
5794: In finite volume, a Euclidean path integral with real action $S_E$ produces weights $e^{-S_E}\ge 0$ and hence a transfer matrix with nonnegative matrix elements in a preferred basis.
5795: In infinite volume, the right condition is \emph{reflection positivity} (Osterwalder--Schrader positivity), which guarantees reconstruction of a Hilbert space and a self-adjoint Hamiltonian with spectrum bounded below.
5796: 
5797: For the purposes of this manuscript (which is explicitly constructive and often finite-dimensional at intermediate stages), it is useful to keep a clean, checkable sufficient condition:
5798: 
5799: \begin{quote}
5800: \emph{If $T$ is symmetric positive definite, then $H=-\frac{1}{a}\log T$ is self-adjoint, and energy positivity reduces to a normalization of the top eigenvalue.}
5801: \end{quote}
5802: 
5803: \section{A wiring-diagram sufficient condition}
5804: 
5805: Total positivity upgrades ``$T$ has nonnegative entries'' to ``every minor of $T$ is positive'', and this stronger property has two practical consequences:
5806: (i) it is stable under local concatenations, and
5807: (ii) it forces the spectrum to be real, positive, and simple.
5808: 
5809: The preceding chapter's total-positivity results immediately yield a Wick-rotation positivity statement.
5810: 
5811: \begin{corollary}[Reflection-symmetric wiring diagram $\Rightarrow$ positive-energy Hamiltonian]
5812: \label{cor:wiring_positive_energy}
5813: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a positive-weight wiring-diagram network whose weight matrix $T=A(\mathcal{N})$ is \emph{symmetric} (e.g.\ the network is invariant under planar reflection exchanging sources and sinks, which is a discrete detailed-balance condition).
5814: Assume $\mathcal{N}$ is such that $T$ is totally positive (Corollary~\ref{cor:wiring_TN}).
5815: Then $H:=-(1/a)\log T$ is self-adjoint and (after a scalar shift/normalization) satisfies $H\succeq 0$.
5816: \end{corollary}
5817: 
5818: \begin{proof}
5819: By Corollary~\ref{cor:wiring_TN}, $T$ is totally positive.
5820: By hypothesis $T$ is symmetric, so Theorem~\ref{thm:tp_positive_energy} applies.
5821: \end{proof}
5822: 
5823: \section{Density-operator viewpoint: Euclidean evolution as a Gibbs state}
5824: 
5825: Given a positive definite transfer matrix $T$, one may form a finite-volume Gibbs state at inverse temperature $\beta$ by
5826: \[
5827: \rho_\beta := \frac{T^\beta}{\Tr(T^\beta)} = \frac{e^{-\beta a H}}{\Tr(e^{-\beta a H})}.
5828: \]
5829: The modular Hamiltonian of $\rho_\beta$ is
5830: \[
5831: K_\beta:=-\log\rho_\beta=\beta a H+\log Z(\beta)\,I,\qquad Z(\beta)=\Tr(e^{-\beta a H}).
5832: \]
5833: Thus, in Euclidean settings the modular Hamiltonian is essentially the physical Hamiltonian (up to an affine transformation), and the ``positivity of energy'' is precisely the statement $K_\beta\succeq 0$ after subtracting its scalar part.
5834: Total positivity provides one constructive route to guarantee that this modular generator is self-adjoint, with good spectral control, \emph{before} taking any thermodynamic limit.
5835:
