8331:   \;=\;
8332:   \langle (Z_d)^m\rangle_{\rho'_v},
8333:   \label{eq:fourier_features}
8334: \end{equation}
8335: where $\rho'_v$ is the reduced state at~$v$ after entangling with neighbors via $U_\theta$.
8336: 
8337: \begin{proposition}[Fourier features as holographic encoding]
8338: \label{prop:fourier_holographic}
8339: The $d$-component feature vector $(\phi_0(v),\phi_1(v),\ldots,\phi_{d-1}(v))$ is the
8340: \emph{discrete Fourier transform of the diagonal of $\rho'_v$ in the computational basis}:
8341: \[
8342:   \phi_m(v)
8343:   \;=\;
8344:   \sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\omega^{mk}\,\rho'_{v,kk},
8345:   \qquad\omega = e^{2\pi i/d},
8346: \]
8347: and is therefore a complete description of the populations (diagonal entries) of the post-interaction
8348: reduced state.
8349: 
8350: Moreover, the storage/retrieval process has an explicit circular convolution structure:
8351: if the input encoding is $Z_d^{\lfloor\kappa x_u\rfloor}\ket{0}$ for each neighbor~$u$, then the
8352: entangling gate $\mathrm{CZ}_d^{(v,u)}$ of \eqref{eq:star_patch_unitary} induces the map
8353: \[
8354:   \phi_m(v)
8355:   \;\sim\;
8356:   \sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}_d}\hat\rho_{v,m-j}\;\cdot\;\hat\eta_j,
8357: \]
8358: where $\hat\rho_{v,\cdot}$ encodes the post-rotation state of the central qudit and $\hat\eta_j$
8359: encodes the Fourier transform of the combined neighbor-encoding contributions.
8360: This is precisely a \emph{circular convolution} in the Fourier domain of the cyclic qudit,
8361: i.e.\ the quantum analog of the holographic reduced representation \eqref{eq:circular_convolution}.
8362: \end{proposition}
8363: 
8364: \begin{proof}
8365: The first identity is immediate from $\langle k|Z_d^m|k\rangle = \omega^{mk}$
8366: and linearity of trace.
8367: For the second, expand the $\mathrm{CZ}_d$ action:
8368: $\mathrm{CZ}_d\ket{a,b}=\omega^{ab}\ket{a,b}$.
8369: After the star circuit \eqref{eq:star_patch_unitary}, the central qudit's state depends
8370: on the neighbors through phases $\omega^{a_v\cdot a_u}$ for each neighbor~$u$.
8371: Tracing over all neighbors and reading out $(Z_d)^m$ yields the stated convolution structure
8372: (a detailed computation parallels the Fourier analysis of controlled-phase gates in quantum
8373: signal processing; we omit the routine but lengthy calculation).
8374: \end{proof}
8375: 
8376: \begin{remark}[Infinite period: the continuous holographic limit]
8377: In the $d=\infty$ rotor model, $\phi_m(v)=\langle e^{im\theta}\rangle$ for $m\in\mathbb{Z}$,
8378: and the circular convolution becomes an ordinary convolution on $L^2(S^1)$.
8379: The Fourier modes then form a complete orthonormal system, and the stored holographic
8380: representation is a genuine infinite-dimensional encoding.
8381: Truncation to $d<\infty$ introduces finite angular resolution but preserves the holographic
8382: distribution property: each Fourier mode $\phi_m$ contains information about all stored patterns.
8383: \end{remark}
8384: 
8385: 
8386: \section{Graph quantum attention as content-addressable memory}
8387: \label{sec:qgat_content_addressable}
8388: 
8389: The attention mechanism of Section~\ref{sec:graph_qattn} admits an even more direct
8390: associative-memory interpretation than quanvolution.
8391: 
8392: \subsection{Query/key/value as address/content/data}
8393: 
8394: In a content-addressable memory (CAM), one provides an \emph{address} (query) and retrieves the
8395: \emph{data} (value) associated with the stored \emph{content} (key) that best matches the address.
8396: The graph quantum attention layer (Section~\ref{sec:qgat_renorm}) implements exactly this:
8397: 
8398: \begin{center}
8399: \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
8400: \begin{tabular}{l@{\qquad$\longleftrightarrow$\qquad}l}
8401: \toprule
8402: \textbf{CAM concept} & \textbf{QGAT on ribbon graph} \\
8403: \midrule
8404: Address (query) & $\ket{q_v}=U_Q(\theta_Q)\ket{\psi(h_v)}$ \\
8405: Content (key) & $\ket{k_u}=U_K(\theta_K)\ket{\psi(h_u)}$ for $u\in N_r(v)$\\
8406: Data (value) & $\ket{v_u}=U_V(\theta_V)\ket{\psi(h_u)}$ \\
8407: Match score & $\alpha_{vu}\propto\exp\!\bigl(-(\langle Z_d^m\rangle_{q_v}-\langle Z_d^m\rangle_{k_u})^2\bigr)$ \\
8408: Retrieved value & $h_v^{\mathrm{out}}=\sigma\!\bigl(\sum_u \alpha_{vu}\,\mathsf{V}_\theta(h_u)\bigr)$ \\
8409: \bottomrule
8410: \end{tabular}
8411: \end{center}
8412: 
8413: The ribbon-graph locality constraint means that each vertex~$v$ can only ``look up'' keys
8414: in its $r$-neighborhood $N_r(v)$.  This is a \emph{local content-addressable memory}, with the
8415: connectivity of the ribbon graph defining the memory's addressing topology.
8416: 
8417: \subsection{Multi-head attention as multi-pattern storage}
8418: 
8419: QGAT \cite{Ning2025QGAT} produces $n_q$ attention heads from a single circuit execution
8420: (Section~\ref{subsec:qgat_recap}): each qudit $k$ in the edge register yields one head's logit
8421: $e_{ij}^{(k)}$.  In the associative-memory interpretation, each head stores and retrieves
8422: \emph{different aspects} of the patterns at each vertex, analogous to multi-slot associative
8423: memory where different features are stored in parallel channels.
8424: 
8425: \begin{proposition}[Capacity of multi-head QGAT as local associative memory]
8426: \label{prop:qgat_capacity}
8427: Let~$v$ be a vertex of degree~$\delta_v$ in a ribbon graph equipped with $n_q$-qudit QGAT.
8428: Interpreting attention as modern Hopfield retrieval (Remark~\ref{rem:attention_hopfield_why}),
8429: the effective number of stored patterns per head is $\delta_v$ (the number of neighbors),
8430: and the retrieval is exponentially accurate in the hidden dimension
8431: $d_k=d^{n_q}$ of the edge-register Hilbert space.
8432: The total memory capacity at vertex~$v$ across all heads is therefore
8433: $\sim n_q\cdot\delta_v\cdot e^{d^{n_q}/2}$ (in the modern Hopfield sense of distinguishable
8434: patterns for a given accuracy).
8435: On a bounded-degree hyperbolic graph with $\delta_v\le\Delta$, this yields a per-vertex
8436: capacity exponential in the qudit Hilbert-space dimension, regardless of graph size.
8437: \end{proposition}
8438: 
8439: \begin{remark}[Why cyclic equivariance matters]
8440: When the attention mechanism respects the cyclic order at each vertex
8441: (Section~\ref{subsec:qgat_ribbon_adaptation}, option~B), the stored patterns inherit a
8442: \emph{cyclic symmetry}: rotating the half-edge labels at~$v$ permutes the stored patterns
8443: but does not change the set of retrievable associations.
8444: This is a rotational equivariance property of the local holographic memory, directly
8445: analogous to the rotational invariance of a physical hologram.
8446: \end{remark}
8447: 
8448: 
8449: \section{Hierarchical holographic memory via renormalization on ribbon graphs}
8450: \label{sec:hierarchical_holographic}
8451: 
8452: \subsection{Pooling as memory compression: from fine to coarse patterns}
8453: 
8454: The iterative pooling/RG process of Sections~\ref{subsec:qgcn_pooling_channel}
8455: and~\ref{subsec:qgat_pooling_rg} produces a hierarchy of ribbon graphs
8456: $\Gamma=\Gamma_0\to\Gamma_1\to\cdots\to\Gamma_L$
8457: with decreasing numbers of vertices.
8458: At each level~$\ell$, the quanvolutional or attention layer implements a local associative
8459: memory with its own set of stored patterns.
8460: The pooling step \emph{compresses} the stored information:
8461: \begin{itemize}
8462: \item \textbf{fine patterns} (many vertices, local features) are stored at level~$\ell$,
8463: \item \textbf{coarse patterns} (fewer vertices, aggregate features) are stored at level~$\ell+1$,
8464: \item the pooling channel $\mathcal{R}_\theta$ maps fine-level stored patterns to coarse-level
8465: stored patterns by tracing out/measuring selected degrees of freedom.
8466: \end{itemize}
8467: 
8468: This is a \emph{hierarchical holographic memory}:
8469: information about fine-scale patterns is not lost but is \emph{encoded} in the effective
8470: parameters and residual entanglement at the coarse scale.
8471: The encoding is ``holographic'' in the precise sense that:
8472: \begin{enumerate}
8473: \item each coarse-level feature $\phi_a(v')$ (where $v'$ is an effective vertex at level $\ell+1$)
8474: depends on a \emph{neighborhood} of fine-level vertices that were pooled together;
8475: \item the information is distributed: no single coarse feature fully determines the fine-level
8476: input, but the collection of coarse features (across all vertices and readout observables)
8477: allows reconstruction (up to the information lost by the pooling channel).
8478: \end{enumerate}
8479: 
8480: \subsection{Connection to AdS/CFT and the holographic principle}
8481: \label{subsec:ads_cft_holographic}
8482: 
8483: The hierarchical holographic memory has a natural interpretation in the language of AdS/CFT
8484: and the tensor-network models of holography (cf.\ the emergent gravity discussion in
8485: Section~\ref{ch:gravity}).
8486: 
8487: In tensor-network models of AdS/CFT
8488: (e.g.\ MERA~\cite{Vidal2007MERA}, HaPPY~\cite{Pastawski2015HAPPY}),
8489: the RG direction (coarse-graining) is identified with the \emph{radial (bulk)} direction in anti-de
8490: Sitter space, and the boundary CFT data are encoded in the fine-scale (UV) degrees of freedom.
8491: The key property of holographic codes is that bulk operators at depth~$\ell$ can be reconstructed
8492: from boundary data on any sufficiently large subregion---this is the \emph{entanglement wedge
8493: reconstruction} property.
8494: 
8495: On a hyperbolic ribbon graph with $\sim 10^5$ cyclic qudits
8496: (Section~\ref{subsec:explicit_hyperbolic_circuits}), the same structure emerges naturally:
8497: 
8498: \begin{center}
8499: \renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}
8500: \begin{tabular}{l@{\qquad$\longleftrightarrow$\qquad}l}
8501: \toprule
8502: \textbf{AdS/CFT concept} & \textbf{QHAM on hyperbolic ribbon graph} \\
8503: \midrule
8504: Boundary CFT data & Fine-scale features $\phi_a(v)$ at level~$0$ \\
8505: Radial (bulk) direction & RG/pooling direction $\ell=0,1,\ldots,L$ \\
8506: Bulk operators & Coarse-scale features $\phi_a(v')$ at level~$\ell>0$ \\
8507: Entanglement wedge & Support of the pooling channel at vertex $v'$ \\
8508: Ryu--Takayanagi surface & Minimal cut in the ribbon graph separating $v'$ from boundary\\
8509: Holographic code & The full RG hierarchy of quanvolution + pooling channels\\
8510: \bottomrule
8511: \end{tabular}
8512: \end{center}
8513: 
8514: \begin{proposition}[Holographic encoding property of the QHAM hierarchy]
8515: \label{prop:holographic_encoding}
8516: Let $\Gamma$ be a degree-$\Delta$ hyperbolic ribbon graph with $N$ vertices, and let
8517: $\Gamma_0\to\Gamma_1\to\cdots\to\Gamma_L$ be the hierarchy produced by $L=O(\log N)$
8518: pooling/RG steps, each contracting a maximal matching.
8519: Then:
8520: \begin{enumerate}
8521: \item $|\Gamma_\ell|=\Theta(N/2^\ell)$, so $|\Gamma_L|=O(1)$ after $L\sim\log_2 N$ steps.
8522: \item The effective stored patterns at level~$\ell$ depend on a ``causal cone'' of
8523: $\Theta(\Delta^\ell)$ fine-scale vertices---i.e., the memory is local in the bulk but
8524: nonlocal on the boundary, with the degree of nonlocality growing exponentially with depth.
8525: \item The total information stored across all levels is bounded by
8526: $\sum_\ell |\Gamma_\ell|\cdot p_\ell\cdot\log d$, where $p_\ell$ is the number of readout
8527: features at level~$\ell$.  For constant $p_\ell$ and $d$, this is $O(N\log d)$, matching the
8528: ``boundary area law'' scaling of holographic codes.
8529: \end{enumerate}
8530: \end{proposition}
8531: 
8532: \begin{proof}
8533: (1) follows from the matching contraction reducing vertex count by at least a factor of~$2$ per step.
8534: (2) follows from the $r$-neighborhood support of each convolution/attention layer: after $\ell$
8535: layers, the effective receptive field at a coarse vertex covers an $\ell$-hop ball whose size
8536: grows as $\Delta^\ell$ on a regular tree (and slower on a hyperbolic graph, but still exponentially).
8537: (3) is an information-theoretic counting argument: each qudit contributes $\log_2 d$ bits of
8538: information, and $p_\ell$ measurements at each of $|\Gamma_\ell|$ vertices yield the stated bound.
8539: \end{proof}
8540: 
8541: 
8542: \section{The cyclic-qudit Fourier structure as holographic encoding}
8543: \label{sec:cyclic_holographic_encoding}
8544: 
8545: The term ``holographic'' is used in two senses in this chapter:
8546: (i) the information-theoretic sense of HRR (Section~\ref{subsec:hrr}), where information is
8547: distributed across all components, and
8548: (ii) the gravitational/AdS-CFT sense of boundary-to-bulk encoding (Section~\ref{subsec:ads_cft_holographic}).
8549: The cyclic-qudit Fourier structure connects both.
8550: 
8551: \subsection{Fourier modes as distributed features}
8552: 
8553: Let $\ket{\psi_v}=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}c_k\ket{k}$ be the state of a cyclic qudit at vertex~$v$
8554: after a quanvolutional layer.
8555: The readout features $\phi_m(v)=\langle(Z_d)^m\rangle=\sum_k |c_k|^2\omega^{mk}$ are the
8556: Fourier modes of the population distribution $\{|c_k|^2\}$.
8557: Each feature~$\phi_m$ depends on \emph{all} $d$ amplitudes, so the information about the
8558: input is distributed---no single Fourier mode determines the input, but the collection
8559: $(\phi_0,\ldots,\phi_{d-1})$ does (up to phase ambiguity).
8560: 
8561: This is the quantum analog of the HRR property: the ``hologram'' is the set of Fourier-mode
8562: readouts, and each mode contains a global imprint of the stored pattern.
8563: 
8564: \subsection{Angular resolution and the truncation/quotient hierarchy}
8565: 
8566: The infinite-period model ($d=\infty$) has an infinite tower of Fourier modes
8567: $\langle e^{im\theta}\rangle$, $m\in\mathbb{Z}$, providing unlimited angular resolution.
8568: Truncation to $d<\infty$ introduces a \emph{Nyquist-type} angular resolution limit:
8569: patterns differing by less than $2\pi/d$ in the angular coordinate at a vertex become
8570: indistinguishable.
8571: 
8572: For the hierarchical holographic memory, this resolution limit interacts with the RG hierarchy:
8573: \begin{itemize}
8574: \item at the fine scale (level~$0$), high angular resolution ($d$ large) captures detailed
8575: local structure;
8576: \item at the coarse scale (level~$L$), effective patterns are sums over many fine-scale inputs,
8577: and only low Fourier modes survive the averaging/pooling---a natural ``low-pass filter''
8578: in the angular direction.
8579: \end{itemize}
8580: This is exactly the behavior expected of a holographic encoding: the UV (fine) data carry high
8581: Fourier modes while the IR (coarse) data are dominated by low modes, paralleling the
8582: high-energy/low-energy split in the holographic renormalization group of AdS/CFT.
8583: 
8584: 
8585: \section{Explicit examples: quantum holographic associative memory on hyperbolic hardware}
8586: \label{sec:qham_examples}
8587: 
8588: \subsection{Example 1: pattern storage and retrieval on a $\{7,3\}$ hyperbolic tiling}
8589: \label{subsec:qham_example_73}
8590: 
8591: Fix a degree-3 hyperbolic tiling ($\{7,3\}$-type) with $N=100$ vertices (a small
8592: patch for illustration) and cyclic qudits of period $d=7$ at each vertex.
8593: 
8594: \paragraph{Storage phase.}
8595: Suppose we wish to store $P=3$ ``patterns'' $\xi^{(\mu)}\in\mathbb{Z}_7^{100}$, $\mu=1,2,3$.
8596: We train a quanvolutional layer (star-patch unitary~\eqref{eq:star_patch_unitary}) by minimizing
8597: a contrastive loss:
8598: \[
8599:   \mathcal{L}(\theta)
8600:   \;=\;
8601:   \sum_{\mu=1}^{3}\sum_v
8602:   \bigl\|
8603:     \Phi_\theta(\xi^{(\mu)})_v - \mathbf{e}_\mu
8604:   \bigr\|^2
8605:   \;+\;
8606:   \lambda\sum_{\mu\neq\nu}\bigl(
8607:     \langle\Phi_\theta(\xi^{(\mu)}),\Phi_\theta(\xi^{(\nu)})\rangle
8608:   \bigr)^2,
8609: \]
8610: where $\mathbf{e}_\mu$ is a one-hot target and the second term encourages orthogonality of stored
8611: representations.
8612: 
8613: \paragraph{Retrieval phase.}
8614: Given a corrupted input $\tilde\xi=\xi^{(1)}+\text{noise}$, evaluate $\Phi_\theta(\tilde\xi)$
8615: on each vertex, aggregate by global average pooling, and apply $\mathrm{argmax}$.
8616: Because the $\{7,3\}$ tiling has logarithmic diameter ($\sim\log_2(100)\approx 7$),
8617: a stack of $\sim 4$ quanvolutional layers (each with pooling) reduces the 100 vertices to
8618: $\sim 6$ effective vertices, after which a single classical readout determines the retrieved
8619: pattern.
8620: 
8621: \paragraph{Circuit cost.}
8622: Each quanvolutional layer requires $\Theta(|E|)=\Theta(N)$ two-qudit gates (with bounded degree,
8623: $|E|=\frac{3}{2}N$).  For $d=7$, each generalized $\mathrm{CZ}_7$ decomposes into
8624: $O(\log_2 7)\approx 3$ two-qubit gates under binary encoding
8625: (Section~\ref{sec:hyperbolic_cyclic_hardware}).
8626: Total circuit depth per layer: $\sim 3\times 3 = 9$ two-qubit gate layers (edge-coloring with
8627: 3 colors $\times$ 3-qubit decomposition depth).
8628: For 4 layers on 100 vertices: $\sim 36$ depth, well within near-term coherence budgets.
8629: 
8630: \subsection{Example 2: hierarchical holographic memory on $\sim 10^5$ cyclic qudits}
8631: \label{subsec:qham_example_1e5}
8632: 
8633: Now consider the full-scale thought experiment: $N=10^5$ vertices on a $\{7,3\}$ hyperbolic
8634: tiling with cyclic qudits of period $d=8$ ($=2^3$, so that binary encoding is clean).
8635: 
8636: \paragraph{RG hierarchy.}
8637: With $\log_2(10^5)\approx 17$, we need $\sim 17$ pooling steps to reach $O(1)$ effective vertices.
8638: In practice, one would stop earlier (say after $L=10$ steps, reaching $\sim 100$ effective vertices)
8639: and apply a few attention layers on the coarse graph before a final readout.
8640: 
8641: \paragraph{Memory organization.}
8642: \begin{itemize}
8643: \item \textbf{Level 0} (fine): $10^5$ vertices, each with a $d=8$ qudit.
8644: Local features: $\phi_m(v)$ for $m=0,\ldots,7$ (8 Fourier modes per vertex).
8645: Total features: $8\times 10^5 = 8\times 10^5$.
8646: \item \textbf{Level 5}: $\sim 3\times 10^3$ effective vertices.
8647: Coarse features capture patterns at the $\sim 2^5=32$-vertex scale.
8648: \item \textbf{Level 10}: $\sim 100$ effective vertices.
8649: Attention layers on this small graph implement a \emph{global associative memory}
8650: with per-vertex capacity exponential in $d^{n_q}=8^{n_q}$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:qgat_capacity}).
8651: \item \textbf{Level 17}: $O(1)$ effective vertices.  A single classical readout determines
8652: the global pattern.
8653: \end{itemize}
8654: 
8655: \paragraph{Holographic property at scale.}
8656: By Proposition~\ref{prop:holographic_encoding}, the total information in the hierarchy is
8657: $O(N\log d)=O(10^5\times 3)\approx 3\times 10^5$ bits,
8658: matching boundary-area scaling.
8659: The effective ``bulk'' patterns at level $\ell=10$ encode nonlocal boundary correlations
8660: spanning $\sim\Delta^{10}=3^{10}\approx 6\times 10^4$ fine-scale vertices---more than half
8661: the device.
8662: 
8663: \paragraph{Circuit implementation.}
8664: Using Circuit~A (Section~\ref{subsec:explicit_hyperbolic_circuits}) for each RG step:
8665: \begin{itemize}
8666: \item star-entangling: $\sim 3N/2$ two-qudit gates per step, parallelized in 4 rounds (edge-coloring).
8667: \item each $\mathrm{CZ}_8$ gate decomposes into $3$ two-qubit gates (binary encoding of $d=8=2^3$).
8668: \item per-step depth: $4\times 3=12$ two-qubit gate layers.
8669: \item 10 RG steps: total depth $\sim 120$ two-qubit layers.
8670: \item readout at each step: single-site $Z$ measurements (negligible depth).
8671: \end{itemize}
8672: This is aggressive but not absurd for a device with $3\times 10^5$ physical qubits
8673: (binary encoding of $10^5$ qudits at $\lceil\log_2 8\rceil=3$ qubits each)
8674: and coherence times supporting $\sim 200$ gate layers.
8675: 
8676: \subsection{Example 3: attention-based pattern retrieval with cyclic equivariance}
8677: \label{subsec:qham_example_attention}
8678: 
8679: On a smaller hyperbolic patch ($N=49$ vertices, $\{7,3\}$ tiling, $d=7$), implement a
8680: QGAT-style attention layer with $n_q=4$ qudits in the edge register.
8681: 
8682: \paragraph{Storage.}
8683: Each vertex stores $n_q=4$ attention heads.  With $\delta_v=3$ neighbors, each head addresses
8684: 3 keys.  The Hilbert-space dimension of the edge register is $d^{n_q}=7^4=2401$, so the
8685: modern-Hopfield capacity per head is $\sim e^{2401/2}$ (astronomically large---in practice
8686: limited by training and noise).
8687: 
8688: \paragraph{Retrieval circuit.}
8689: For each edge $(i,j)$:
8690: \begin{enumerate}
8691: \item Amplitude-encode edge features into 4 qudits of period~7.  Under binary encoding, this
8692: requires $4\times\lceil\log_2 7\rceil=12$ qubits per edge register.
8693: \item Apply a depth-6 strongly entangling block ($6\times 4=24$ parameterized one-qudit gates plus
8694: $6\times 3=18$ two-qudit entanglers per layer).
8695: \item Measure $(Z_7)_k$ on each of the 4 qudits, yielding 4 logits per edge.
8696: \item Softmax over neighbors: $\alpha_{ij}^{(k)}=\exp(e_{ij}^{(k)})/\sum_{j'}\exp(e_{ij'}^{(k)})$.
8697: \end{enumerate}
8698: 
8699: \paragraph{Associative-memory interpretation.}
8700: The 4-head attention at vertex~$i$ simultaneously queries 4 ``aspects'' of the stored patterns
8701: at each of its 3 neighbors.  The softmax retrieval selects, for each head, the neighbor whose
8702: key best matches the query.  Because the scoring uses Fourier modes of cyclic qudits, the
8703: matching is \emph{angular}: it compares periodic features of the input encoding, providing
8704: natural equivariance under the cyclic order at each vertex.
8705: 
8706: This makes the ribbon-graph attention memory a \emph{rotation-equivariant content-addressable
8707: memory}, where ``rotation'' refers to the cyclic half-edge permutation at each vertex.
8708: 
8709: \subsection{Connecting QHAM to the emergent-gravity program}
8710: \label{subsec:qham_gravity}
8711: 
8712: The quantum holographic associative memory framework connects directly to the
8713: emergent-gravity program of Section~\ref{ch:gravity}:
8714: 
8715: \begin{enumerate}
8716: \item \textbf{Entanglement $\to$ geometry.}
8717: The attention weights $\alpha_{vu}$ define an effective metric on the ribbon graph
8718: (Section~\ref{subsec:qgat_pooling_rg}): vertices with high mutual attention are ``close''.
8719: This data-dependent metric is the QHAM analog of the Ryu--Takayanagi surface in AdS/CFT.
8720: 
8721: \item \textbf{RG $\to$ radial direction.}
8722: The pooling hierarchy $\Gamma_0\to\cdots\to\Gamma_L$ is the QHAM analog of the radial
8723: (holographic) direction.  Coarse-graining ``deeper into the bulk'' produces effective
8724: variables that are increasingly nonlocal on the boundary.
8725: 
8726: \item \textbf{Clock holonomy $\to$ time.}
8727: At each RG level, the clock operators $S_v$ induce time holonomy
8728: (Section~\ref{ch:gluing}).  The QHAM hierarchy thus equips the emergent bulk with a
8729: \emph{clock structure at each scale}---and the consistency of clocks across scales
8730: (detected by multiparameter persistence) is the QHAM analog of bulk diffeomorphism
8731: invariance.
8732: 
8733: \item \textbf{Memory retrieval $\to$ bulk reconstruction.}
8734: The associative-memory retrieval process (query $\to$ attention $\to$ value) is the QHAM
8735: analog of bulk operator reconstruction: given boundary data (the query), the hierarchy
8736: retrieves the bulk encoding (the value) that best matches the query.
8737: The fact that this works for corrupted inputs (noise robustness of associative memory)
8738: parallels the error-correcting property of holographic codes.
8739: \end{enumerate}
8740: 
8741: \begin{remark}[A cautious synthesis]
8742: \label{rem:cautious_synthesis}
8743: We do not claim that QHAM \emph{is} quantum gravity.
8744: We claim something weaker but precise:
8745: \emph{the mathematical structure of learned quantum graph convolution and attention on ribbon
8746: graphs, with cyclic-qudit degrees of freedom and hierarchical pooling, naturally realizes the
8747: same abstract properties (boundary-area scaling, hierarchical nonlocality, error correction,
8748: data-dependent geometry) that characterize holographic codes and tensor-network models of AdS/CFT.}
8749: Whether this structural parallel has physical content is an empirical question addressable by
8750: the experiments in Section~\ref{ch:expts} and the persistence diagnostics of
8751: Section~\ref{ch:persistence}.
8752: \end{remark}

\chapter{Experiments and circuits under realistic quantum hardware constraints (\texorpdfstring{$\sim 10^4$}{~1e4} qubits)} · lines 8757–9149
8757: \chapter{Experiments and circuits under realistic quantum hardware constraints (\texorpdfstring{$\sim 10^4$}{~1e4} qubits)}
8758: 
8759: \label{ch:expts}
8760: 
8761: 
8762: The  main body proposes hardware experiments up to $\sim 10^4$ qubits ( Chapter~12).
8763: Here we expand the engineering layer in three directions:
8764: 
8765: \begin{enumerate}
8766: \item \textbf{Clock operators as circuits:} how to implement finite cyclic shifts, twisted shifts, and their truncations under unitary/noisy constraints.
8767: \item \textbf{Holonomy constraints:} how to enforce or diagnose global time holonomy on a graph embedded in limited connectivity.
8768: \item \textbf{Persistence pipelines at scale:} concrete resource estimates for measuring $W_\psi$ and building bifiltered complexes.
8769: \end{enumerate}
8770: 
8771: \subsection{Hardware model and the ``logical surface-order graph''}
8772: \label{sec:hardware_model}
8773: 
8774: Let $G_{\mathrm{hw}}=(V_{\mathrm{hw}},E_{\mathrm{hw}})$ be the physical connectivity graph of the device.
8775: We assume:
8776: \begin{itemize}
8777: \item $|V_{\mathrm{hw}}|=N\sim 10^4$,
8778: \item two-qubit gates are natively available only on edges in $E_{\mathrm{hw}}$,
8779: \item measurement is in the computational basis with optional pre-rotations.
8780: \end{itemize}
8781: 
8782: A surface-order experiment starts from a \emph{logical} embedded graph $\Gamma\subset \Sigma$ (triangulated surface, hyperbolic patch, or modular dessin quotient).
8783: We require an embedding (possibly with SWAP routing)
8784: \[
8785: \iota:V(\Gamma)\hookrightarrow V_{\mathrm{hw}}.
8786: \]
8787: 
8788: \begin{remark}[Connectivity mismatch is the default]
8789: Most interesting $\Gamma$ are not subgraphs of $G_{\mathrm{hw}}$.
8790: Therefore, the practical design principle is:
8791: \begin{quote}
8792: \emph{Choose $\Gamma$ to be topologically interesting but routing-friendly: planar patches with handles encoded by long-range logical edges realized via SWAP networks.}
8793: \end{quote}
8794: \end{remark}
8795: 
8796: 
8797: \subsection{Biomolecular motif-scaffold hardware: building a ribbon-graph QPU from peptides and proteins}
8798: \label{sec:biomolecular_qpu}
8799: 
8800: The default hardware mental model for this manuscript is ``standard'' qubit technology (superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms).
8801: However, the \emph{surface-order} viewpoint is more abstract: it only needs a graph $\Gamma$ of interacting local Hilbert spaces and the ability to
8802: (i) implement local ``clock'' primitives and (ii) estimate correlation/entropy proxies on edges.
8803: That abstraction admits an additional, chemically realizable route to hardware:
8804: 
8805: \begin{quote}
8806: \emph{Use biomolecules (peptides/proteins) as programmable nanoscale scaffolds that place and couple spin qubits at prescribed locations,
8807: so that the physical device \emph{is literally} a ribbon graph in three-dimensional space.}
8808: \end{quote}
8809: 
8810: This route becomes particularly concrete when combined with modern \emph{motif scaffolding} generative models for protein backbones.
8811: 
8812: \subsubsection{Peptidic lanthanide spin qubits as ``vertex motifs''}
8813: A physically grounded starting point is the platform developed in \cite{Rosaleny2017PeptideQC}:
8814: short \emph{Lanthanide Binding Tag} (LBT) peptides (length $\sim 15$--$17$ amino acids) that chelate trivalent lanthanide ions (e.g.\ Nd, Gd) and act as molecular spin qubits.
8815: 
8816: The key hardware-relevant observations from \cite{Rosaleny2017PeptideQC} are:
8817: 
8818: \begin{itemize}
8819: \item \textbf{Coherence is measurable at the motif level.}
8820: For NdLBT and GdLBT, pulsed-EPR measurements report relaxation times on the order of microseconds (e.g.\ $T_1\sim 10\,\mu$s and $T_2\sim 2\,\mu$s for GdLBT, with somewhat shorter values for NdLBT),
8821: and coherent Rabi oscillations can be observed for $\sim 20$ cycles under suitable conditions (Hartmann--Hahn tuning).%
8822: \footnote{In state-vector terms, these correspond to the ability to prepare superpositions $\ket{\psi}=\alpha\ket{0}+\beta\ket{1}$ and maintain their relative phase over many gate times, as witnessed by Ramsey/echo signals and sustained driven Rabi oscillations.}
8823: 
8824: \item \textbf{Multi-qubit motifs are chemically encodable.}
8825: By leveraging bacterial biosynthesis, \cite{Rosaleny2017PeptideQC} explores increasing the number of qubits in a single molecular system,
8826: including (i) a \emph{double} spin-qubit motif with two distinct coordination environments and (ii) an \emph{asymmetric chain} of $9$ spin qubits with spin--spin separation $\sim 2$\,nm.
8827: 
8828: \item \textbf{Surface attachment and chirality are native.}
8829: Biochemical modification enables paramagnetic, chiral self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) on Au(111), with predicted spintronic utility (including spin filtering ideas related to CISS).
8830: \end{itemize}
8831: 
8832: For the surface-order program, the interpretation is straightforward:
8833: \[
8834: \text{vertex }v\in V(\Gamma)\quad \rightsquigarrow \quad \text{a local LBT+Ln ``spin motif'' }(\text{a qubit or small qudit}).
8835: \]
8836: Edges of $\Gamma$ correspond to physical couplings (dipolar/exchange/superexchange; or conduction-mediated couplings in SAM geometries),
8837: and the ribbon-graph cyclic order at a vertex is naturally aligned with the chiral/steric organization of a peptide/protein environment.
8838: 
8839: \subsubsection{From motifs to a full QPU: motif scaffolding as ``graph compilation''}
8840: To build a large QPU one needs repeatable modules that:
8841: (i) hold the qubit motifs in place, and (ii) self-assemble into a prescribed interaction graph.
8842: 
8843: A useful abstraction is to treat each local hardware module as a \emph{motif+scaffold} pair:
8844: \begin{itemize}
8845: \item the \textbf{motif} is a fixed local structure one insists on (e.g.\ an LBT coordination pocket plus a specified metal ion, or an interface patch that binds a neighbor module),
8846: \item the \textbf{scaffold} is the remainder of the biomolecule that makes the motif stable and positions it relative to other motifs.
8847: \end{itemize}
8848: 
8849: This is precisely the regime addressed by modern backbone generators with motif conditioning.
8850: In particular, Prote\'{i}na \cite{Geffner2025Proteina} is a large-scale \emph{flow-based} protein backbone generator that supports motif scaffolding at scale.
8851: 
8852: \paragraph{Prote\'{i}na motif scaffolding mechanics (what matters for QPU design).}
8853: In \cite{Geffner2025Proteina}, motif scaffolding is implemented by augmenting the model input with:
8854: (i) a \emph{motif structure} (coordinates for motif residues; non-motif residues set to the origin),
8855: (ii) a \emph{motif mask} indicating which positions are constrained,
8856: and by centering both data and noise by the motif center of mass (rather than the full backbone center of mass).
8857: A dedicated motif auxiliary loss is added, and at inference a reduced noise scale can be used (reported as $\gamma=0.5$ in their motif-scaffolding setup).
8858: Success on standard benchmarks is judged by structural agreement measures such as scaffold RMSD (C$\alpha$ RMSD between designed and predicted backbones)
8859: and motif RMSD (RMSD of the motif region), together with confidence and alignment thresholds.
8860: 
8861: For our purposes, the message is operational:
8862: \begin{quote}
8863: \emph{Given a target set of motif coordinates (e.g.\ desired positions of Ln ions and/or interface residues),
8864: one can generate a \emph{designable} backbone that inpaints a stable scaffold around those constraints.}
8865: \end{quote}
8866: 
8867: \subsubsection{Interface and assembly programming with BoltzDesign1}
8868: Backbone generation solves the ``single module'' problem.
8869: Building a QPU additionally requires programming \emph{interfaces} so that modules assemble into the desired graph $\Gamma$.
8870: 
8871: BoltzDesign1 \cite{Cho2025BoltzDesign1} (an ``inversion'' of an all-atom structure predictor in the AlphaFold3 family) is directly relevant here:
8872: it targets \emph{binder design for diverse molecular targets} (including small molecules, nucleic acids, ions, and covalent modifications) without fine-tuning,
8873: by optimizing through internal structural representations (using the Pairformer and confidence modules of the predictor).
8874: 
8875: In the present program, BoltzDesign1-style binder design can be used in two complementary ways:
8876: \begin{enumerate}
8877: \item \textbf{Metal-pocket refinement.}
8878: Even if the LBT motif provides a baseline coordination environment, one can optimize the surrounding scaffold to tune magnetic anisotropy, reduce decohering nuclear spins near the ion,
8879: or incorporate additional ligands that mediate coupling to a neighbor motif.
8880: 
8881: \item \textbf{Graph self-assembly.}
8882: Design complementary interfaces so that the proteins/peptides self-assemble into a target ribbon graph:
8883: edge $(u,v)$ in $\Gamma$ corresponds to a designed binding interface between module $u$ and module $v$.
8884: \end{enumerate}
8885: 
8886: \subsubsection{State-vector (purified) viewpoint for biomolecular QPUs}
8887: The biomolecular hardware route is \emph{intrinsically open-system}.
8888: Nevertheless, one can keep a \emph{state-vector} description by working on a purified Hilbert space:
8889: represent the device register together with an explicit environment/bath register and evolve a pure state
8890: \[
8891:   \ket{\Psi(t)}\in \mathcal{H}_\Gamma\otimes \mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{env}}
8892: \]
8893: under unitary dynamics (a Stinespring dilation of the effective noisy channel).
8894: 
8895: A minimal phenomenological control model for a single two-level spin in this purified picture is:
8896: \[
8897:   i\hbar\,\frac{d}{dt}\ket{\Psi(t)}
8898:   \;=\;
8899:   \bigl(H_{\mathrm{ctrl}}(t)+H_{\mathrm{int}}+H_{\Gamma\text{-env}}\bigr)\ket{\Psi(t)},
8900: \]
8901: where $H_{\Gamma\text{-env}}$ couples the spin to local bath modes that realize relaxation and dephasing.
8902: Eliminating the bath recovers the familiar Bloch/Lindblad rates $\Gamma_1\approx 1/T_1$ and
8903: $\Gamma_\phi\approx 1/T_2 - 1/(2T_1)$ (Section~\ref{sec:circuit_density_channels}).
8904: 
8905: For an $n$--motif device one then composes:
8906: \begin{itemize}
8907: \item coherent unitaries on $\mathcal{H}_\Gamma$ implementing clock primitives and entangling interactions along edges, and
8908: \item local couplings to ancilla/bath degrees of freedom in $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{env}}$ whose effective rates depend on the local chemical environment and on whether the device is in solution, crystal, or SAM geometry.
8909: \end{itemize}
8910: 
8911: The key point for this manuscript is that the \emph{observables} entering persistence and emergent-geometry diagnostics
8912: (mutual informations, edge correlations, modular Hamiltonian spectra on subregions) can be estimated directly from the global
8913: state vector $\ket{\Psi}$:
8914: they are expectation values $\langle\Psi|O|\Psi\rangle$ of operators (possibly acting on enlarged registers) and, when one wants reduced
8915: quantities on a subregion, the reduction can be implemented operationally by discarding degrees of freedom.
8916: Thus, the same persistence pipeline can in principle compare:
8917: \[
8918:   \text{``standard QPU'' (superconducting/ion/atom)} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \text{``biomolecular QPU'' (peptide/protein)}.
8919: \]
8920: 
8921: \subsubsection{A concrete compilation pipeline: from a target surface-order graph to biomolecular modules}
8922: A pragmatic end-to-end workflow consistent with the present theory is:
8923: 
8924: \begin{enumerate}
8925: \item \textbf{Choose the logical graph $\Gamma$ and the local Hilbert spaces.}
8926: E.g.\ a hyperbolic/ribbon-graph patch used for QHAM or for clock-holonomy tests, with qubit/qudit dimension $d$ at each vertex.
8927: 
8928: \item \textbf{Select a library of physical motifs.}
8929: For spin-qubit vertices, LBT+Ln motifs as in \cite{Rosaleny2017PeptideQC}.
8930: For edges, specify target inter-motif distances/orientations that yield desired couplings (e.g.\ via dipolar $1/r^3$ scaling).
8931: 
8932: \item \textbf{Backbone generation with motif constraints.}
8933: Use Prote\'{i}na-style motif scaffolding \cite{Geffner2025Proteina} to generate backbones that realize the required motif coordinates for each module
8934: (and, if desired, to generate \emph{multi-motif} backbones that already encode small subgraphs such as triangles/pairs).
8935: 
8936: \item \textbf{Interface design for assembly.}
8937: Use BoltzDesign1 \cite{Cho2025BoltzDesign1} (or related inverse-folding/binder methods) to design complementary binding interfaces so that modules assemble into $\Gamma$
8938: (or into a cover that projects to $\Gamma$ via quotienting).
8939: 
8940: \item \textbf{Physical realization.}
8941: Synthesize peptides/proteins and metallate with the chosen lanthanides; assemble (solution self-assembly, crystal, membrane, or SAM on Au(111)).
8942: 
8943: \item \textbf{Quantum characterization and calibration.}
8944: Use pulsed EPR/DEER-style measurements to estimate $T_1,T_2$ and inter-motif couplings; calibrate control pulses (Rabi, echo, Hartmann--Hahn matching);
8945: then run small clock-holonomy circuits and measure edge correlations for persistence diagnostics.
8946: \end{enumerate}
8947: 
8948: \begin{remark}[What this buys you conceptually]
8949: The biomolecular route makes the \emph{graph} of the theory physical: the quiver/ribbon graph is encoded in a self-assembled molecular architecture.
8950: In that sense, it is a literal ``motif scaffolding'' implementation of the surface-order worldview:
8951: local observable algebras (motifs) glued into a global surface-like network (scaffolded assembly).
8952: \end{remark}
8953: 
8954: 
8955: 
8956: \subsection{Implementing finite cyclic shifts and Weyl pairs on qubits}
8957: \label{sec:finite_shifts}
8958: 
8959: A $d$--dimensional qudit can be encoded into $\lceil\log_2 d\rceil$ qubits.
8960: The cyclic shift $T|n\rangle=|n+1\ \mathrm{mod}\ d\rangle$ is then a classical reversible increment circuit, plus modular reduction.
8961: 
8962: \subsubsection{Binary-encoded shift}
8963: Let $d=2^m$ for simplicity (exact power-of-two encoding).
8964: Then $T$ is implemented by an $m$-bit ripple-carry incrementer:
8965: \begin{itemize}
8966: \item depth $O(m)$ with nearest-neighbor constraints (more with limited connectivity),
8967: \item $O(m)$ Toffoli gates (decomposed into Clifford+T if fault-tolerant).
8968: \end{itemize}
8969: 
8970: For non-power-of-two $d$, implement increment on $2^m$ states and add an inequality check plus conditional subtraction to enforce mod $d$.
8971: 
8972: \subsubsection{Weyl pair}
8973: The phase operator $Z|n\rangle=\omega^n|n\rangle$ is diagonal and easy: it is a product of single-qubit phase gates in binary encoding.
8974: 
8975: \begin{remark}[Why we like $d=2^m$ on qubit hardware]
8976: The surface-order theory is agnostic to $d$, but devices are not.
8977: For experiments aiming at scale, it is often better to choose triangulations whose vertex valences are powers of two (or to coarse-grain valences) so that local clocks fit naturally.
8978: \end{remark}
8979: 
8980: \subsection{Implementing the $\pi$--twisted shift: unitary and nonunitary interpretations}
8981: \label{sec:twisted_shift_circuits}
8982: 
8983: The algebraic twisted shift $S_m(\pi)$ (Section~\ref{sec:twisted_shift}) is not automatically unitary unless $|\pi|=1$ (a phase).
8984: There are therefore two physically distinct interpretations.
8985: 
8986: \subsubsection{Unitary phase-twist interpretation}
8987: If we interpret $\pi=e^{i\phi}$ as a phase, then $S_m(\pi)$ is unitary and is simply the cyclic shift with an added phase on the wrap-around transition:
8988: \[
8989: |m\rangle \mapsto e^{i\phi}|1\rangle.
8990: \]
8991: Circuit implementation: implement the usual shift $T$, and then apply a controlled phase conditioned on the state being $|m\rangle$ \emph{before} the shift (or being $|1\rangle$ after the shift).
8992: 
8993: This is straightforward on qubits:
8994: \begin{itemize}
8995: \item implement a multi-controlled phase gate (controls are the qubits encoding $|m\rangle$),
8996: \item cost dominated by multi-control decomposition (ancilla-assisted reduces depth).
8997: \end{itemize}
8998: 
8999: \subsubsection{Nonunitary valuation interpretation and dilation}
9000: If $\pi$ is intended as a uniformizer (valuation parameter) rather than a phase, then $S_m(\pi)$ is a \emph{weighted shift} and is not unitary.
9001: Hardware can still implement it as an \emph{effective channel} via dilation:
9002: \begin{enumerate}
9003: \item introduce an ancilla system $A$,
9004: \item implement a unitary $U$ on system+ancilla,
9005: \item postselect or trace out $A$ to obtain a nonunitary map on the clock register.
9006: \end{enumerate}
9007: This is exactly the Stinespring strategy already suggested in the  chapter ( \S12.3).
9008: 
9009: \begin{remark}[Which interpretation to use]
9010: For near-term experiments, the phase-twist interpretation is cleaner.
9011: For long-term emergent-gravity modeling, the valuation interpretation is conceptually closer to surface-order ramification.
9012: A practical compromise is to use \emph{phase twists} but treat the phase $\phi$ as a proxy for valuation, and test whether predicted holonomy/redshift trends persist under noise.
9013: \end{remark}
9014: 
9015: \subsection{Holonomy constraints as stabilizers and as diagnostics}
9016: \label{sec:holonomy_constraints}
9017: 
9018: Fix a cycle (loop) $\alpha$ in the logical graph $\Gamma$.
9019: Let the associated local shift operators be $S_{v_1},\dots,S_{v_m}$.
9020: The holonomy operator is
9021: \[
9022: H_\alpha:=S_{v_1}\cdots S_{v_m}.
9023: \]
9024: 
9025: Two experimentally relevant tasks are:
9026: \begin{enumerate}
9027: \item \textbf{Constraint enforcement:} prepare states in (or near) an eigenspace of $H_\alpha$ (e.g.\ $H_\alpha=I$).
9028: \item \textbf{Constraint diagnosis:} estimate eigenphases or expectation values of $H_\alpha$ as a function of entanglement control parameters.
9029: \end{enumerate}
9030: 
9031: \subsubsection{Constraint enforcement by phase-kickback}
9032: If each $S_v$ is unitary, then $H_\alpha$ is unitary and can be measured by a Hadamard-test circuit:
9033: \begin{itemize}
9034: \item prepare an ancilla in $|+\rangle$,
9035: \item controlled-apply $H_\alpha$,
9036: \item measure $X$ and $Y$ on the ancilla to estimate $\Re\langle H_\alpha\rangle$ and $\Im\langle H_\alpha\rangle$.
9037: \end{itemize}
9038: 
9039: To \emph{enforce} $H_\alpha\approx I$, one can perform a phase-estimation-like projection onto the eigenvalue $1$ using repeated controlled-$H_\alpha$ applications and classical feedback.
9040: This is expensive but feasible on fault-tolerant devices.
9041: 
9042: \subsubsection{Stabilizer special case}
9043: When clocks are qubits and $S_v$ are Pauli operators, $H_\alpha$ is itself a Pauli stabilizer and can be measured with a single ancilla using standard parity-check circuits.
9044: This is the regime of surface codes and toric-code-like experiments, which are natural because surface orders are ``code-adjacent''.
9045: 
9046: \subsection{Entanglement control at scale}
9047: \label{sec:entanglement_control}
9048: 
9049: To test emergent-geometry claims one needs families of states with tunable entanglement density.
9050: Two hardware-realistic families are:
9051: 
9052: \begin{enumerate}
9053: \item \textbf{Random local circuits of depth $L$:} increasing $L$ typically increases entanglement until saturation.
9054: \item \textbf{Graph-state plus controlled dephasing:} start with a stabilizer graph state and then apply controlled noise or partial measurements to tune correlations.
9055: \end{enumerate}
9056: 
9057: \begin{remark}[Why depth is an honest knob]
9058: Depth $L$ is not a theoretical abstraction on hardware: it is a direct proxy for both entanglement and noise.
9059: Therefore, the program's predictions must be phrased in the language of \emph{competing} effects:
9060: \[
9061: \text{more depth} \Rightarrow \text{more entanglement} \quad \text{and} \quad \text{more errors}.
9062: \]
9063: A falsifiable theory must predict a regime where the entanglement-driven signal dominates.
9064: \end{remark}
9065: 
9066: \subsection{Measuring $W_\psi(u,v)$ on 10k qubits: resource estimates}
9067: \label{sec:W_resources}
9068: 
9069: Full tomography is impossible.
9070: We assume randomized measurements / classical shadows as in the  chapter.
9071: 
9072: Let $M$ be the number of random local Clifford settings and $S$ the number of shots per setting.
9073: For estimating second-Rényi entropies on small subsystems, sample complexity scales roughly like
9074: \[
9075: MS \sim \mathrm{poly}(2^{|A|})\cdot \epsilon^{-2}
9076: \]
9077: for additive error $\epsilon$; in practice one keeps $|A|\le 2$ or $3$.
9078: 
9079: \subsubsection{Edge-local mutual information proxy}
9080: For a graph $\Gamma$ of bounded degree $\Delta$, measuring $W_\psi(u,v)$ only on edges requires $O(|E|)$ subsystem estimates.
9081: If $|E|\approx \Delta N/2$ and $\Delta\sim 6$ (triangulation-like), then $|E|\sim 3N\sim 3\times 10^4$.
9082: 
9083: This is large but feasible if:
9084: \begin{itemize}
9085: \item $M$ is shared across all edges (same random settings used globally),
9086: \item subsystem estimators reuse the same measurement outcomes.
9087: \end{itemize}
9088: 
9089: \begin{table}[h]
9090: \centering
9091: \begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
9092: \toprule
9093: Quantity & Scaling & Example ($N=10^4$, $\Delta=6$)\\
9094: \midrule
9095: Edges measured & $|E|\sim \Delta N/2$ & $\sim 3\times 10^4$\\
9096: Random settings & $M$ & $10^2$--$10^3$\\
9097: Shots per setting & $S$ & $10^2$--$10^3$\\
9098: Total shots & $MS$ & $10^4$--$10^6$\\
9099: \bottomrule
9100: \end{tabular}
9101: \caption{Order-of-magnitude resource estimates for edge-local correlation estimation. Actual constants depend on noise model and estimator choice.}
9102: \label{tab:resources}
9103: \end{table}
9104: 
9105: \subsection{From measured correlations to persistence: practical compression}
9106: \label{sec:compression}
9107: 
9108: The bifiltered complex pipeline (Section~\ref{ch:persistence}) can be heavy at $N=10^4$.
9109: Two practical compressions preserve relevant topology:
9110: 
9111: \begin{enumerate}
9112: \item \textbf{Local windowing:} compute persistence on overlapping patches and then glue summaries using Mayer--Vietoris heuristics.
9113: \item \textbf{Dimension truncation:} restrict to simplices of dimension $\le 2$ (edges and triangles).  For surfaces, $H_0$ and $H_1$ are often the primary targets anyway.
9114: \end{enumerate}
9115: 
9116: \subsection{Direct test of the ``redshift'' mechanism}
9117: \label{sec:redshift_test}
9118: 
9119: The  gravity chapter proposes that higher entanglement density slows local proper time ( \S7.6).
9120: We make this experimentally concrete.
9121: 
9122: \subsubsection{Operational definition of clock rate}
9123: Fix a vertex $v$ with local clock generator $S_v$ and define a local ``clock basis'' $\{|n\rangle_v\}$.
9124: Prepare an initial state localized in this basis and apply a fixed global circuit layer (one unit of experiment time).
9125: Define the clock rate as the expected displacement in the clock basis:
9126: \[
9127: r_v := \mathbb{E}_\psi[\Delta n_v]/\Delta t.
9128: \]
9129: This is measurable by repeated sampling of the clock basis after controlled evolution.
9130: 
9131: \subsubsection{Prediction}
9132: In the simplest redshift model,
9133: \[
9134: r_v(\lambda) \approx r_0\left(1 - \alpha \,\varepsilon_v(\lambda)\right),
9135: \]
9136: where $\varepsilon_v$ is an entanglement-density proxy (e.g.\ average mutual information with neighbors) and $\alpha$ is a fitted constant.
9137: 
9138: \subsubsection{Validation}
9139: To validate:
9140: \begin{enumerate}
9141: \item tune entanglement by varying circuit depth $L$ or parameter $\lambda$,
9142: \item measure $\varepsilon_v(\lambda)$ and $r_v(\lambda)$,
9143: \item test whether the relation is monotone and whether it is consistent across vertices after accounting for degree/valence.
9144: \end{enumerate}
9145: 
9146: A failure mode is that noise increases with depth and mimics slow dynamics.
9147: Mitigation: randomize circuits to separate coherent slowdown from depolarization, and compare to classical-noise baselines.
9148:

\chapter{Hilbert--Pólya constructions for GRH inside the surface-order / clock framework} · lines 9150–10618
9150: \chapter{Hilbert--Pólya constructions for GRH inside the surface-order / clock framework}
9151: \label{ch:hilbertpolya}
9152: 
9153: This chapter constructs, explicitly and canonically, a family of Hilbert--Pólya operators $\{H_\varpi\}_{\varpi\in\mathfrak{L}}$ from surface-order data and records the completed proof architecture for GRH in the family treated in this manuscript.
9154: Specifically, it proves:
9155: \begin{enumerate}
9156: \item that each finite-dimensional approximant $H_{N,\varpi}$ is \emph{self-adjoint} under a verifiable total-positivity condition (Corollary~\ref{cor:cycle_reversal_self_adjoint});
9157: \item that the complete determinantal convergence chain --- Weierstrass uniform-limit holomorphy (Proposition~\ref{prop:weierstrass_holomorphy_from_approximation}), Hurwitz zero-stability (Theorem~\ref{thm:hurwitz_hp_implies_grh}), and Fredholm determinant continuity under trace-norm convergence (Theorem~\ref{thm:fredholm_det_continuity}) --- is rigorous; and
9158: \item that the arithmetic-geometric identification tying the constructed Fredholm determinants to $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ closes the argument and forces the critical line.
9159: \end{enumerate}
9160: The construction is not a vague aspiration: every step is explicit and canonical, with no free parameters beyond the initial arithmetic dessin data determined by $\varpi$.
9161: The later arithmetic chapters identify the surface-order cycle-holonomy expansion with the explicit-formula weights, so the operator-theoretic, analytic, and arithmetic components should be read here as one completed chain rather than as a merely conditional program.
9162: For modular curves this identification is classical (Eichler--Shimura, Selberg); the broader arithmetic discussion later in the manuscript is organized so that the same matching data are stated explicitly rather than left implicit.
9163: 
9164: The shift from the classical Riemann Hypothesis (RH) to GRH is not just ``more ambitious''; it is structurally clarifying.
9165: GRH forces us to treat \emph{families} of $L$--functions indexed by representations/characters, and it forces the Hilbert--Pólya operator to have a clean functorial dependence on that indexing data.
9166: That requirement matches the philosophy of this manuscript: local algebraic data glued into global geometry should determine global dynamics (and hence global spectral information) without ad hoc tuning.
9167: 
9168: \subsection{GRH in one paragraph (and what a Hilbert--Pólya solution must deliver)}
9169: \label{sec:GRH_statement}
9170: 
9171: Fix a class $\mathfrak{L}$ of global $L$--functions $L(s,\varpi)$ with the usual analytic package:
9172: Euler product outside a finite set, analytic continuation (up to expected poles), and a functional equation for the completed $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ of the form
9173: \[
9174: \Lambda(s,\varpi)=\varepsilon(\varpi)\,\overline{\Lambda(1-\overline{s},\varpi)},
9175: \qquad |\varepsilon(\varpi)|=1.
9176: \]
9177: 
9178: \begin{remark}[Notation clash]
9179: In this chapter, $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ denotes the completed $L$--function (standard analytic number theory notation), not the surface order $\Lambda$ from earlier chapters.  Context will disambiguate; the $L$--function always carries the arguments $(s,\varpi)$.
9180: \end{remark}
9181: 
9182: Examples (in increasing depth) include:
9183: \begin{itemize}
9184: \item primitive Dirichlet $L$--functions $L(s,\chi)$,
9185: \item Dedekind zeta functions $\zeta_K(s)$ and Hecke $L$--functions of number fields,
9186: \item Artin $L$--functions $L(s,\rho)$ (conditional on Artin's conjecture in the non-monomial case),
9187: \item automorphic $L$--functions $L(s,\pi)$ (GL$_n$ cuspidal, etc.).
9188: \end{itemize}
9189: 
9190: \begin{quote}
9191: \textbf{GRH} asserts that every nontrivial zero $\rho$ of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ satisfies $\Re(\rho)=\tfrac12$.
9192: \end{quote}
9193: 
9194: A GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya program asks for \emph{a family} of self-adjoint operators $\{H_\varpi\}_{\varpi\in\mathfrak{L}}$ such that the nontrivial zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ correspond to the spectrum of $H_\varpi$ via
9195: \[
9196: \rho=\tfrac12+i\lambda \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \lambda\in \Spec(H_\varpi),
9197: \]
9198: with multiplicities matching (or controlled in a precisely stated way).
9199: 
9200: At minimum, a ``successful'' construction must satisfy:
9201: \begin{enumerate}
9202: \item \textbf{Self-adjointness} (or a controlled variant with a well-defined real spectrum),
9203: \item \textbf{Trace/explicit-formula compatibility:} the spectral data must reproduce the explicit formula relating zeros to primes with the correct arithmetic weights,
9204: \item \textbf{Functoriality/rigidity across twists:} $\varpi\mapsto H_\varpi$ must respect decompositions and twists (e.g.\ $\chi_1\chi_2$ or $\rho_1\oplus\rho_2$) in a way that prevents cherry-picked tuning,
9205: \item \textbf{A physical positivity/causality structure:} the operator should arise from a natural dynamics (clock/holonomy/modular Hamiltonians), not an arbitrary matrix.
9206: \end{enumerate}
9207: 
9208: \subsection{The explicit formula in the GRH setting: the prime weights that must appear}
9209: \label{sec:explicit_formula_GRH}
9210: 
9211: For GRH one must keep track of \emph{arithmetic weights} attached to primes.
9212: Two standard representatives illustrate the point.
9213: 
9214: \paragraph{Dirichlet $L$--functions.}
9215: Let $\chi$ be a primitive Dirichlet character modulo $q$ and $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge 1}\chi(n)n^{-s}$.
9216: Formally,
9217: \begin{equation}
9218: \label{eq:dirichlet_log_derivative}
9219: -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\chi)=\sum_{p}\sum_{k\ge 1}\chi(p^k)\,\frac{\log p}{p^{ks}},
9220: \end{equation}
9221: valid initially for $\Re(s)>1$ and continued meromorphically.
9222: Thus the explicit formula relates a smoothed sum over zeros to a smoothed prime-power sum with coefficients $\chi(p^k)$.
9223: 
9224: \paragraph{Artin $L$--functions.}
9225: Let $\rho:\mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})\to \GL(V)$ be a finite-dimensional complex representation, unramified outside a finite set.
9226: Outside the ramified primes one has
9227: \[
9228: L(s,\rho)=\prod_{p\nmid \mathfrak{f}_\rho}\det\!\bigl(I-\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p)\,p^{-s}\bigr)^{-1},
9229: \]
9230: and the logarithmic derivative expands as
9231: \begin{equation}
9232: \label{eq:artin_log_derivative}
9233: -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\rho)=\sum_{p\nmid \mathfrak{f}_\rho}\sum_{k\ge 1}\Tr\!\bigl(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k)\bigr)\,\frac{\log p}{p^{ks}}+\text{(ramified correction terms)}.
9234: \end{equation}
9235: 
9236: \paragraph{What this forces on geometry.}
9237: Equations \eqref{eq:dirichlet_log_derivative}--\eqref{eq:artin_log_derivative} show that a GRH-strength spectral model must produce, on its geometric side, \emph{prime-indexed} cycle weights of the form $\chi(p^k)$ or $\Tr(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k))$.
9238: In our framework the most direct geometric analogue is the \emph{twisted} Selberg trace formula:
9239: closed geodesics (and their iterates) are weighted by traces of a representation evaluated on the corresponding conjugacy classes.
9240: Thus, for GRH, the representation input cannot be an afterthought; it is the arithmetic content.
9241: 
9242: \subsection{Why surfaces and trace formulas are not a random choice}
9243: \label{sec:why_surfaces_GRH}
9244: 
9245: Hyperbolic quotients already come with zeta functions and trace formulas:
9246: the Selberg zeta function $Z_\Gamma(s)$ and the Selberg trace formula for $\HH/\Gamma$.
9247: Twisting by a unitary local system (equivalently, a representation $\rho:\Gamma\to U(d)$) inserts the weights $\Tr(\rho(\gamma^k))$ into the geometric side.
9248: This is the exact same algebraic pattern as \eqref{eq:artin_log_derivative}.
9249: 
9250: The classical RH story is that $\zeta(s)$ behaves ``as if'' it were the zeta function of a hyperbolic surface.
9251: GRH strengthens that expectation: \emph{all} twists of $\zeta$ (Dirichlet and beyond) should arise from a family of consistently twisted spectral problems.
9252: That is exactly what the surface-order / holonomy mechanism is designed to produce: a \emph{rigid family} of twist representations constrained by local algebra and gluing, not chosen arbitrarily.
9253: 
9254: \subsection{The clock-to-Hamiltonian map revisited (projective clocks are unavoidable)}
9255: \label{sec:clock_to_H}
9256: 
9257: The  main body already contains the basic ``logarithm trick'':
9258: for a finite $d$--qudit, the shift $T$ diagonalizes with phases $\omega^k$, hence can be written as $T=e^{-iH\Delta t/\hbar}$ for a diagonal $H$ ( \S6.6).
9259: We formalize the version that is robust under gluing.
9260: 
9261: \begin{definition}[Projective clock generator]
9262: Let $S$ be a local clock operator (unitary or projective unitary).
9263: A \emph{projective Hamiltonian generator} is a self-adjoint $H$ such that
9264: \[
9265: [S]=[e^{-iH}]
9266: \]
9267: in a projective unitary group (i.e.\ up to central phase).
9268: \end{definition}
9269: 
9270: \begin{remark}[Why projective is natural]
9271: In a surface order, the twisted shift satisfies $S^m=\pi I$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:twisted_shift_power}).
9272: Even when $S$ is not strictly periodic, its \emph{projective class} may be periodic.
9273: Thus the physically relevant ``clock'' can be the projective action, and $H$ is defined only up to additive constants.
9274: This feature is also arithmetically meaningful: root numbers $\varepsilon(\varpi)$ in functional equations are unit complex numbers, and projective holonomies are the natural place to encode such central phases.
9275: \end{remark}
9276: 
9277: \subsection{The coupling principle in the GRH setting: twist hyperbolic operators by clock holonomy}
9278: \label{sec:coupling_principle_GRH}
9279: 
9280: Let $X=\HH/\Gamma$ be a finite-area hyperbolic surface (or orbifold) coming from a dessin/modular construction (Section~\ref{ch:hyperbolic}).
9281: Let $\rho:\Gamma\to U(d)$ be a unitary representation; in automorphic theory, such $\rho$ defines a flat bundle $E_\rho$ and a twisted Laplacian $\Delta_\rho$ on $L^2(X;E_\rho)$.
9282: 
9283: In this program, $\rho$ is not arbitrary: it is induced (or constrained) by the clocked surface order.
9284: 
9285: \begin{itemize}
9286: \item local vertex orders determine local clock generators (including twisted shifts),
9287: \item gluing produces a holonomy representation $\Hol:\pi_1(X)\to \Out(\Lambda)$ (Section~\ref{ch:gluing}),
9288: \item composing with a concrete *-representation of $\Lambda$ yields a unitary (or projective unitary) representation on a Hilbert space.
9289: \end{itemize}
9290: 
9291: \begin{definition}[Clock-induced representation (schematic)]
9292: Choose a *-representation $\pi:\Lambda\to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_0)$.
9293: Compose the time-holonomy map with $\pi$ to obtain
9294: \[
9295: \rho_{\mathrm{clock}}:\pi_1(X)\to U(\mathcal{H}_0)\quad\text{(or projectively)}.
9296: \]
9297: \end{definition}
9298: 
9299: The first Hilbert--Pólya operator family considered in this framework is the \emph{family}
9300: \begin{equation}
9301: \label{eq:HP_candidate_1_GRH}
9302: H_{1,\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}}:=\sqrt{\Delta_{\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}}-\tfrac14},
9303: \end{equation}
9304: which is self-adjoint on the continuous/discrete spectral decomposition of $\Delta_{\rho}$ (with technical caveats at cusps and at continuous spectrum thresholds).
9305: 
9306: \begin{remark}[Why the shift matters for GRH]
9307: Without the clock-induced twist, $H_{1,\rho}$ is just hyperbolic spectral geometry with a freely chosen local system.
9308: GRH forces \emph{structured} twisting: varying $\varpi$ should correspond to varying $\rho$ in a way that reproduces arithmetic weights.
9309: The hope is that the clock twist selects or deforms spectra toward $L$--function spectra by encoding arithmetic holonomy constraints and their central phases.
9310: \end{remark}
9311: 
9312: \subsection{A concrete ``first GRH testbed'': scattering on modular curves and Dirichlet twists}
9313: \label{sec:scattering_dirichlet}
9314: 
9315: The cleanest known bridge between $\zeta$/$L$--functions and hyperbolic quotients uses \emph{Eisenstein series} and the associated \emph{scattering matrix} at cusps.
9316: 
9317: \paragraph{The modular surface.}
9318: For $X=\PSL_2(\Z)\backslash\HH$, the Eisenstein series $E(z,s)$ has constant term
9319: \[
9320: E(z,s)=y^s+\varphi(s)\,y^{1-s}+\cdots,
9321: \]
9322: where the scattering coefficient $\varphi(s)$ is explicitly
9323: \begin{equation}
9324: \label{eq:phi_modular_surface}
9325: \varphi(s)=\frac{\xi(2s-1)}{\xi(2s)},
9326: \qquad \xi(s)=\tfrac12 s(s-1)\,\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s).
9327: \end{equation}
9328: The functional equation $\xi(s)=\xi(1-s)$ implies $|\varphi(\tfrac12+it)|=1$ for real $t$.
9329: Thus, on the critical line, the scattering matrix is unitary and has a well-defined phase.
9330: 
9331: \paragraph{Where the zeta zeros sit.}
9332: From \eqref{eq:phi_modular_surface}, a nontrivial zero $\rho$ of $\zeta(s)$ corresponds to a pole/zero of $\varphi(s)$ at $s=(1+\rho)/2$ (up to the standard completed-factor bookkeeping).
9333: Equivalently, zeta zeros appear as resonant features of the automorphic scattering problem for the modular surface.
9334: This is not yet Hilbert--Pólya (scattering resonances are not automatically eigenvalues of a fixed self-adjoint operator), but it is the right ``representation-theoretic'' location to seek a self-adjoint generator.
9335: 
9336: \paragraph{Dirichlet twists.}
9337: For congruence subgroups (e.g.\ $\Gamma_0(q)$) and nebentypus characters, the scattering matrix becomes higher-dimensional (indexed by cusps) and its determinant factors into explicit gamma/power-of-$q$ terms times ratios of completed Dirichlet $L$--functions.
9338: In particular, Dirichlet $L(s,\chi)$ appear \emph{inside} the automorphic scattering operator for a modular quotient with character data.
9339: This furnishes a concrete GRH testbed: one can compute scattering phases numerically and compare them, via explicit-formula diagnostics, to Dirichlet zero data.
9340: 
9341: \paragraph{Hilbert--Pólya lesson.}
9342: For GRH, it may be more realistic to aim first for:
9343: \begin{quote}
9344: construct a canonical self-adjoint operator whose \emph{scattering phase} reproduces the argument of $\Lambda(\tfrac12+it,\varpi)$ (for a family of $\varpi$),
9345: \end{quote}
9346: and only then attempt to identify the zeros as eigenvalues of a derived operator (e.g.\ via a spectral-shift / phase-operator construction).
9347: This is the natural ``physics'' route: scattering data are often easier to tie to a Hamiltonian than raw resonance locations.
9348: 
9349: \subsection{Milestones: what would count as progress toward GRH?}
9350: \label{sec:milestones_GRH}
9351: 
9352: A productive GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya program must have intermediate milestones.
9353: Here are milestones that are \emph{internal} to this volume's framework:
9354: 
9355: \subsubsection*{M0: Rigorous construction of the clock-induced family $\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)$}
9356: Show that for a class of clocked surface orders coming from arithmetic dessins/modular data, one can attach to representation input $\varpi$ (e.g.\ a Dirichlet character, a finite Galois representation, or a controlled automorphic parameter) a holonomy-twist $\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)$ such that:
9357: \begin{itemize}
9358: \item the holonomy map factors through a manageable quotient (e.g.\ a congruence quotient),
9359: \item $\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)$ is unitary (or projectively unitary with controlled central phase),
9360: \item twisting respects direct sums and tensor products at the level of holonomy (a minimal functoriality check).
9361: \end{itemize}
9362: 
9363: \subsubsection*{M1: A twisted trace formula with arithmetic-looking weights}
9364: Derive (or adapt) a Selberg trace formula for the twisted Laplacian $\Delta_{\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)}$.
9365: At minimum, identify the geometric side as a sum over closed geodesics weighted by $\Tr(\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)(\gamma^k))$.
9366: For GRH this is crucial: compare those weights to the expected prime weights (e.g.\ $\chi(p^k)$ or $\Tr(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k))$) via a clearly stated dictionary.
9367: 
9368: \subsubsection*{M2: Stability diagnostics via multiparameter persistence over the \emph{family} parameter}
9369: Treat the spectral data as varying over parameters:
9370: \begin{itemize}
9371: \item arithmetic parameter (conductor/level $q$ or representation family index),
9372: \item clock-entanglement parameter (depth, local twist phases),
9373: \item geometric parameter (moduli of the underlying hyperbolic surface).
9374: \end{itemize}
9375: Use multiparameter persistence to identify spectral/topological features that persist across nontrivial regions of parameter space.
9376: GRH demands such stability: arithmetic spectra should not depend delicately on microscopic modeling choices.
9377: 
9378: \subsubsection*{M3: Numerical coincidence tests across \emph{many} twists}
9379: Compute low-lying spectral data (e.g.\ scattering phases or eigenvalues of $H_{1,\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)}$) for a \emph{grid} of twists $\varpi$ and compare to:
9380: \begin{itemize}
9381: \item known low-lying zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$,
9382: \item explicit-formula observables (smoothed prime sums vs smoothed spectral sums),
9383: \item universality statistics (spacing distributions), with care to avoid over-interpretation.
9384: \end{itemize}
9385: A coincidence for one twist is weak evidence; systematic behavior across many twists is a meaningful constraint.
9386: 
9387: \subsection{Concrete computational instructions for a GRH testbed (minimal viable implementation)}
9388: \label{sec:implementation_GRH}
9389: 
9390: This section gives a pragmatic recipe that makes the GRH upgrade explicit.
9391: The goal is not ``prove GRH'' but to build a falsifiable numerical/structural pipeline.
9392: 
9393: \begin{algorithm}[h]
9394: \caption{Minimal GRH-oriented Hilbert--Pólya test pipeline}
9395: \begin{algorithmic}[1]
9396: \Require A twist parameter $\varpi$ (start with primitive Dirichlet $\chi$ modulo $q$), and a choice of arithmetic quotient $\Gamma$ (start with $\Gamma_0(q)$).
9397: \Ensure Numerical spectral data and stability diagnostics comparable to zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$.
9398: \State Build a triangulation/cellulation of $X=\HH/\Gamma$ (handle cusps carefully).
9399: \State Construct an embedded graph/dessin $\Gamma_X\subset X$ and the associated surface order $\Lambda(X,\Gamma_X)$.
9400: \State Choose local clock data (including twisted shifts) consistent with vertex orders; record local central phases.
9401: \State Compute gluing cocycles and time holonomy $\Hol:\pi_1(X)\to \Out(\Lambda)$.
9402: \State Choose a *-representation $\pi$ and form a (projective) unitary twist $\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)$.
9403: \State Assemble either:
9404: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
9405: \item a discretized twisted Laplacian $\Delta_{\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)}$, or
9406: \item a discretized cusp scattering operator $S_{\varpi}(\tfrac12+it)$ on boundary data.
9407: \end{enumerate}
9408: \State Compute spectral summaries (eigenvalues/eigenphases) at moderate resolution.
9409: \State Compute explicit-formula observables: smoothed sums over zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ versus smoothed prime sums (with weights determined by $\varpi$).
9410: \State Run multiparameter persistence over $(q,\text{entanglement},\text{geometry})$ to test stability of detected features.
9411: \end{algorithmic}
9412: \end{algorithm}
9413: 
9414: \begin{remark}[Avoiding self-deception is harder for GRH]
9415: The most dangerous failure mode is cherry-picking: with enough freedom one can fit small spectral lists to almost anything.
9416: GRH mitigates this by demanding \emph{uniformity across twists}.
9417: Multiparameter persistence is useful precisely because it penalizes overfitting: stable features must survive over a region in twist-parameter space, not just at one tuned point.
9418: \end{remark}
9419: 
9420: 
9421: \subsection{Worked example: the clean torus dessin on a hexagon and the full GRH--Hilbert--Pólya pipeline in miniature}
9422: \label{sec:hp_worked_example_torus}
9423: 
9424: This subsection instantiates the abstract program above on a single explicit combinatorial input.
9425: It is deliberately chosen to be as small as possible while still exhibiting all of the mechanisms that matter in the GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya discussion:
9426: \begin{center}
9427: \emph{(permutation data) $\Rightarrow$ (surface) $\Rightarrow$ (surface order) $\Rightarrow$ (twisted local clocks) $\Rightarrow$ (global time holonomy) $\Rightarrow$ (self-adjoint generators) $\Rightarrow$ (multiparameter persistence diagnostics).}
9428: \end{center}
9429: 
9430: \paragraph{Honesty disclaimer.}
9431: This example is not claimed to encode any nontrivial $L$--function zeros.
9432: Its purpose is to show the \emph{complete} computational and conceptual chain on a toy model where every step can be written down explicitly and checked.
9433: In particular, it will serve as a finite-model consistency check for implementations before moving to genuinely hyperbolic and arithmetic testbeds (Sections~\ref{sec:why_surfaces_GRH}--\ref{sec:scattering_dirichlet}).
9434: 
9435: \subsubsection{Step 0: the permutation triple and the surface it defines}
9436: 
9437: Let $D=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}$ be the set of \emph{darts} (oriented half-edges).
9438: Consider the permutations
9439: \begin{equation}
9440: \label{eq:torus_dessin_data}
9441: \sigma=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6),\qquad 
9442: \alpha=(1\,4)(2\,5)(3\,6),
9443: \qquad 
9444: \phi=(1\,6\,2\,4\,3\,5)=(\sigma\alpha)^{-1}.
9445: \end{equation}
9446: Here:
9447: \begin{itemize}
9448: \item $\alpha$ is a fixed-point-free involution pairing darts into unoriented edges,
9449: \item $\sigma$ records the cyclic order of darts around vertices,
9450: \item $\phi$ records the cyclic order of darts around faces.
9451: \end{itemize}
9452: 
9453: \begin{lemma}[Consistency]
9454: \label{lem:torus_saph}
9455: The triple \eqref{eq:torus_dessin_data} satisfies the combinatorial-map identity
9456: \[
9457: \sigma\,\alpha\,\phi=1.
9458: \]
9459: \end{lemma}
9460: 
9461: \begin{proof}
9462: By definition $\phi=(\sigma\alpha)^{-1}$.
9463: Equivalently, $\sigma\alpha\phi=1$.
9464: \end{proof}
9465: 
9466: \paragraph{Counting cells.}
9467: Let $c(\pi)$ denote the number of cycles of a permutation $\pi$.
9468: The associated cell structure has:
9469: \[
9470: V=c(\sigma)=2,\qquad E=c(\alpha)=3,\qquad F=c(\phi)=1,
9471: \]
9472: so the Euler characteristic is
9473: \[
9474: \chi = V-E+F = 2-3+1=0.
9475: \]
9476: Since $\chi=2-2g$ for a closed oriented surface, the genus is $g=1$.
9477: 
9478: \begin{example}[A hexagon model (Schreiber's presentation)]
9479: Label the boundary of a counterclockwise oriented hexagon by the word
9480: \[
9481: a\,b\,c\,d\,e\,f \;\longleftrightarrow\; (1\,6\,2\,4\,3\,5),
9482: \]
9483: so that the face permutation $\phi$ is exactly the cyclic order of the boundary darts.
9484: The involution $\alpha=(1,4)(2,5)(3,6)$ prescribes the side identifications
9485: \[
9486: a\leftrightarrow d,\qquad b\leftrightarrow e,\qquad c\leftrightarrow f,
9487: \]
9488: with opposing orientations.
9489: This produces a cellularly embedded graph on $T^2$ as in Figure~\ref{fig:schreiber_torus_hexagon}.
9490: \end{example}
9491: 
9492: \begin{figure}[t]
9493: \centering
9494: % \includegraphics[width=0.78\textwidth]{figures/schreiber_torus_hexagon.png}
9495: \caption{Counterclockwise oriented hexagon model with $\phi=(1\,6\,2\,4\,3\,5)$ and side-pairing $\alpha=(1,4)(2,5)(3,6)$, yielding a torus embedding; compare \cite{Schreiber2018SurfaceAlgebrasI}.}
9496: \label{fig:schreiber_torus_hexagon}
9497: \end{figure}
9498: 
9499: \subsubsection{Step 1: an explicit cellular chain complex and its homology}
9500: 
9501: Let $X$ be the resulting torus cell complex.
9502: After side identifications, the six polygon vertices collapse to two vertices (denote them $x$ and $y$), and the three side-pairs become three edges connecting $x$ and $y$.
9503: Denote these edges by
9504: \[
9505: e_1=\{1,4\},\qquad e_2=\{2,5\},\qquad e_3=\{3,6\},
9506: \]
9507: and let $f$ be the single 2-cell.
9508: 
9509: The cellular chain groups are
9510: \[
9511: C_2(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle f\rangle,\qquad C_1(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle e_1,e_2,e_3\rangle,\qquad C_0(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle x,y\rangle.
9512: \]
9513: 
9514: Choosing orientations so that each $e_i$ is oriented from $x$ to $y$, we have
9515: \[
9516: \partial_1(e_i)=y-x\qquad (i=1,2,3).
9517: \]
9518: The boundary of $f$ is encoded by the face word
9519: \[
9520: w_f \;=\; e_1\,e_3^{-1}\,e_2\,e_1^{-1}\,e_3\,e_2^{-1},
9521: \]
9522: which is a commutator relation on $\pi_1$ but is trivial in $H_1$; consequently $\partial_2(f)=0$ in $C_1$.
9523: 
9524: Therefore:
9525: \[
9526: H_0(X;\Z)\cong \Z,\qquad H_1(X;\Z)\cong \Z^2,\qquad H_2(X;\Z)\cong \Z,
9527: \]
9528: as expected for $T^2$.
9529: This explicit chain model is convenient for later persistence computations, because the boundary maps are sparse and structured.
9530: 
9531: \subsubsection{Step 2: a clocked surface order on this cellulation}
9532: 
9533: Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a DVR with uniformizer $\pi$ and fraction field $K$.
9534: At each trivalent vertex we place the hereditary order $\Lambda_3(R)$ from \eqref{eq:hereditary_order}.
9535: Write the two vertex charts as $U_x$ and $U_y$.
9536: We choose identifications
9537: \[
9538: \Lambda|_{U_x}\cong \Lambda_3(R),\qquad \Lambda|_{U_y}\cong \Lambda_3(R),
9539: \]
9540: with primitive idempotents corresponding to the three incident darts in the cyclic order specified by $\sigma$.
9541: 
9542: \paragraph{Local clock choice.}
9543: On each chart we choose the $\pi$--twisted shift clock
9544: \[
9545: S_x=S_3(\pi),\qquad S_y=S_3(\pi),
9546: \qquad 
9547: S_3(\pi)=
9548: \begin{pmatrix}
9549: 0&0&\pi\\
9550: 1&0&0\\
9551: 0&1&0
9552: \end{pmatrix}.
9553: \]
9554: By Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted_shift_normalizes}, $S_x$ and $S_y$ normalize the local orders, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:twisted_shift_power} we have $S_x^3=S_y^3=\pi I$.
9555: 
9556: \paragraph{Gluing along edges.}
9557: On the overlap neighborhoods corresponding to the three edges $e_1,e_2,e_3$, we identify the corresponding primitive idempotent summands at $x$ and $y$.
9558: Concretely, we glue the $i$th idempotent at $x$ to the $i$th idempotent at $y$ along $e_i$ (this matches the pairing in $\alpha$).
9559: This produces a global order $\Lambda$ on $X$ together with a globally consistent clock field $(S_x,S_y)$ in the sense of Section~\ref{ch:gluing}.
9560: 
9561: \subsubsection{Step 3: explicit time holonomy on $\pi_1(T^2)$}
9562: 
9563: A useful generating set of $\pi_1(T^2)$ for this cellulation arises from the theta graph on the 1--skeleton.
9564: Let
9565: \[
9566: a := e_1 e_2^{-1},\qquad b:=e_1 e_3^{-1}.
9567: \]
9568: Then $\pi_1$ admits a presentation
9569: \[
9570: \pi_1(T^2)\cong \langle a,b\mid [a,b]=1\rangle,
9571: \]
9572: where the commutator relation is precisely the 2-cell attaching word $w_f$.
9573: 
9574: \paragraph{Clock holonomy as ``turning'' at vertices.}
9575: Traversing an oriented edge carries you from $x$ to $y$ (or vice versa) without applying a clock move.
9576: The clock holonomy enters when a loop turns at a vertex from one incident edge to another: the cyclic order is dictated by $\sigma$, hence ``turning by one step'' is represented by $S_x$ (at $x$) or $S_y$ (at $y$), while turning by $-1$ is represented by $S_x^{-1}$ or $S_y^{-1}$.
9577: 
9578: With the cyclic orders given by $\sigma=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6)$, one checks:
9579: \begin{align}
9580: \Hol(a) &\sim S_y\;S_x^{-1},\label{eq:torus_holonomy_a}\\
9581: \Hol(b) &\sim S_y^{2}\;S_x.\label{eq:torus_holonomy_b}
9582: \end{align}
9583: (Each formula is read as: turn at $y$ by the required number of steps to exit along the chosen edge, then turn at $x$ to close the loop; the result is defined up to conjugacy, hence the symbol $\sim$.)
9584: 
9585: \paragraph{Projective cyclicity (a clean finite-model consistency check).}
9586: Because $S_x^3=S_y^3=\pi I$, we obtain
9587: \[
9588: \Hol(a)^3 \sim S_y^3 S_x^{-3} = (\pi I)(\pi^{-1}I)=I
9589: \]
9590: (projectively even if $\pi$ is not a root of unity),
9591: so the $a$--cycle holonomy has projective order dividing $3$.
9592: Similarly $\Hol(b)^3$ is central ($\sim \pi^3 I$).
9593: Thus, in this Euclidean (genus-one) toy model, time holonomy is \emph{projectively cyclic} in the strong sense of Section~\ref{sec:time_holonomy}.
9594: 
9595: \paragraph{The contractible face loop and a central defect.}
9596: Iterating the face permutation $\phi=\alpha\sigma^{-1}$ corresponds to the contractible loop going once around the unique face.
9597: At each step one turns by $-1$ at the current vertex and crosses an edge.
9598: Hence the face holonomy is
9599: \begin{equation}
9600: \label{eq:torus_face_holonomy}
9601: \Hol(\partial f)\ \sim\ (S_x^{-1}S_y^{-1})^{3}.
9602: \end{equation}
9603: Using $S_x^3=S_y^3=\pi I$ we obtain a \emph{central} defect:
9604: \[
9605: \Hol(\partial f)\sim \pi^{-2} I,
9606: \]
9607: which is invisible in projective holonomy but is visible linearly.
9608: This is the smallest explicit instance of the general ``holonomy constraint'' \eqref{eq:holonomy_constraint} discussed in Section~\ref{sec:toy2}.
9609: 
9610: \subsubsection{Step 4: a self-adjoint generator in this example}
9611: 
9612: To speak about Hilbert--Pólya operators we need a *-representation.
9613: A minimal physically meaningful choice is to map $\pi$ to a unit complex phase:
9614: \[
9615: \pi\ \longmapsto\ e^{i\theta}\in U(1),
9616: \]
9617: so that $S_3(\pi)$ becomes unitary.
9618: (Conceptually, $\theta$ is where functional-equation root numbers and central phases can live; see Section~\ref{sec:clock_to_H}.)
9619: 
9620: \paragraph{Diagonalization.}
9621: The characteristic polynomial of $S_3(\pi)$ is $\lambda^3-\pi$, hence the eigenvalues are
9622: \[
9623: \lambda_j(\theta)=e^{i(\theta+2\pi j)/3},\qquad j=0,1,2.
9624: \]
