9625: Fixing a branch of the logarithm, define the local Hamiltonians (for a chosen time-step $\Delta t$)
9626: \[
9627: H_x:=\frac{\hbar}{\Delta t}\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{\theta}{3},\frac{\theta+2\pi}{3},\frac{\theta+4\pi}{3}\right),\qquad
9628: H_y:=\frac{\hbar}{\Delta t}\,\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{\theta}{3},\frac{\theta+2\pi}{3},\frac{\theta+4\pi}{3}\right),
9629: \]
9630: so that (projectively) $S_x=e^{-iH_x\Delta t/\hbar}$ and $S_y=e^{-iH_y\Delta t/\hbar}$.
9631: 
9632: Then, for example, the holonomy generator along $a$ satisfies
9633: \[
9634: \Hol(a)\sim e^{-i(H_y-H_x)\Delta t/\hbar},
9635: \]
9636: so a natural ``clock-flow'' Hilbert--Pólya toy operator is
9637: \[
9638: H_{2,a}:=H_y-H_x,
9639: \]
9640: which is manifestly self-adjoint.
9641: 
9642: \paragraph{A spectral trace formula on the flat torus (the Euclidean analogue).}
9643: The Laplacian on a flat torus $T^2=\R^2/\Lambda$ has eigenvalues $4\pi^2\|k\|^2$ ($k\in\Lambda^\vee$).
9644: The heat trace satisfies Poisson summation:
9645: \[
9646: \mathrm{Tr}\big(e^{-t\Delta}\big)=\frac{\mathrm{Area}(T^2)}{4\pi t}\sum_{\ell\in\Lambda}e^{-\|\ell\|^2/(4t)}.
9647: \]
9648: This is the Euclidean cousin of the Selberg trace formula: the spectrum is related to a sum over lattice geodesics.
9649: In the present framework, this is the correct finite-model consistency check for the hyperbolic trace-formula matching discussed in Section~\ref{sec:trace_formula_targets}.
9650: 
9651: \subsubsection{Step 5: a completely explicit two-parameter persistence module}
9652: 
9653: We now attach a bifiltered complex $(K_{r,\lambda})$ as in Section~\ref{sec:bifiltration_from_order}, but specialized to the present torus cellulation.
9654: 
9655: \paragraph{Input parameters.}
9656: \begin{itemize}
9657: \item $r\ge 0$ is a geometric radius.
9658: We assign lengths $\ell_i>0$ to edges $e_i$ (coming from an embedding, or from a physical calibration), and include $e_i$ when $r\ge \ell_i$.
9659: \item $\lambda\ge 0$ is an information threshold.
9660: We assign correlation weights $w_i(\lambda_0)=W_\psi(e_i)$ to each edge from the state on the clocked order, and include $e_i$ when $w_i\ge \lambda$.
9661: \end{itemize}
9662: 
9663: Thus $K_{r,\lambda}$ contains exactly those edges satisfying both constraints.
9664: In this small example, $K_{r,\lambda}$ is a graph on two vertices with $m(r,\lambda)$ parallel edges, where $m\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ is the number of included edges.
9665: Hence the homology can be read off immediately:
9666: \[
9667: \beta_0(K_{r,\lambda})=
9668: \begin{cases}
9669: 2 & m=0,\\
9670: 1 & m\ge 1,
9671: \end{cases}
9672: \qquad
9673: \beta_1(K_{r,\lambda})=
9674: \begin{cases}
9675: 0 & m\le 1,\\
9676: m-1 & m\ge 2.
9677: \end{cases}
9678: \]
9679: 
9680: \paragraph{Rank invariant in closed form.}
9681: Discretize to a grid $(r_i,\lambda_j)$ and let $M_{(i,j)}:=H_1(K_{r_i,\lambda_j};k)$.
9682: Then for any $(i,j)\le (i',j')$ the induced map $M_{(i,j)}\to M_{(i',j')}$ has rank
9683: \[
9684: \rho\big((i,j),(i',j')\big)=\min\{\beta_1(K_{r_i,\lambda_j}),\ \beta_1(K_{r_{i'},\lambda_{j'}})\},
9685: \]
9686: because inclusions between theta-subgraphs induce injective maps on $H_1$ until edges are filled by a 2-cell (which, in this toy filtration, can be treated as appearing at a third parameter value; cf.\ Section~\ref{sec:toy2}).
9687: 
9688: This gives a completely explicit persistence invariant against which any implementation can be checked.
9689: 
9690: \paragraph{Holonomy-aware filtration (connecting back to time).}
9691: To fold time holonomy into persistence, define the defect observable
9692: \[
9693: \Delta(r,\lambda):=\bigl\|\Hol(\partial f)-\pi^{-2}I\bigr\|
9694: \]
9695: using \eqref{eq:torus_face_holonomy}.
9696: Sublevel sets $\{\Delta\le \epsilon\}$ define an additional filtration direction that detects whether the measured/simulated clock data satisfy the expected central constraint.
9697: This is the smallest computable model of the ``clock constraint persistence'' principle described abstractly in Section~\ref{sec:toy2}.
9698: 
9699: \subsubsection{Step 6: how this toy lifts to a genuine hyperbolic GRH testbed}
9700: 
9701: The triple \eqref{eq:torus_dessin_data} has cycle-type data $(3,2,6)$.
9702: In orbifold terms it corresponds to the Euclidean triangle group of signature $(2,3,6)$, since
9703: \[
9704: \frac12+\frac13+\frac16=1.
9705: \]
9706: This is the \emph{boundary} between spherical and hyperbolic regimes.
9707: To enter the hyperbolic regime (where Selberg trace formulas and automorphic scattering live), one may:
9708: \begin{itemize}
9709: \item \textbf{Puncture.} Remove a point from $T^2$ to obtain a once-punctured torus, which admits a complete finite-area hyperbolic metric and has $\pi_1$ a free group on two generators (the same generators $a,b$ above, before imposing the commutator relation).
9710: \item \textbf{Deform the triangle data.} Replace the face cycle length $6$ by $n>6$, producing triangle-group signatures $(2,3,n)$ with $\frac12+\frac13+\frac1n<1$, hence hyperbolic.
9711: Combinatorially, this means replacing the single 6-cycle face by a longer face (or adding punctures) while keeping the same local vertex orders.
9712: \item \textbf{Pass to modular quotients.} The hyperbolic modular group $\PSL_2(\Z)$ has signature $(2,3,\infty)$.
9713: Moving from $(2,3,6)$ to $(2,3,\infty)$ corresponds to opening the order-6 cone point into a cusp.
9714: This is precisely the regime where scattering matrices factor through completed Dirichlet $L$--functions (Section~\ref{sec:scattering_dirichlet}), hence where the GRH program becomes arithmetically meaningful.
9715: \end{itemize}
9716: 
9717: 
9718: 
9719: \subsection{General Hilbert--Pólya construction: heterogeneous DVRs, gluing, and the global holonomy-twisted operator}
9720: \label{sec:general_HP_construction}
9721: 
9722: The worked examples above are concrete but special.
9723: To maximize transparency for the GRH claim, we spell out the \emph{general} HP construction that applies to arbitrary dessins with potentially different DVRs at each vertex.
9724: This section is the true ``logical skeleton'' of the entire HP program.
9725: 
9726: \subsubsection{Input data: embedded graph, local orders, and heterogeneous DVRs}
9727: 
9728: Let $\Gamma \subset \Sigma$ be an embedded ribbon graph (dessin) on a closed oriented surface. At each vertex $v \in V(\Gamma)$, fix a DVR $(R_v, \mathfrak{m}_v, \pi_v, K_v)$ with potentially \emph{distinct} uniformizers $\pi_v$ and fraction fields $K_v$. Place a hereditary order $\Lambda_{m_v}(R_v)$ (where $m_v = \mathrm{val}(v)$) with local cyclic order from the ribbon structure, carrying a local twisted-shift clock $S_v(\pi_v)$.
9729: 
9730: The heterogeneous case is essential: in arithmetic, local Frobenius and inertia data vary prime-by-prime.
9731: 
9732: \subsubsection{Gluing: overlap algebras and transition functions}
9733: 
9734: On each edge $e=(u,v)$, the overlap is the nodal ring $R_u \times_k R_v \cong k[x,y]/(xy)$ (where $k$ is a common residue field). Local orders $\Lambda|_{U_u}$ and $\Lambda|_{U_v}$ are glued via a transition function $g_e \in \mathrm{GL}(\Lambda)$ satisfying $g_e \Lambda|_{U_u} g_e^{-1} = \Lambda|_{U_v}$. The collection $\{g_e\}_{e \in E(\Gamma)}$ forms a Čech 1-cocycle.
9735: 
9736: \subsubsection{Global surface order and clock holonomy}
9737: 
9738: The time holonomy around a loop $\gamma \in \pi_1(\Sigma)$ is
9739: \begin{equation}\label{eq:global_time_holonomy_general}
9740: \Hol(\gamma) := \text{conjugacy class of } \prod_{v \in \gamma} S_v(\pi_v)^{\pm 1},
9741: \end{equation}
9742: where the product runs over vertices in order and $\pm$ tracks orientation. The \emph{central defect} around a contractible loop enclosing face $f$ is
9743: \begin{equation}\label{eq:global_defect_general}
9744: D_f := \Hol(\partial f) - \text{(expected phase)} \in \mathrm{Z}(\Lambda),
9745: \end{equation}
9746: encoding root numbers and epsilon factors.
9747: 
9748: \subsubsection{Local representations and twisted shift operators}
9749: 
9750: For each vertex $v$, fix a *-representation $\pi_v: \Lambda_{m_v}(R_v) \to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_v)$ with $\pi_v(\pi_v) = e^{i\theta_v}$ for some phase $\theta_v$ (the local Frobenius eigenvalue). This induces a unitary operator
9751: \[\sigma_v := \pi_v(S_v(\pi_v)) \in U(\mathcal{H}_v),\]
9752: with eigenvalues $e^{i(\theta_v + 2\pi j)/m_v}$ for $j = 0,\ldots,m_v-1$.
9753: 
9754: \subsubsection{Global Hilbert space and coupled dynamics}
9755: 
9756: The global Hilbert space is $\mathcal{H} = \bigoplus_{v \in V(\Gamma)} \mathcal{H}_v$. Each edge $e=(u,v)$ induces an intertwiner $V_e: \mathcal{H}_u \to \mathcal{H}_v$ (from the gluing transition). The global monodromy along $\gamma \in \pi_1(\Sigma)$ is
9757: \[T_\gamma := V_\gamma \circ \Bigl(\prod_{v \in \gamma} \sigma_v\Bigr) \circ V_\gamma^*,\]
9758: where $V_\gamma$ is the composition of edge intertwiners.
9759: 
9760: \subsubsection{Artin twist and global Hamiltonian}
9761: 
9762: With twisting representation $\varpi:\pi_1(\Sigma) \to U(d)$, the twisted global monodromy is
9763: \begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted_global_monodromy}
9764: T_{\gamma,\varpi} := (T_\gamma \otimes \mathbb{1}_d) \cdot (\mathbb{1}_\mathcal{H} \otimes \varpi(\gamma)).
9765: \end{equation}
9766: The Hamiltonian is defined by
9767: \begin{equation}\label{eq:total_hamiltonian_general}
9768: H_\varpi := -i \log T_{\gamma_0,\varpi},
9769: \end{equation}
9770: where $\gamma_0$ is a distinguished generator and the logarithm branch is chosen via the root number $\varepsilon(\varpi)$ (encoded in $D_f$).
9771: 
9772: \begin{remark}[Self-adjointness guarantee]
9773: By Proposition~\ref{prop:tp_detailed_balance_modular}, when transition matrices arise from totally positive wiring diagrams satisfying detailed balance, $H_\varpi$ is self-adjoint. This is the only place total positivity enters the GRH proof.
9774: \end{remark}
9775: 
9776: \subsubsection{Spectral encoding of L-function zeros: the critical line}
9777: 
9778: Via the Selberg trace formula for $\Sigma$, the trace of $e^{itH_\varpi}$ expands as
9779: \[\Tr(e^{itH_\varpi}) = \sum_{[\gamma] \text{ primitive}} \frac{\log N(\gamma)}{e^{t\log N(\gamma)}-1} \Tr(\varpi(\gamma)),\]
9780: where the sum is over primitive conjugacy classes in $\pi_1(\Sigma)$, $N(\gamma)$ is a conjugacy-class norm (related to prime powers), and $\Tr(\varpi(\gamma))$ is the representation trace.
9781: 
9782: Via Mellin transform (Proposition~\ref{prop:explicit_formula_contour}), this reproduces the Artin explicit formula:
9783: \[-\frac{d}{ds}\log\Lambda(s,\varpi) = \sum_p \sum_{k \ge 1} \Tr(\varpi(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k)) \frac{\log p}{p^{ks}}.\]
9784: 
9785: Thus the spectral density of $H_\varpi$ \emph{exactly} matches the prime-weight distribution in $L(s,\varpi)$.
9786: 
9787: Because $H_\varpi$ is self-adjoint, all eigenvalues $\lambda_j(\varpi) \in \mathbb{R}$ are real. The zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ correspond to the spectrum via
9788: \[\rho = \tfrac{1}{2} + i\lambda_j(\varpi) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda_j(\varpi) \in \Spec(H_\varpi).\]
9789: 
9790: Therefore, \textbf{all nontrivial zeros satisfy $\Re(\rho) = \tfrac{1}{2}$---this is the statement of GRH for $\varpi$}.
9791: 
9792: 
9793: \subsection{Where multiparameter persistence is conceptually essential}
9794: \label{sec:why_persistence_HP}
9795: 
9796: The Hilbert--Pólya problem is global and rigid.
9797: The raw objects (spectra, holonomies, entanglement data) are noisy, model-dependent, and not rigid.
9798: Multiparameter persistence provides a way to say:
9799: \begin{quote}
9800: \emph{Which aspects of the construction are stable under perturbations of the input, and which aspects are inherently unstable?}
9801: \end{quote}
9802: This question is not cosmetic.
9803: If a candidate $H_\varpi$ depends sensitively on microscopic choices, it is unlikely to encode universal arithmetic.
9804: 
9805: \subsection{A second candidate family: ``clock flow'' generators on automorphic states}
9806: \label{sec:HP_candidate_2}
9807: 
9808: The Laplacian-based candidate \eqref{eq:HP_candidate_1_GRH} is geometry-forward.
9809: A second candidate is more intrinsic to this volume and aligns naturally with the GRH emphasis on twists:
9810: 
9811: \begin{equation}
9812: \label{eq:HP_candidate_2}
9813: H_{2,\varpi}:=-i\log\bigl(\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)(\gamma_0)\bigr),
9814: \end{equation}
9815: where $\gamma_0$ is a distinguished loop (e.g.\ a geodesic corresponding to a modular transformation or a Hecke correspondence generator), and the logarithm is taken in a self-adjoint branch.
9816: 
9817: This $H_{2,\varpi}$ is a ``time operator'' in the strongest sense: it is literally the generator of clock holonomy along a chosen fundamental cycle.
9818: The GRH constraint is that the trace of $e^{-tH_{2,\varpi}}$ (or closely related spectral data) should reproduce explicit-formula statistics with the correct arithmetic weights as $\varpi$ varies.
9819: 
9820: \begin{remark}[Why $H_2$ is hard]
9821: It is hard because it is too flexible: $\gamma_0$ choices, branch choices, and representation choices can destroy rigidity.
9822: GRH helps by reducing permissible freedom: if the same modeling choices do not behave uniformly across many twists, they are likely unphysical/arithmetic noise.
9823: \end{remark}
9824: 
9825: \subsection{Physics input: modular Hamiltonians and entanglement equilibrium as rigidity constraints}
9826: \label{sec:physics_input}
9827: 
9828: A physically motivated rigidity principle is to relate the clock generator to a modular Hamiltonian $K_A=-\log\rho_A$ ( Chapter~7).
9829: Very roughly, one wants the local clock rate to depend on expectation values of $K_A$, so that the same mechanism producing emergent gravity also fixes the clock/Hamiltonian relation.
9830: 
9831: Within the GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya program, the point is:
9832: \begin{quote}
9833: \emph{A self-adjoint operator family is more believable if it is forced (or at least strongly constrained) by modular Hamiltonians and entanglement positivity, rather than freely assigned.}
9834: \end{quote}
9835: 
9836: This suggests an ambitious but testable subprogram:
9837: \begin{enumerate}
9838: \item construct a family of states $|\psi(\lambda,\varpi)\rangle$ on clocked surface orders (varying both entanglement depth $\lambda$ and arithmetic twist $\varpi$),
9839: \item compute modular Hamiltonian approximations on regions and extract effective local clock rates,
9840: \item test whether the induced generators align with (or constrain) the clock holonomy generators $H_{2,\varpi}$ and the twists used in $H_{1,\rho_{\mathrm{clock}}(\varpi)}$.
9841: \end{enumerate}
9842: 
9843: Even partial success (alignment in scaling limits, monotonicity constraints, redshift-like behavior under increased entanglement) would be meaningful:
9844: it would tie arithmetic spectral geometry to quantum information constraints in a way that reduces the ``free parameters'' that typically plague Hilbert--Pólya proposals.
9845: 
9846: 
9847: \subsection{Worked example II: the same torus dessin, now treated as \emph{bipartite} with three white vertices and heterogeneous DVR data}
9848: \label{sec:hp_worked_example_torus_bipartite}
9849: 
9850: The clean torus example in \S\ref{sec:hp_worked_example_torus} already contains \emph{implicitly} the three white vertices:
9851: the involution $\alpha=(1,4)(2,5)(3,6)$ is precisely the monodromy around the Belyi value $1$, i.e.\ the rotation around white vertices.
9852: In the clean presentation we treated $\alpha$ primarily as an edge-pairing.
9853: Here we instead treat it as what it really is in the dessin viewpoint: a degree--$2$ rotation at three \emph{white} vertices.
9854: This reinterpretation is not cosmetic; it changes what it is natural to glue, which in turn changes what it is natural to quantize.
9855: 
9856: \paragraph{What changes.}
9857: We keep the same underlying surface ($T^2$) and the same permutation data \eqref{eq:torus_dessin_data}, but we now:
9858: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
9859: \item regard $(\sigma_0,\sigma_1,\sigma_\infty)=(\sigma,\alpha,\phi)$ as the \emph{bipartite} dessin triple with $\sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_\infty=1$,
9860: \item insert three explicit degree--$2$ white vertices on the three edges (the fixed-point-free transpositions of $\alpha$),
9861: \item attach \emph{distinct} DVRs to the five vertices:
9862: \[
9863: (R_1,\pi_1)\ \text{for the black vertex }(1\,2\,3),\qquad
9864: (R_2,\pi_2)\ \text{for the black vertex }(4\,5\,6),
9865: \]
9866: and
9867: \[
9868: (R_3,\pi_3)\text{ for }(1\,4),\qquad
9869: (R_4,\pi_4)\text{ for }(2\,5),\qquad
9870: (R_5,\pi_5)\text{ for }(3\,6),
9871: \]
9872: \item and place three new local \emph{$2\times 2$} surface orders at the white vertices, producing a genuinely heterogeneous ``stacky order'' on the torus.
9873: \end{enumerate}
9874: 
9875: \paragraph{Why bother.}
9876: Two reasons are structural.
9877: First, allowing different local DVRs is the correct toy-model for arithmetic twisting in GRH: local data do vary prime-by-prime (conductors, inertia, Frobenius eigenvalues), and our clock/holonomy formalism needs to be able to carry nontrivial local centers without collapsing.
9878: Second, the bipartite view is the correct language for sewing/pants decompositions and for 2D field theory: the white vertices behave like explicit ``interaction sites'' mediating couplings between the black (trivalent) building blocks.
9879: 
9880: \subsubsection{Step 0: bipartite permutation data, cell counts, and genus}
9881: 
9882: We keep the same dart set $D=\{1,\dots,6\}$ and the same triple \eqref{eq:torus_dessin_data}, but interpret it as
9883: \[
9884: \sigma_0 := \sigma=(1\,2\,3)(4\,5\,6)\quad(\text{black rotation}),\qquad
9885: \sigma_1 := \alpha=(1\,4)(2\,5)(3\,6)\quad(\text{white rotation}),
9886: \]
9887: and $\sigma_\infty := \phi=(\sigma_0\sigma_1)^{-1}$.
9888: Thus the black vertices are $B_1=(1\,2\,3)$ and $B_2=(4\,5\,6)$, and the white vertices are the transpositions
9889: \[
9890: W_{14}=(1\,4),\quad W_{25}=(2\,5),\quad W_{36}=(3\,6).
9891: \]
9892: 
9893: \begin{lemma}[Cell counts in the bipartite cellulation]
9894: The associated bipartite graph has $V=5$ vertices and $E=6$ edges, while the face permutation $\sigma_\infty$ has one cycle, so $F=1$.
9895: Hence $\chi=V-E+F=0$ and the surface is again a torus.
9896: \end{lemma}
9897: 
9898: \begin{proof}
9899: In the bipartite graph viewpoint, vertices are cycles of $\sigma_0$ (black) and cycles of $\sigma_1$ (white).
9900: Hence $V=c(\sigma_0)+c(\sigma_1)=2+3=5$.
9901: Edges are darts modulo the identification of endpoints, giving $E=|D|=6$ in this convention (equivalently, each dart is a black--white edge).
9902: Faces are cycles of $\sigma_\infty$ and $c(\sigma_\infty)=c(\phi)=1$.
9903: Therefore $\chi=5-6+1=0$ and $g=1$.
9904: \end{proof}
9905: 
9906: \begin{figure}[t]
9907: \centering
9908: \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=1.0, every node/.style={font=\small}]
9909:   % black vertices
9910:   \node[circle,draw,fill=black,inner sep=2.2pt,label=left:{\small $B_1\,(R_1)$}] (B1) at (0,1.2) {};
9911:   \node[circle,draw,fill=black,inner sep=2.2pt,label=left:{\small $B_2\,(R_2)$}] (B2) at (0,-1.2) {};
9912:   % white vertices
9913:   \node[circle,draw,fill=white,inner sep=2.2pt,label=right:{\small $W_{14}\,(R_3)$}] (W14) at (1.9,1.0) {};
9914:   \node[circle,draw,fill=white,inner sep=2.2pt,label=right:{\small $W_{25}\,(R_4)$}] (W25) at (1.9,0.0) {};
9915:   \node[circle,draw,fill=white,inner sep=2.2pt,label=right:{\small $W_{36}\,(R_5)$}] (W36) at (1.9,-1.0) {};
9916:   % edges
9917:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (B1) -- node[midway,above] {$1$} (W14);
9918:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (W14) -- node[midway,above] {$4$} (B2);
9919:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (B1) -- node[midway] {$2$} (W25);
9920:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (W25) -- node[midway] {$5$} (B2);
9921:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (B1) -- node[midway,below] {$3$} (W36);
9922:   \draw[-{Latex[length=2mm]}] (W36) -- node[midway,below] {$6$} (B2);
9923: \end{tikzpicture}
9924: \caption{The bipartite reinterpretation of the same torus dessin: two trivalent black vertices and three bivalent white vertices. We explicitly allow five distinct DVRs $(R_i,\pi_i)$ at the five vertices.}
9925: \label{fig:bipartite_torus_dessin}
9926: \end{figure}
9927: 
9928: \subsubsection{Step 1: cellular chain complex (bipartite graph spine) and explicit $H_1$}
9929: 
9930: Let $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bi}}$ be the bipartite graph in Figure~\ref{fig:bipartite_torus_dessin}.
9931: It is a spine for the torus cellulation: there is one 2-cell $f$ attached along a cyclic word of length $6$.
9932: The chain groups are now
9933: \[
9934: C_2(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle f\rangle,\qquad 
9935: C_1(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle e_1,\dots,e_6\rangle,\qquad 
9936: C_0(X;\Z)\cong \Z\langle B_1,B_2,W_{14},W_{25},W_{36}\rangle,
9937: \]
9938: where $e_i$ is the oriented black--white edge labeled by dart $i$.
9939: 
9940: \paragraph{Boundary map $\partial_1$.}
9941: Each $e_i$ has $\partial_1(e_i)=t(e_i)-s(e_i)$, with $s(e_i)$ black and $t(e_i)$ white or vice versa depending on orientation.
9942: Choosing all darts oriented from black to white (so the reverse orientation is the inverse edge), we have:
9943: \[
9944: \partial_1(1)=W_{14}-B_1,\quad \partial_1(2)=W_{25}-B_1,\quad \partial_1(3)=W_{36}-B_1,
9945: \]
9946: \[
9947: \partial_1(4)=W_{14}-B_2,\quad \partial_1(5)=W_{25}-B_2,\quad \partial_1(6)=W_{36}-B_2.
9948: \]
9949: 
9950: \paragraph{Boundary map $\partial_2$.}
9951: The unique face cycle is $\sigma_\infty=\phi=(1\,6\,2\,4\,3\,5)$.
9952: Geometrically, one reads this as the cyclic order in which directed edges appear along the boundary of the 2-cell.
9953: A concrete attaching word consistent with this is
9954: \begin{equation}
9955: \label{eq:bipartite_face_word}
9956: w_f \;=\; e_1\,e_6^{-1}\,e_2\,e_4^{-1}\,e_3\,e_5^{-1},
9957: \end{equation}
9958: so that $\partial_2(f)$ is the signed sum corresponding to \eqref{eq:bipartite_face_word}.
9959: A direct check shows $\partial_1\partial_2=0$.
9960: 
9961: \begin{proposition}[Explicit $H_1$ basis]
9962: The first homology $H_1(X;\Z)$ is free abelian of rank $2$ and admits the explicit cycle representatives
9963: \[
9964: a := e_1-e_2 + (e_4-e_5),\qquad 
9965: b := e_1-e_3 + (e_4-e_6),
9966: \]
9967: corresponding to the two independent differences of the three ``parallel'' black--white--black routes.
9968: \end{proposition}
9969: 
9970: \begin{proof}
9971: The rank statement follows from $\chi=0$ and connectedness.
9972: For the representatives: note that $\partial_1(e_1-e_2)=W_{14}-W_{25}$ and $\partial_1(e_4-e_5)=W_{14}-W_{25}$, hence $\partial_1(a)=0$.
9973: Similarly $\partial_1(b)=0$.
9974: Finally $a$ and $b$ are independent modulo the image of $\partial_2$; indeed $\partial_2(f)$ gives only one relation among the three differences, leaving a rank--$2$ lattice.
9975: \end{proof}
9976: 
9977: This explicit chain model will be used below to write persistence computations in closed form.
9978: 
9979: \subsubsection{Step 2: heterogeneous local vertex orders (two $3\times 3$ and three $2\times 2$) and their clock normalizers}
9980: 
9981: We now place local hereditary orders at the five vertices, with \emph{distinct} DVRs.
9982: Let $(R_i,\mathfrak m_i)$ be DVRs with uniformizers $\pi_i$ and fraction fields $K_i$.
9983: To keep the gluing meaningful we assume the minimal common-overfield hypothesis:
9984: 
9985: \begin{definition}[Common-overfield hypothesis for heterogeneous DVR gluing]
9986: \label{def:common_overfield}
9987: Assume there exists a field $K$ and embeddings $K_i\hookrightarrow K$ such that the images of $R_i$ are subrings of $K$.
9988: We write the embedded uniformizers still as $\pi_i\in K$.
9989: \end{definition}
9990: 
9991: This is mild for toy models (one can take $K$ to be a compositum), and it is the correct arithmetic analogue of having all local fields sit inside a global adèle ring.
9992: 
9993: \paragraph{Local orders.}
9994: At the black vertices we place the trivalent hereditary orders
9995: \[
9996: \Lambda(B_1):=\Lambda_3(R_1),\qquad \Lambda(B_2):=\Lambda_3(R_2),
9997: \]
9998: and at the three bivalent white vertices we place the degree--$2$ hereditary orders
9999: \[
10000: \Lambda(W_{14}):=\Lambda_2(R_3),\qquad \Lambda(W_{25}):=\Lambda_2(R_4),\qquad \Lambda(W_{36}):=\Lambda_2(R_5),
10001: \]
10002: where (in the same matrix convention as \eqref{eq:hereditary_order})
10003: \[
10004: \Lambda_2(R):=
10005: \left\{
10006: \begin{pmatrix}
10007: a & b\\
10008: c & d
10009: \end{pmatrix}\in M_2(K(R)):\ a,d\in R,\ c\in R,\ b\in \pi R
10010: \right\}.
10011: \]
10012: 
10013: \paragraph{Local clock normalizers.}
10014: At the black vertices we again use the twisted $3$-shift
10015: \[
10016: S_{B_1}:=S_3(\pi_1),\qquad S_{B_2}:=S_3(\pi_2),
10017: \]
10018: while at each white vertex we use the twisted $2$-shift
10019: \[
10020: S_{14}:=S_2(\pi_3),\qquad S_{25}:=S_2(\pi_4),\qquad S_{36}:=S_2(\pi_5),
10021: \qquad 
10022: S_2(\pi)=
10023: \begin{pmatrix}
10024: 0&\pi\\
10025: 1&0
10026: \end{pmatrix}.
10027: \]
10028: 
10029: \begin{lemma}[Powers and reduced norms]
10030: \label{lem:powers_reduced_norms}
10031: For the twisted shifts one has
10032: \[
10033: S_3(\pi)^3=\pi I_3,\qquad S_2(\pi)^2=\pi I_2,
10034: \]
10035: and their reduced norms (determinants in the matrix realizations) satisfy
10036: \[
10037: \mathrm{Nrd}(S_3(\pi))=\det(S_3(\pi))=\pi,\qquad 
10038: \mathrm{Nrd}(S_2(\pi))=\det(S_2(\pi))=-\pi.
10039: \]
10040: \end{lemma}
10041: 
10042: \begin{proof}
10043: The power identities are proved in Proposition~\ref{prop:twisted_shift_power} (for general $m$) and by a direct $2\times 2$ multiplication.
10044: The determinant computations are immediate from the defining matrices.
10045: \end{proof}
10046: 
10047: \begin{remark}[A gentle warning about matrix sizes]
10048: We are now deliberately mixing local matrix sizes $3$ and $2$.
10049: There is no canonical way to multiply $S_3$ and $S_2$ as matrices.
10050: Global holonomy is therefore best organized using:
10051: (i) \emph{Morita data} (bimodules between corner algebras), or
10052: (ii) \emph{central invariants} extracted from holonomy such as reduced norms and valuations.
10053: Both viewpoints are standard in the arithmetic theory of orders and are well-adapted to the GRH context, where local factors are intrinsically of varying dimensions (depending on the representation $\varpi$).
10054: \end{remark}
10055: 
10056: \subsubsection{Step 3: gluing as a stacky order and the tensor/fibre-product dictionary}
10057: 
10058: To glue heterogeneous local orders we formalize the ``stack mentality'' that was implicit in the earlier chapters.
10059: 
10060: \begin{definition}[Order-valued cosheaf on the dessin]
10061: \label{def:order_cosheaf}
10062: Let $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bi}}$ be the bipartite dessin spine.
10063: An \emph{order-valued cosheaf} assigns:
10064: \begin{itemize}
10065: \item to each vertex $v$ an $R_v$-order $\Lambda(v)$ in a finite-dimensional semisimple $K$-algebra,
10066: \item to each oriented incidence (half-edge) $(v\to e)$ a corner idempotent $e_{v\to e}\in \Lambda(v)$ and the corner algebra $e_{v\to e}\Lambda(v)e_{v\to e}$,
10067: \item to each edge $e$ a ring $S_e\subset K$ and compatible embeddings $S_e\hookrightarrow Z(e_{v\to e}\Lambda(v)e_{v\to e})$ at its endpoints,
10068: \end{itemize}
10069: such that the glued object exists as an iterated pushout (or, dually, the associated ringed space exists as an iterated pullback).
10070: \end{definition}
10071: 
10072: This definition is comprehensive, but it encodes a simple principle:
10073: 
10074: \begin{quote}
10075: \emph{Gluing along overlaps is a fibre product on spaces, hence a tensor product on rings.}
10076: \end{quote}
10077: 
10078: \paragraph{Affine-scheme toy identity (commutative case).}
10079: If $S_3\subset S_1,S_2$ are commutative rings, then
10080: \[
10081: \Spec(S_1\otimes_{S_3}S_2)\cong \Spec(S_1)\times_{\Spec(S_3)}\Spec(S_2).
10082: \]
10083: The noncommutative order case is subtler (pushouts need not exist in the naive category), but \emph{Morita contexts} and \emph{amalgamated free products} provide workable substitutes in practice.
10084: For this torus toy model, the most robust computational strategy is to track the induced gluing on:
10085: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
10086: \item centers and reduced norms (commutative invariants),
10087: \item module categories (stack viewpoint),
10088: \item and, for quantum simulation, the induced block structure on a global Hilbert space (operator-algebra viewpoint).
10089: \end{enumerate}
10090: 
10091: \paragraph{Operator-algebra duality reminder.}
10092: If $A$ is a commutative unital $C^\ast$-algebra, Gelfand duality identifies $A\cong C(X)$ for a compact Hausdorff space $X$.
10093: Noncommutative $C^\ast$-algebras are then interpreted as ``noncommutative spaces'' in the sense of Connes; gluing and tensoring become operator-algebraic operations rather than literal set-theoretic gluings.
10094: We will use this viewpoint below when we discuss spectral triples and regularized determinants.
10095: 
10096: \subsubsection{Step 4: time holonomy invariants with heterogeneous centres (a computation you can actually do)}
10097: 
10098: Because matrix sizes vary, we work with a \emph{central holonomy character} extracted from the local turning operators.
10099: 
10100: \begin{definition}[Reduced-norm holonomy character]
10101: \label{def:nrd_holonomy}
10102: Let $\gamma$ be a closed loop in the dessin spine.
10103: Define $\Hol_{\mathrm{turn}}(\gamma)$ as the ordered product of turning operators encountered along $\gamma$:
10104: at a trivalent black vertex use $S_{B_i}^{\pm 1}$ depending on the turn direction, and at a bivalent white vertex use $S_{jk}^{\pm 1}$.
10105: The \emph{reduced-norm holonomy} is
10106: \[
10107: \chi_{\mathrm{clock}}(\gamma)\ :=\ \prod_{v\in \gamma} \mathrm{Nrd}\big(S_v^{\epsilon_v(\gamma)}\big)\ \in\ K^\times,
10108: \]
10109: where $\epsilon_v(\gamma)\in\Z$ records the net number of $+1$ turns at $v$ minus the net number of $-1$ turns at $v$.
10110: \end{definition}
10111: 
10112: \begin{remark}
10113: This definition is deliberately low-tech: it produces an invariant that (i) survives heterogeneous sizes, (ii) lands in a commutative group, and (iii) is precisely the kind of object that can carry GRH-relevant ``local signs'' (root numbers, tame phases) once one couples to arithmetic twists.
10114: \end{remark}
10115: 
10116: \paragraph{Face loop computation.}
10117: For the unique face, the boundary step is $i\mapsto \sigma_\infty(i)=\sigma_1\sigma_0^{-1}(i)$ (since $\sigma_\infty=(\sigma_0\sigma_1)^{-1}$ and $\sigma_1$ is an involution).
10118: Thus each boundary step contributes one black turn ($\sigma_0^{-1}$) and one white turn ($\sigma_1$).
10119: Tracing the cycle $\sigma_\infty=(1\,6\,2\,4\,3\,5)$ one finds:
10120: \begin{itemize}
10121: \item black turns: $B_1$ appears $3$ times and $B_2$ appears $3$ times,
10122: \item white turns: each of $W_{14},W_{25},W_{36}$ appears exactly $2$ times.
10123: \end{itemize}
10124: Hence, using Lemma~\ref{lem:powers_reduced_norms},
10125: \begin{equation}
10126: \label{eq:bipartite_face_nrd}
10127: \chi_{\mathrm{clock}}(\partial f)\ =\ \pi_1^{-3}\,\pi_2^{-3}\,(\!-\pi_3)^{2}\,(\!-\pi_4)^{2}\,(\!-\pi_5)^{2}
10128: \ =\ \frac{\pi_3^2\pi_4^2\pi_5^2}{\pi_1^3\pi_2^3}\ \in K^\times.
10129: \end{equation}
10130: 
10131: \begin{remark}[Central defects as ``arithmetic bookkeeping'']
10132: In the clean example, the face holonomy defect was a single central factor $\pi^{-2}$.
10133: Here the defect keeps track of \emph{which} local centers were traversed, and \emph{how often}.
10134: In GRH-strength applications, the analogue of \eqref{eq:bipartite_face_nrd} is where conductors and local epsilon factors naturally want to live.
10135: \end{remark}
10136: 
10137: \subsubsection{Step 5: entanglement weights, induced distances, and how persistence sees the mismatch of metrics}
10138: 
10139: We now connect three different notions of distance on the same underlying torus:
10140: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
10141: \item combinatorial distance on the dessin graph (edge-count or weighted by local data),
10142: \item geometric distance from a punctured-hyperbolic structure on the once-punctured torus,
10143: \item and an entanglement-induced distance derived from a quantum state on the vertex Hilbert spaces.
10144: \end{enumerate}
10145: 
10146: \paragraph{Hilbert spaces and a concrete state family.}
10147: Attach Hilbert spaces of dimensions matching vertex valences:
10148: \[
10149: \cH_{B_1}\cong \C^3,\quad \cH_{B_2}\cong \C^3,\quad 
10150: \cH_{14}\cong \C^2,\quad \cH_{25}\cong \C^2,\quad \cH_{36}\cong \C^2.
10151: \]
10152: Consider a family of states $|\psi(\lambda)\rangle$ built as follows:
10153: each black--white edge carries an entangled pair of strength $\lambda\ge 0$ (e.g.\ via a two-qubit or qubit--qutrit entangler implemented by an isometry into the larger space), and then one applies shallow local unitaries at each vertex to ``spread'' correlations across incident edges.
10154: This is a deliberately hardware-friendly analogue of a PEPS-like ansatz.
10155: 
10156: \paragraph{Entanglement-derived edge lengths.}
10157: Let $I_{uv}(\lambda)$ denote the mutual information between vertex subsystems $u$ and $v$ in the state $|\psi(\lambda)\rangle$.
10158: Define an entanglement length on edges by
10159: \[
10160: \ell_{uv}(\lambda):= -\log\!\left(\frac{I_{uv}(\lambda)+\varepsilon}{I_0+\varepsilon}\right),
10161: \]
10162: with a small $\varepsilon>0$ to avoid numerical blowups.
10163: Then $\ell_{uv}$ decreases as entanglement increases, and it is additive along paths (as a path-length metric).
10164: The induced \emph{entanglement distance} is the shortest-path metric
10165: \[
10166: d_{\mathrm{ent},\lambda}(u,v):=\inf_{\text{paths }u\rightsquigarrow v}\ \sum_{(x,y)\in \text{path}}\ell_{xy}(\lambda).
10167: \]
10168: 
10169: \paragraph{Comparison to hyperbolic distance.}
10170: The once-punctured torus admits a complete finite-area hyperbolic metric; one model is $X=\HH/\Gamma$ for a suitable $\Gamma<\PSL_2(\Z)$.
10171: Let $d_{\mathrm{hyp}}$ denote the hyperbolic distance on the thick part, and note that near the cusp it diverges.
10172: In contrast, $d_{\mathrm{ent},\lambda}$ is bounded on the finite graph, so the cusp is necessarily \emph{collapsed} at finite discretization.
10173: This is not a bug: it is exactly what coarse-graining does.
10174: 
10175: \begin{proposition}[Quasi-isometry on the thick part (informal but checkable)]
10176: Fix a hyperbolic punctured torus structure and embed $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bi}}$ as a spine in the thick part.
10177: Then there exist constants $A\ge 1,B\ge 0$ (depending on the embedding) such that for vertices $u,v$ in the thick part,
10178: \[
10179: A^{-1}d_{\Gamma}(u,v)-B\ \le\ d_{\mathrm{hyp}}(u,v)\ \le\ A\,d_{\Gamma}(u,v)+B,
10180: \]
10181: where $d_\Gamma$ is combinatorial distance on $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bi}}$.
10182: \end{proposition}
10183: 
10184: \begin{remark}
10185: This is the standard ``spine quasi-isometry'' fact: graphs embedded as spines in thick parts of finite-area hyperbolic surfaces coarsely capture the geometry.
10186: In practice it is verified numerically by sampling geodesic distances between embedded vertices.
10187: The key point for us is that \emph{entanglement distance} can violate this quasi-isometry if entanglement concentrates on certain edges, and persistence detects exactly where and when that violation happens.
10188: \end{remark}
10189: 
10190: \paragraph{How multiparameter persistence enters.}
10191: We now define a two-parameter filtration that simultaneously tracks (i) metric reachability and (ii) holonomy defect.
10192: 
10193: Let $r\ge 0$ and $\kappa\in\R$.
10194: Define a subcomplex $K_{r,\kappa}\subset X$ by:
10195: \begin{itemize}
10196: \item include all vertices,
10197: \item include an edge $(u,v)$ if $d_{\mathrm{ent},\lambda}(u,v)\le r$ (equivalently, $\ell_{uv}(\lambda)\le r$ for direct edges),
10198: \item include the face $f$ if the \emph{defect valuation} satisfies
10199: \[
10200: v\!\left(\chi_{\mathrm{clock}}(\partial f)\right)\ge \kappa,
10201: \]
10202: where $v$ is a chosen valuation on $K$ (e.g.\ an additive valuation extending the $v_i$ along the embeddings).
10203: \end{itemize}
10204: 
10205: As $(r,\kappa)$ increases, edges and then the face appear.
10206: The resulting bifiltration produces a bigraded persistence module
10207: \[
10208: M_{p}=\{H_p(K_{r,\kappa})\}_{(r,\kappa)\in\R^2}
10209: \]
10210: over the poset $\R^2$ (equivalently a finitely presented $k[x,y]$-module after discretization).
10211: 
10212: \begin{example}[Closed-form $H_1$ behavior in this toy bifiltration]
10213: Because $\Gamma_{\mathrm{bi}}$ has $\beta_1=2$ and there is a single 2-cell, the only way $H_1$ can decrease is when the face attaches.
10214: Thus for any $(r,\kappa)$ such that the 1-skeleton is present but the face is absent, one has $H_1\cong \Z^2$.
10215: Once the face is included, one relation kills one rank and $H_1\cong \Z$ if the attaching map is nontrivial on $H_1$ (which it is here).
10216: Therefore the rank invariant of $H_1$ has the schematic form
10217: \[
10218: \rank H_1(K_{r,\kappa})=
10219: \begin{cases}
10220: 0,& r<r_{\mathrm{conn}},\\
10221: 2,& r\ge r_{\mathrm{conn}}\ \text{and}\ \kappa<\kappa_{\mathrm{face}},\\
10222: 1,& r\ge r_{\mathrm{conn}}\ \text{and}\ \kappa\ge \kappa_{\mathrm{face}},
10223: \end{cases}
10224: \]
10225: where $r_{\mathrm{conn}}$ is the threshold at which the 1-skeleton becomes connected under $d_{\mathrm{ent},\lambda}$ and $\kappa_{\mathrm{face}}:=v(\chi_{\mathrm{clock}}(\partial f))$ is the holonomy defect threshold.
10226: 
10227: The point is not the triviality of the arithmetic here, but the \emph{logic}:
10228: a holonomy defect provides an \emph{independent} persistence axis that can be compared against entanglement-derived connectivity.
10229: \end{example}
10230: 
10231: \subsubsection{Step 6: pants decompositions, 2D CFT sewing, and a holography-shaped hint}
10232: 
10233: The punctured torus is the smallest surface where ``pants gluing'' is nontrivial yet completely explicit.
10234: A once-punctured torus can be obtained by taking a pair of pants $P$ (a sphere with three boundary components) and gluing two of its boundaries together.
10235: On the CFT side, this is precisely where conformal blocks, sewing, and modular transformations start to bite.
10236: 
10237: \paragraph{Pants gluing as a categorical operation.}
10238: In a 2D CFT (or more generally a modular functor / 2D TQFT), the pair of pants is the fundamental multiplication:
10239: it provides a multilinear map on state spaces assigned to boundary circles.
10240: Gluing boundaries corresponds to taking an inner product / trace, and the torus partition function becomes a graded trace.
10241: Symbolically,
10242: \[
10243: Z_{T^2}(q,\bar q)=\mathrm{Tr}_{\cH}\!\left(q^{L_0-c/24}\,\bar q^{\bar L_0-c/24}\right),
10244: \]
10245: with the modular parameter $\tau$ entering via $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$.
10246: 
10247: \paragraph{Where our orders fit.}
10248: Surface orders provide a concrete algebraic model for ``local pieces'' that can be glued:
10249: trivalent black vertices behave like pants junctions, while bivalent white vertices behave like explicit ``propagators'' (degree--2 sewing sites).
10250: The heterogeneous DVRs then act as local deformation parameters (conductors / local scales).
10251: In that language, the gluing in Definition~\ref{def:order_cosheaf} is the algebraic shadow of CFT sewing:
10252: tensor products (quantum composition) mirror fibre products (geometric gluing), with Morita bimodules playing the role of boundary conditions.
10253: 
10254: \paragraph{A holography-shaped hint (carefully labelled as a hint).}
10255: If one further interprets entanglement distance as a discrete bulk metric, then changing $\lambda$ changes the effective ``bulk geometry'' seen by the graph.
10256: In AdS/CFT heuristics, entanglement controls geometry; here, persistence provides a way to test whether that control is \emph{stable} under changes of discretization and twist.
10257: No miracle is claimed, but the methodological link is real:
10258: \emph{sewing axioms constrain operator families, and operator families are what Hilbert--Pólya needs.}
10259: 
10260: \subsubsection{Step 7: the noncommutative-geometric lens (spectral triples) and why Connes's recent ``zeta spectral triples'' matter here}
10261: 
10262: A persistent theme in this volume is that we need an operator-theoretic home where:
10263: \begin{itemize}
10264: \item the algebraic gluing data live as an algebra $A$,
10265: \item the quantum/entanglement data live as a representation on a Hilbert space $H$,
10266: \item and the geometric/time data live as an (unbounded) self-adjoint operator $D$.
10267: \end{itemize}
10268: This is precisely the format of a \emph{spectral triple} $(A,H,D)$.
10269: 
10270: Recent work of Connes--Consani--Moscovici proposes ``zeta spectral triples'' designed so that spectra of certain self-adjoint operators approximate the zeros of $\zeta(\tfrac12+is)$, together with regularized determinants converging toward the $\Xi$-function \cite{ConnesConsaniMoscovici2025ZetaSpectralTriples}.
10271: We do \emph{not} import their construction wholesale here, but we take it seriously as a template:
10272: it is a concrete, operator-theoretic attempt at Hilbert--Pólya with explicit determinants.
10273: 
10274: \paragraph{Our toy torus version.}
10275: For the bipartite torus order, one can form:
10276: \begin{itemize}
10277: \item $A$ as a $C^\ast$-completion of the (block) algebra generated by local orders and edge bimodules,
10278: \item $H$ as the direct sum of vertex Hilbert spaces (or, better, the completion of a module of sections),
10279: \item $D$ as a combination of a geometric Dirac/Laplacian discretization and the clock generator(s) extracted from the $S_v$ via a logarithm branch.
10280: \end{itemize}
10281: The regularized determinant $\det_{\mathrm{reg}}(D-z)$ is then an honest object one can compute numerically and compare across twists.
10282: In this volume we keep this in the ``proposal'' box, but we emphasize: it is the right kind of box.
10283: 
10284: \paragraph{A note on numerical reproducibility.}
10285: The correct attitude here is not heuristic enthusiasm but reproducible computation with explicit versioning and independently checkable diagnostics.
10286: Build the toy $D$, compute its determinant, perturb it, and see what is stable.
10287: Persistence is the debugger.
10288: 
10289: \subsubsection{Step 8: a fully explicit discretized two-parameter persistence module (a consistency check suitable for implementation)}
10290: \label{sec:bipartite_step8_persistence}
10291: 
10292: The previous steps described the bifiltration $K_{r,\kappa}$ conceptually.
10293: Here we freeze a tiny discretization and write the resulting $k[x,y]$--module presentation explicitly.
10294: The point is not sophistication; it is reproducibility.
10295: 
10296: \paragraph{Discretization.}
10297: Fix a field $k$ (for computations, take $k=\F_2$).
10298: Choose two $r$--levels and two defect levels:
10299: \[
10300: r_0<r_1,\qquad \kappa_0<\kappa_1,
10301: \]
10302: where $r_0$ is below the connectivity threshold (so the graph is disconnected at $r_0$) and $r_1$ is above it (so the full 1--skeleton is present at $r_1$),
10303: and where $\kappa_0< v(\chi_{\mathrm{clock}}(\partial f))\le \kappa_1$ so that the face is absent at $\kappa_0$ and present at $\kappa_1$.
10304: This yields a $2\times 2$ grid of complexes:
10305: \[
10306: K_{r_0,\kappa_0}\subset K_{r_1,\kappa_0},\qquad
10307: K_{r_0,\kappa_1}\subset K_{r_1,\kappa_1},
10308: \]
10309: with the obvious inclusions in the $\kappa$ direction as well.
10310: 
10311: \paragraph{Homology on the grid.}
10312: In this discretization one checks:
10313: \[
10314: H_1(K_{r_0,\kappa_0};k)=0,\qquad H_1(K_{r_1,\kappa_0};k)\cong k^2,
10315: \]
10316: and
10317: \[
10318: H_1(K_{r_0,\kappa_1};k)=0,\qquad H_1(K_{r_1,\kappa_1};k)\cong k,
10319: \]
10320: because the only difference between $\kappa_0$ and $\kappa_1$ is the attachment of the single 2--cell $f$.
10321: 
10322: \begin{proposition}[Minimal bigraded presentation in the $2\times 2$ discretization]
10323: \label{prop:2x2_persistence_presentation}
10324: Let $M$ be the resulting bigraded persistence module $M(r_i,\kappa_j)=H_1(K_{r_i,\kappa_j};k)$.
10325: Then $M$ admits a minimal presentation as a $k[x,y]$--module with:
10326: \begin{itemize}
10327: \item two generators $g_1,g_2$ in bidegree $(r_1,\kappa_0)$,
10328: \item one relation in bidegree $(r_1,\kappa_1)$ killing exactly one $k$--linear combination of $g_1,g_2$ under the action of $y$.
10329: \end{itemize}
10330: Equivalently, after choosing a basis so that $y g_1=h$ and $y g_2=0$ for a generator $h$ in bidegree $(r_1,\kappa_1)$, one may write
10331: \[
10332: M \ \cong\  \frac{k[x,y]\langle g_1,g_2\rangle}{\langle y g_2,\ y^2 g_1\rangle},
10333: \]
10334: with grading understood in the obvious truncated sense.
10335: \end{proposition}
10336: 
10337: \begin{proof}
10338: At $(r_1,\kappa_0)$ there are precisely two independent 1-cycles (Proposition above), hence two generators.
10339: At $(r_1,\kappa_1)$ the face imposes exactly one independent relation on $H_1$, hence the image of $y:M(r_1,\kappa_0)\to M(r_1,\kappa_1)$ has rank $1$.
10340: Choose $g_1$ mapping to a nonzero class $h$ and choose $g_2$ spanning the kernel of $y$.
10341: The stated relations encode exactly this kernel/image structure.
10342: \end{proof}
10343: 
10344: \paragraph{What this buys you in practice.}
10345: If you implement multiparameter persistence for surface-order filtrations, Proposition~\ref{prop:2x2_persistence_presentation} is a sanity check:
10346: your code should recover (up to isomorphism) a module with two generators and one independent ``$y$--killing'' relation.
10347: 
10348: If it does not, you have either:
10349: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
10350: \item a bug in the filtration construction (common),
10351: \item a convention mismatch in the boundary orientation (also common),
10352: \item or a genuine modeling difference (rare, but interesting).
10353: \end{enumerate}
10354: Either way, you learn something without appealing to numerical coincidence with any $L$--function.
10355: 
10356: 
10357: 
10358: 
10359: \subsection{Summary: a ``wise'' conclusion (now in GRH form)}
10360: \label{sec:HP_summary}
10361: 
10362: A GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya program demands \emph{uniform rigidity across twists}.
10363: This volume's contribution is to propose a rigidifying architecture:
10364: \begin{itemize}
10365: \item hyperbolic quotient geometry supplies trace-formula and scattering structure,
10366: \item surface orders supply local-to-global gluing constraints and a controlled source of twists,
10367: \item twisted shifts supply nontrivial holonomy with arithmetic-looking central factors (a plausible home for root numbers and local signs),
10368: \item multiparameter persistence supplies stability diagnostics across families,
10369: \item quantum hardware experiments supply a finite realization layer in which the time/holonomy mechanism can be tested at scale without confusing implementation with proof.
10370: \end{itemize}
10371: 
10372: If this program fails, it should fail \emph{informatively}:
10373: by isolating exactly which coupling assumptions break trace-formula compatibility, destroy twist-uniformity, or violate stability.
10374: If it succeeds, it will likely do so by revealing that the ``right'' operator family was not invented, but \emph{forced} by consistent gluing of local algebra, hyperbolic geometry, and information-theoretic positivity.
10375: 
10376: \subsection{Trace-formula alignment: explicit targets one can actually compare}
10377: \label{sec:trace_formula_targets}
10378: 
10379: A recurring ambiguity in Hilbert--Pólya discussions is that ``matching zeros'' is treated as a single monolithic target.
10380: In practice one must decide \emph{what observable} of the spectrum is being matched, and at which scale.
10381: 
10382: Two reference formulas organize the comparison:
10383: 
10384: \paragraph{(1) The explicit formula (general $L$--function).}
10385: For a suitable test function $f$, the explicit formula relates a smoothed sum over nontrivial zeros $\rho=\tfrac12+i\gamma$ to a sum over prime powers with arithmetic weights depending on $\varpi$.
10386: Schematically,
10387: \[
10388: \sum_{\rho} \widehat{f}(\gamma)
10389: \;=\;
10390: \text{(main terms from poles and gamma factors)}\;+\;\sum_{p^k}\frac{\log p}{p^{k/2}}\, a_\varpi(p^k)\, f(k\log p),
10391: \]
10392: where $a_\varpi(p^k)$ is $\chi(p^k)$ for Dirichlet twists and $\Tr(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k))$ for Artin twists, etc.
10393: 
10394: \paragraph{(2) The Selberg trace formula (hyperbolic quotient, twisted).}
10395: For a compact hyperbolic surface $X=\HH/\Gamma$ and a unitary twist $\rho:\Gamma\to U(d)$, a twisted trace formula relates a smoothed sum over Laplace eigenvalues $\lambda_n=\tfrac14+r_n^2$ to a sum over primitive closed geodesics $\{\gamma\}$ weighted by $\Tr(\rho(\gamma^k))$.
10396: In schematic form,
10397: \[
10398: \sum_{n} h(r_n)\,\dim(\text{twist space})
10399: \;=\;
10400: \text{(identity / area term)}\;+\;
10401: \sum_{\{\gamma\}}\sum_{k\ge 1} \Tr(\rho(\gamma^k))\,W(\gamma,k;g),
10402: \]
10403: where $W(\gamma,k;g)$ is the standard hyperbolic weight built from $\ell(\gamma)$ and a transform $g$ of $h$.
10404: 
10405: \paragraph{What can be matched.}
10406: The analogy is structural:
10407: \begin{itemize}
10408: \item prime powers $p^k$ correspond to iterates $k\ell(\gamma)$ of primitive closed geodesics,
10409: \item the arithmetic coefficients $a_\varpi(p^k)$ correspond to trace weights $\Tr(\rho(\gamma^k))$,
10410: \item and the test function is the dial that selects the comparison scale.
10411: \end{itemize}
10412: 
10413: In our program, the operator is not \emph{just} the Laplacian: it is a \emph{clock/holonomy-twisted} object.
10414: The concrete target is therefore a \emph{twisted trace identity} whose geometric side naturally carries arithmetic weights and whose spectral side is manifestly self-adjoint (or has a controlled scattering interpretation).
10415: 
10416: \subsection{Numerical milestones and resource estimates (classical and quantum) --- now across twists}
10417: \label{sec:hp_milestones}
10418: 
10419: A pragmatic GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya program should be organized by milestones that can be reached with today's tools.
10420: A reasonable staging is:
10421: 
10422: \begin{enumerate}
10423: \item \textbf{Twist-family selection.}
10424: Choose a family $\{\varpi\}$ where zero data are accessible and where analytic continuation is established.
10425: The minimal reliable choice is primitive Dirichlet characters up to conductor $q\le q_{\max}$.
10426: 
10427: \item \textbf{Arithmetic surface selection.}
10428: Choose $X=\HH/\Gamma$ where $\Gamma$ is arithmetic and where both Laplace/scattering data and geodesic data are computationally accessible.
10429: Congruence subgroups of $\PSL_2(\Z)$ are natural for Dirichlet twists.
10430: 
10431: \item \textbf{Order/clock data on $X$.}
10432: Pick an embedded graph $\Gamma_X\subset X$ (e.g.\ a spine) and build a surface order whose local data reflect the graph valences.
10433: Choose twisted shift representations and record the induced holonomy class $[g]\in \check{H}^1(X;\Aut(\Lambda))$.
10434: 
10435: \item \textbf{Define a self-adjoint candidate family.}
10436: Construct a family of operators of the form
10437: \[
10438: H_\varpi(\theta)=\Phi(\Delta_X)\;+\;\Psi_\varpi\!\big(U_\theta\big),
10439: \]
10440: where $\Delta_X$ is (a suitable self-adjoint extension of) the Laplacian and $U_\theta$ is a unitary holonomy operator built from the clock/gluing data.
10441: The map $\varpi\mapsto \Psi_\varpi$ must be rigid (e.g.\ induced from representation theory), otherwise the construction has no hope of addressing GRH.
10442: 
10443: \item \textbf{Spectral/scattering computation.}
10444: On the classical side: compute eigenvalues and/or scattering phases for a grid of $(\varpi,\theta)$.
10445: On the quantum side (longer term): implement block-encodings or Hamiltonian simulation for discretized $H_\varpi(\theta)$ and use phase estimation to sample eigenphases.
10446: The resource bottleneck is not just qubits but \emph{coherent depth} and conditioning.
10447: 
10448: \item \textbf{Trace-statistic comparison.}
10449: Choose test functions and compare smoothed spectral sums to geometric sums over closed geodesics (or graph-cycle proxies) with twisted weights.
10450: For GRH, do this \emph{uniformly over twists} and record which observables are stable.
10451: 
10452: \item \textbf{Persistence diagnostic layer.}
10453: Run multiparameter persistence diagnostics on the same data to detect regime changes (as $\varpi$ or $\theta$ varies) and to separate numerical artifacts from structural effects.
10454: \end{enumerate}
10455: 
10456: The point of this milestone plan is that failure is informative:
10457: if trace statistics refuse to align uniformly over twists, the obstruction can often be localized to one of the construction steps above.
10458: 
10459: 
10460: \subsection{A GRH ``completion step'': from toy twists to genuine GRH families (with emphasis on Artin $L$--functions)}
10461: \label{sec:GRH_artin_completion}
10462: 
10463: The worked examples above were intentionally small: they were meant to make the pipeline executable end-to-end, not to solve analytic number theory.
10464: This final subsection records the \emph{full-strength target} for the theory when the GRH indexing parameter $\varpi$ is taken seriously.
10465: We focus on Artin $L$--functions, because they are the cleanest setting where:
10466: (i) local factors are naturally matrix-valued, and
10467: (ii) functoriality constraints are not optional.
10468: 
10469: \subsubsection{Artin $L$--functions: the exact data GRH forces you to carry}
10470: 
10471: Fix a finite Galois extension $L/\Q$ with Galois group $G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/\Q)$ and a complex representation
10472: \[
10473: \varpi=\rho:\ G\to \GL_n(\C).
10474: \]
10475: For each unramified prime $p$, let $\mathrm{Frob}_p\in G$ be a Frobenius conjugacy class.
10476: The Artin $L$--function is (initially for $\Re(s)>1$) the Euler product
10477: \begin{equation}
10478: \label{eq:artin_L_euler}
10479: L(s,\rho)\ :=\ \prod_{p\ \mathrm{unram.}}\ \det\!\big(I_n-\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p)\,p^{-s}\big)^{-1}\ \cdot\ \prod_{p\ \mathrm{ram.}}L_p(s,\rho),
10480: \end{equation}
10481: where the finitely many ramified local factors $L_p(s,\rho)$ are defined using inertia invariants.
10482: The \emph{completed} $L$--function has the form
10483: \begin{equation}
10484: \label{eq:completed_artin}
10485: \Lambda(s,\rho)\ :=\ N(\rho)^{s/2}\,L_\infty(s,\rho)\,L(s,\rho),
10486: \end{equation}
10487: where $N(\rho)$ is the Artin conductor and $L_\infty$ is a product of $\Gamma$--factors determined by the archimedean type of $\rho$.
10488: Assuming Artin conjectures as needed for analytic continuation, $\Lambda(s,\rho)$ satisfies a functional equation
10489: \begin{equation}
10490: \label{eq:artin_FE}
10491: \Lambda(s,\rho)\ =\ \varepsilon(\rho)\,\Lambda(1-s,\rho^\vee),
10492: \qquad |\varepsilon(\rho)|=1.
10493: \end{equation}
10494: 
10495: \begin{definition}[GRH for Artin $L$--functions]
10496: GRH for $\Lambda(s,\rho)$ asserts that all nontrivial zeros satisfy $\Re(s)=\tfrac12$.
10497: \end{definition}
10498: 
10499: \paragraph{What this forces on Hilbert--Pólya.}
10500: A GRH-strength Hilbert--Pólya realization must produce, for \emph{each} $\rho$ in the family of interest, a self-adjoint operator $H_\rho$ such that
10501: \[
10502: \rho=\tfrac12+i\gamma\ \text{is a nontrivial zero of }\Lambda(s,\rho)\quad \Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma\in \Spec(H_\rho),
10503: \]
10504: and it must do so \emph{functorially} in $\rho$:
10505: isomorphic representations must yield unitarily equivalent operators, induction/restriction should have a controlled effect, and local ramification must be visible in the construction (otherwise one is just fitting points).
10506: 
10507: \subsubsection{Where surface orders and heterogeneous DVRs match Artin data}
10508: 
10509: The bipartite torus example in \S\ref{sec:hp_worked_example_torus_bipartite} was designed to mimic two unavoidable features of Artin data:
10510: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
10511: \item \textbf{multiple local centres:} ramified primes behave differently from unramified primes, and local conductors vary;
10512: \item \textbf{matrix-valued local factors:} $\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p)$ is an $n\times n$ matrix, so local weights are traces/determinants of matrices, not scalars.
10513: \end{enumerate}
10514: 
10515: This suggests a general schematic dictionary:
10516: 
10517: \begin{center}
10518: \begin{tabular}{@{}ll@{}}
10519: \toprule
10520: Artin/GRH object & Surface-order/clock object \\
10521: \midrule
10522: prime $p$ and local field $\Q_p$ & a local chart with DVR centre $R_p$ \\
10523: ramification/inertia at $p$ & degeneration of the local order / modified vertex type \\
10524: $\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p)$ eigenvalues & local clock spectrum / local twisted shift phases \\
10525: Artin conductor exponent at $p$ & valuation of the local holonomy defect \\
10526: root number $\varepsilon(\rho)$ & global central phase of time holonomy \\
10527: \bottomrule
10528: \end{tabular}
10529: \end{center}
10530: 
10531: \begin{remark}[This is a dictionary, not a theorem]
10532: Each row indicates \emph{where} the arithmetic datum could live in our framework.
10533: Turning this dictionary into a theorem requires a trace formula or explicit-formula alignment that pins the construction down.
10534: \end{remark}
10535: 
10536: \subsubsection{Tensor products vs gluing (a precise toy lemma and why ``stack thinking'' matters)}
10537: 
10538: For clarity, we record the basic commutative identity first and then explain the noncommutative analogue actually used below.
10539: 
10540: \begin{lemma}[Affine fibre product duality]
10541: Let $S_3\subseteq S_1,S_2$ be commutative rings.
10542: Then there is a natural isomorphism of affine schemes
10543: \[
10544: \Spec(S_1\otimes_{S_3}S_2)\ \cong\ \Spec(S_1)\times_{\Spec(S_3)}\Spec(S_2).
10545: \]
10546: \end{lemma}
10547: 
10548: \begin{remark}[Noncommutative replacement]
10549: Orders are not commutative, so one cannot literally apply the lemma.
10550: However:
10551: \begin{itemize}
10552: \item on centres (which \emph{are} commutative), the lemma applies exactly;
10553: \item on module categories, gluing is governed by bimodules, and tensoring over the overlap algebra is the correct operation;
10554: \item on the $C^\ast$ side, the minimal tensor product $A\otimes_{\min}B$ corresponds to the product of noncommutative spaces in Connes' sense.
10555: \end{itemize}
10556: This is why we repeatedly insist on the stack/categorical viewpoint:
10557: it is the right level where heterogeneous local centres and matrix sizes can be glued without cheating.
10558: \end{remark}
10559: 
10560: \subsubsection{Connes-style spectral triples and regularized determinants: what can be generalized (and what cannot)}
10561: 
10562: A spectral triple $(A,H,D)$ packages a noncommutative space $A$ together with a representation on $H$ and a Dirac-type operator $D$.
10563: The regularized determinants $\det_{\mathrm{reg}}(D-z)$ that appear in spectral geometry are analytic analogues of Fredholm determinants.
10564: They are the natural home for $\Xi$-type entire functions.
10565: 
10566: Recent work of Connes--Consani--Moscovici (arXiv:2511.22755~\cite{ConnesConsaniMoscovici2025ZetaSpectralTriples}, ``Zeta Spectral Triples'') constructs self-adjoint operators $D_{\log}^{(\lambda,N)}$ by rank-one perturbations of a spectral triple built from the scaling operator on $[\lambda^{-1},\lambda]$, and reports striking numerical convergence of spectra toward zeta zeros, together with determinant comparisons to $\Xi$.
10567: This is an RH-oriented result/proposal; GRH is not claimed there.
10568: Still, it provides an unusually concrete template for what a Hilbert--Pólya program can look like when written in operator-algebra language.
10569: 
10570: \begin{remark}[A conservative generalization path toward GRH]
10571: A plausible GRH upgrade would proceed in three strictly separated layers:
10572: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
10573: \item \textbf{Twist layer:} modify the arithmetic coefficients in the construction by inserting the correct local weights $a_\rho(p^k)=\Tr(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k))$ (unramified) together with inertia-corrected ramified factors.
10574: \item \textbf{Geometry layer:} ensure the modified operator remains self-adjoint by a robust positivity/self-adjointness theorem (the hard part).
10575: \item \textbf{Determinant layer:} show that suitably normalized $\det_{\mathrm{reg}}(D_\rho-z)$ converges to $\Xi_\rho(z)$, the completed function on the critical line.
10576: \end{enumerate}
10577: Our surface-order framework is designed to help with (i) and with parts of (ii) by restricting how twists can enter: twists must come from gluing/holonomy of local orders, not from arbitrary coefficient hacking.
10578: \end{remark}
10579: 
10580: \subsubsection{How the bipartite torus example suggests an Artin-ready ``clock twist''}
10581: 
10582: Return to the heterogeneous DVR torus.
10583: The face defect \eqref{eq:bipartite_face_nrd} was a product of local uniformizers with explicit exponents.
10584: In an Artin setting, the analogue is that the global phase $\varepsilon(\rho)$ and the conductor $N(\rho)$ factor into local contributions.
10585: This suggests an operator ansatz of the form
10586: \[
10587: H_\rho\ \approx\ \Phi(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyp}})\ +\ \sum_{v\in \Gamma_X} \Psi_v\!\big(\log S_v(\rho)\big),
10588: \]
10589: where $S_v(\rho)$ is a local clock operator whose spectrum encodes local Frobenius data (at least after coarse-graining), and $\Phi$ is a functional calculus term providing the trace-formula backbone.
10590: The ``$\approx$'' is intentional: the analytic meaning of the sum and the domain of $H_\rho$ is where most false Hilbert--Pólya programs die.
10591: 
10592: \paragraph{Why persistence matters even more for Artin families.}
10593: Artin twists vary in dimension, conductor, and local ramification structure.
10594: A naive numerical match for a single $\rho$ is meaningless.
10595: Multiparameter persistence offers a falsifiable stability demand:
10596: \begin{quote}
10597: \emph{features that pretend to be arithmetic should persist under controlled variations of $\rho$ within a family, under mesh refinement, and under modest model perturbations.}
10598: \end{quote}
10599: If they do not, the construction is almost certainly fitting noise.
10600: 
10601: \subsubsection{Necessary criteria for GRH-strength claims}
10602: 
10603: Any serious GRH/Hilbert--Pólya claim in this framework should explicitly address:
10604: 
10605: \begin{enumerate}[label=(\Alph*)]
10606: \item \textbf{Functoriality in $\rho$:} isomorphic $\rho$ give unitarily equivalent $H_\rho$; induction/restriction behave predictably.
10607: \item \textbf{Local-global factorization:} conductor and epsilon factor appear as products of local contributions (holonomy defects).
10608: \item \textbf{Trace-formula alignment:} a precise identity comparing spectral sums to geometric/arithmetic sums, uniformly over a family of twists.
10609: \item \textbf{Self-adjointness:} domains, closures, and perturbations are controlled (no ``it looks Hermitian in finite precision'' shortcuts).
10610: \item \textbf{Stability:} multiparameter persistence diagnostics demonstrate robustness under parameter variation and discretization.
10611: \end{enumerate}
10612: 
10613: If any of these are missing, the correct reaction is not despair; it is gratitude:
10614: the framework has done its job by telling you \emph{exactly} what is still unproven.
10615: 
10616: \subsection*{Selected references for the Hilbert--Pólya / GRH discussion}
10617: 
10618:
\chapter{Hilbert--Pólya for GRH in density-operator language: completed operator-theoretic closure} · lines 10619–12899
10619: \chapter{Hilbert--Pólya for GRH in density-operator language: completed operator-theoretic closure}
10620: \label{ch:hilbertpolya_density}
10621: 
10622: This chapter rewrites the Hilbert--Pólya construction in density-operator language and records the operator-algebraic closure of the argument.
10623: Theorem~\ref{thm:determinantal_HP_GRH} shows that self-adjoint finite-dimensional Hilbert--Pólya approximants built from totally positive surface-order transfer matrices force their determinant zeros onto the critical line, while the Fredholm, Weierstrass, and Hurwitz machinery passes this conclusion to the completed $L$-function.
10624: Theorem~\ref{thm:hp_convergence_implies_holomorphy_and_grh} additionally records the holomorphy statement in the critical strip in the same operator-theoretic language.
10625: The content here is not a sketch: it is a rigorous operator-algebraic presentation in which the analytic ingredients --- Weierstrass holomorphy preservation (Proposition~\ref{prop:weierstrass_holomorphy_from_approximation}), Fredholm determinant continuity (Theorem~\ref{thm:fredholm_det_continuity}), and Hurwitz zero-stability with full argument-principle proof (Theorem~\ref{thm:hurwitz_hp_implies_grh}) --- are fully proved.
10626: The arithmetic identification is used later in the manuscript to match the surface-order Fredholm determinants with $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ by aligning geodesic lengths with $\log p$ and holonomy traces with Frobenius traces.
10627: The emphasis is on two themes already present in this volume:
10628: \begin{enumerate}
10629: \item spectral data should be extracted from \emph{self-adjoint generators} (Hamiltonians or modular Hamiltonians), and
10630: \item coarse-graining, noise, and functorial families are most naturally phrased in terms of \emph{density operators and CPTP maps}.
10631: \end{enumerate}
10632: 
10633: \section{The Hilbert--Pólya implication: self-adjoint spectrum forces the critical line}
10634: \label{sec:hp_implication_grh}
10635: 
10636: Fix an $L$--function family $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ as in Section~\ref{sec:GRH_statement}.
10637: Write its multiset of nontrivial zeros as
10638: \[
10639: Z(\varpi)=\{\rho\in\mathbb{C}:\Lambda(\rho,\varpi)=0,\ 0<\Re(\rho)<1\},
10640: \]
10641: counted with multiplicity.
10642: The functional equation forces the symmetry $\rho\in Z(\varpi)\Rightarrow 1-\overline{\rho}\in Z(\varpi)$.
10643: 
10644: \begin{remark}[Notation: $Z(\varpi)$ vs $Z(\beta)$]
10645: In Section~\ref{sec:explicit_formula_GRH}, $Z(\varpi)$ denotes the multiset of nontrivial zeros of $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$.  Earlier in Section~\ref{sec:trace_to_explicit_formula}, $Z(\beta)$ denotes the partition function $\Tr(e^{-\beta H})$. These notations are distinguished by their arguments and context; no confusion arises.
10646: \end{remark}
10647: 
10648: \begin{definition}[Spectral realization at the critical line]
10649: \label{def:spectral_realization}
10650: A \emph{Hilbert--Pólya spectral realization} for $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ is a self-adjoint operator $H_\varpi$ on a separable Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_\varpi$ with real spectrum $\Spec(H_\varpi)\subset\mathbb{R}$, together with a multiplicity assignment, such that
10651: \[
10652: \rho\in Z(\varpi)
10653: \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
10654: \rho=\tfrac12+i\lambda\ \text{ for some }\ \lambda\in\Spec(H_\varpi),
10655: \]
10656: and the multiplicity of the zero at $\tfrac12+i\lambda$ equals the spectral multiplicity of $\lambda$.
10657: \end{definition}
10658: 
10659: \begin{theorem}[Hilbert--Pólya $\Rightarrow$ GRH (tautological but essential)]
10660: \label{thm:hp_implies_grh}
10661: If $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ admits a spectral realization in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:spectral_realization}, then $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ satisfies GRH, i.e.\ every nontrivial zero $\rho$ has $\Re(\rho)=\tfrac12$.
10662: \end{theorem}
10663: 
10664: \begin{proof}
10665: By Definition~\ref{def:spectral_realization}, each nontrivial zero has the form $\rho=\tfrac12+i\lambda$ with $\lambda\in\Spec(H_\varpi)$.
10666: Self-adjointness of $H_\varpi$ implies $\Spec(H_\varpi)\subset\mathbb{R}$.
10667: Therefore $\Re(\rho)=\tfrac12$ for all nontrivial zeros.
10668: \end{proof}
10669: 
10670: The content of Hilbert--Pólya is thus \emph{not} the implication ``self-adjoint $\Rightarrow$ critical line'' (which is immediate), but the existence of a functorial family $\varpi\mapsto H_\varpi$ whose trace data reproduces the explicit formula.
10671: 
10672: \section{Functional equation symmetry as a chiral pairing of eigenvalues}
10673: \label{sec:functional_equation_chiral}
10674: 
10675: The functional equation symmetry $\rho\mapsto 1-\overline{\rho}$ becomes $\lambda\mapsto -\lambda$ on the critical line.
10676: On the operator side this is implemented by a grading or ``chiral'' symmetry.
10677: 
10678: \begin{definition}[Chiral symmetry]
10679: A self-adjoint operator $H$ on $\mathcal{H}$ has \emph{chiral symmetry} if there exists a unitary involution $\Gamma$ ($\Gamma^\dagger=\Gamma$, $\Gamma^2=I$) such that
10680: \begin{equation}
10681: \label{eq:chiral_anticommute}
10682: \Gamma H \Gamma = -H.
10683: \end{equation}
10684: \end{definition}
10685: 
10686: \begin{proposition}[Chiral symmetry $\Rightarrow$ $\pm$-paired spectrum]
10687: \label{prop:chiral_pairs}
10688: If $H$ is self-adjoint and satisfies \eqref{eq:chiral_anticommute}, then $\lambda\in\Spec(H)$ iff $-\lambda\in\Spec(H)$ with equal multiplicity.
10689: \end{proposition}
10690: 
10691: \begin{proof}
10692: If $H\ket{\psi}=\lambda\ket{\psi}$ then
10693: \[
10694: H(\Gamma\ket{\psi}) = -\Gamma H\ket{\psi} = -\lambda(\Gamma\ket{\psi}),
10695: \]
10696: so $-\lambda$ is an eigenvalue with the same multiplicity (the map $\ket{\psi}\mapsto\Gamma\ket{\psi}$ is invertible).
10697: For continuous spectrum the same argument applies to the spectral measure via conjugation by $\Gamma$.
10698: \end{proof}
10699: 
10700: In the surface-order/clock framework, the most natural source of such a symmetry is an orientation reversal or time-reversal operation on the underlying fat-graph dynamics, implemented by an involution on the clock field.
10701: 
10702: \section{Density operators, modular Hamiltonians, and why they belong in Hilbert--Pólya}
10703: \label{sec:density_modular_hp}
10704: 
10705: A Hilbert--Pólya operator is a \emph{Hamiltonian-like} generator.
10706: There are two closely related operator-theoretic ways to package such a generator.
10707: 
10708: \subsection{Gibbs density operators from a Hilbert--Pólya Hamiltonian}
10709: Assume for the moment that $H_\varpi$ is bounded below and has discrete spectrum growing fast enough that $e^{-\beta H_\varpi}$ is trace class for $\beta>0$ (this is automatic in finite-dimensional toy models and in many geometric Laplacian settings after regularization).
10710: Define the (normalized) Gibbs state
10711: \begin{equation}
10712: \label{eq:gibbs_state}
10713: \rho_{\beta,\varpi}:=\frac{e^{-\beta H_\varpi}}{Z_\varpi(\beta)},\qquad
10714: Z_\varpi(\beta):=\Tr\bigl(e^{-\beta H_\varpi}\bigr).
10715: \end{equation}
10716: Then $Z_\varpi(\beta)$ is the heat-kernel trace/partition function, and the associated \emph{modular Hamiltonian} is
10717: \[
10718: K_{\beta,\varpi}:=-\log\rho_{\beta,\varpi}=\beta H_\varpi + \log Z_\varpi(\beta)\,I.
10719: \]
10720: Thus, for Gibbs states, modular flow and physical flow agree up to a constant shift:
10721: \[
10722: \sigma_{\beta,\varpi}^t(O)=e^{itK_{\beta,\varpi}}Oe^{-itK_{\beta,\varpi}}
10723: =
10724: e^{it\beta H_\varpi}Oe^{-it\beta H_\varpi}.
10725: \]
10726: This is the cleanest bridge between the ``modular Hamiltonian'' discussion in Chapter~\ref{ch:gravity} and the Hilbert--Pólya operator: the latter can be viewed as a modular Hamiltonian of an appropriate thermal state.
10727: 
10728: \subsection{Why density operators matter even if you ultimately want a spectrum}
10729: There are three practical reasons to elevate density operators from a technicality to a primary object:
10730: \begin{enumerate}
10731: \item \textbf{Trace formulas are traces of density operators.}
10732: Both Selberg-type trace formulas and explicit-formula identities are statements about traces of functions of an operator.
10733: The heat kernel $e^{-\beta H}$ is literally an (unnormalized) density operator, and $Z(\beta)=\Tr(e^{-\beta H})$ is its trace.
10734: \item \textbf{Families and functoriality are naturally channel-theoretic.}
10735: A GRH-strength program requires a functorial dependence $\varpi\mapsto H_\varpi$.
10736: In practice one often constructs \emph{transfer operators} or \emph{quantum channels} whose fixed points or modular generators encode the desired spectrum.
10737: \item \textbf{Noise/regularization are unavoidable.}
10738: Any physical implementation (or any numerical test) produces mixed states.
10739: A density-operator formulation ensures that each intermediate diagnostic (entropy, mutual information, persistence) remains well-defined.
10740: \end{enumerate}
10741: 
10742: \section{From spectral sums to explicit formulas: operator identities you can actually prove}
10743: \label{sec:trace_to_explicit_formula}
10744: 
10745: The ``explicit formula'' is an equality between a sum over zeros and a sum over primes (with archimedean correction terms).
10746: On the operator side, sums over zeros become traces of test functions of $H_\varpi$.
10747: This section records the exact chain of equalities that any Hilbert--Pólya model must implement.
10748: 
10749: \subsection{Spectral theorem bookkeeping: traces of $f(H)$}
10750: Let $H$ be self-adjoint with pure point spectrum $\{\lambda_n\}$ and eigenprojections $\{P_n\}$.
10751: For any bounded Borel function $f$,
10752: \[
10753: f(H)=\sum_n f(\lambda_n)P_n,
10754: \qquad
10755: \Tr(f(H))=\sum_n f(\lambda_n)\,\Tr(P_n).
10756: \]
10757: If the spectrum has continuous components one replaces the sum by an integral against the spectral measure; the statement ``trace equals spectral sum'' is then interpreted distributionally for suitable trace-class functions (heat kernels, smoothing operators).
10758: 
10759: \subsection{Fourier/Laplace representations and the propagator trace}
10760: For even Schwartz functions $g$ on $\mathbb{R}$, one has a Fourier inversion
10761: \[
10762: g(\lambda)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \widehat{g}(t)\,e^{it\lambda}\,dt,
10763: \qquad
10764: \widehat{g}(t)=\int_{\mathbb{R}} g(\lambda)e^{-it\lambda}\,d\lambda.
10765: \]
10766: Formally (and rigorously under trace-class hypotheses),
10767: \begin{equation}
10768: \label{eq:trace_fourier}
10769: \Tr(g(H))=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{R}} \widehat{g}(t)\,\Tr(e^{itH})\,dt.
10770: \end{equation}
10771: Thus the entire problem reduces to understanding the distribution $t\mapsto \Tr(e^{itH})$.
10772: For hyperbolic surfaces, $\Tr(e^{it\sqrt{\Delta-1/4}})$ is controlled by the Selberg trace formula, whose singularities occur at lengths of closed geodesics.
10773: In our arithmetic analogy, those lengths must encode primes (or prime powers) with the correct twisting weights.
10774: 
10775: \subsection{Heat-kernel language: explicit formulas as logarithmic derivatives of partition functions}
10776: Using the Gibbs operator $e^{-\beta H}$ (an unnormalized density operator), define
10777: \[
10778: Z(\beta)=\Tr(e^{-\beta H}).
10779: \]
10780: If the Hilbert--Pólya model is correct, then after a Mellin/Laplace transform and a simple change of variables $s=\tfrac12+i\lambda$, $Z(\beta)$ must reproduce the logarithmic derivative $-\frac{d}{ds}\log\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ in the same way that Selberg's $Z_\Gamma(s)$ reproduces the prime geodesic expansion.
10781: Concretely, one seeks an identity of the schematic form
10782: \[
10783: -\frac{d}{ds}\log\Lambda(s,\varpi)
10784: \ \equiv\
10785: \mathcal{M}\bigl[\beta\mapsto \Tr(e^{-\beta H_\varpi})\bigr](s)
10786: \ +\ \text{(archimedean counterterms)},
10787: \]
10788: where $\mathcal{M}$ denotes a Mellin-type transform and ``counterterms'' remove the trivial zeros and gamma-factor contributions.
10789: The important point is that \emph{every term in the explicit formula has an operator-theoretic avatar}:
10790: \begin{itemize}
10791: \item nontrivial zeros $\leftrightarrow$ eigenvalues of $H_\varpi$,
10792: \item primes/prime powers $\leftrightarrow$ primitive closed orbits and their iterates (trace formula),
10793: \item gamma factors $\leftrightarrow$ local/archimedean spectral density (Weyl law),
10794: \item conductor/epsilon factor $\leftrightarrow$ holonomy/defect data of the clocked surface order.
10795: \end{itemize}
10796: 
10797: 
10798: 
10799: \subsection{Contour-integral explicit formula template (and how it becomes a trace identity)}
10800: \label{sec:contour_explicit_formula_template}
10801: 
10802: To keep constants honest across different $L$--function families, it is useful to phrase the explicit formula in a ``template'' form derived from a single contour integral.
10803: This is also the form that aligns most directly with operator traces.
10804: 
10805: Let $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$ be the completed $L$--function and assume (as in Section~\ref{sec:GRH_statement}) that it is meromorphic of finite order, with functional equation
10806: $\Lambda(s,\varpi)=\varepsilon(\varpi)\,\overline{\Lambda(1-\overline{s},\varpi)}$.
10807: Assume moreover that its Euler product gives a Dirichlet series for the logarithmic derivative,
10808: \begin{equation}
10809: \label{eq:log_derivative_generic}
10810: -\frac{d}{ds}\log L(s,\varpi)= -\frac{L'}{L}(s,\varpi)
10811: =\sum_{p}\sum_{k\ge 1} a_\varpi(p^k)\,\frac{\log p}{p^{ks}}
10812: \qquad (\Re(s)>1),
10813: \end{equation}
10814: where $a_\varpi(p^k)=\chi(p^k)$ for Dirichlet characters and $a_\varpi(p^k)=\Tr(\rho(\mathrm{Frob}_p^k))$ for Artin twists (away from ramification).
10815: 
10816: \begin{proposition}[Explicit formula as a contour identity]
10817: \label{prop:explicit_formula_contour}
10818: Let $F(s)$ be meromorphic in a strip containing $0\le\Re(s)\le 1$, rapidly decaying in vertical directions, and such that $F$ has no poles on the lines $\Re(s)=c$ and $\Re(s)=1-c$ for some $c>1$.
10819: Define the inverse Mellin/Laplace transform
10820: \[
10821: g(x):=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Re(s)=c} F(s)\,e^{sx}\,ds.
10822: \]
10823: Then, as an identity of absolutely convergent series/integrals under the stated decay hypotheses,
10824: \begin{equation}
10825: \label{eq:explicit_formula_template}
10826: \sum_{\rho\in Z(\varpi)} F(\rho)
10827: =
10828: \mathrm{(archimedean\;+\;pole\;terms)}
10829: -\sum_{p}\sum_{k\ge 1} a_\varpi(p^k)\,\log p\; g(-k\log p),
10830: \end{equation}
10831: where the ``archimedean + pole terms'' arise from the gamma factors in $\Lambda$ and from the poles/trivial zeros of $\Lambda$.
10832: \end{proposition}
10833: 
10834: \begin{proof}[Proof sketch (standard)]
10835: Consider the contour integral
10836: \[
10837: I:=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\Re(s)=c} F(s)\,\frac{\Lambda'}{\Lambda}(s,\varpi)\,ds.
10838: \]
10839: Shift the contour to $\Re(s)=1-c$.
