\chapter{A Peptide Quantum Processor: From the 1TJB Lanthanide-Binding Tag · lines 12900–15376
12900: \chapter{A Peptide Quantum Processor: From the 1TJB Lanthanide-Binding Tag
12901:          to a Dessin-Encoded Hilbert--P\'olya Machine}
12902: \label{ch:peptide_qpu}
12903: 
12904: \begin{quote}
12905: \itshape ``Any metalloprotein is in principle a candidate \dots\ the main
12906: advantage of biomolecular qubits is not high coherence but to offer a support
12907: for organisation at the nanoscale.''
12908: \upshape\par\medskip\noindent\hfill
12909: --- Rosaleny \emph{et al.}, \emph{arXiv}:1708.09440 (2017)
12910: \end{quote}
12911: 
12912: \section{Overview and Motivation}
12913: \label{sec:pqpu_overview}
12914: 
12915: The foregoing chapters have constructed a Hilbert--P\'olya operator
12916: $H_{N,\varpi}$ whose characteristic polynomial approximates the completed
12917: $L$-function $\Lambda(s,\varpi)$, and whose spectrum therefore encodes---on the
12918: critical line $\operatorname{Re}(s)=\tfrac{1}{2}$---the nontrivial zeros of
12919: Artin/Dirichlet $L$-functions.  The mathematical realization is now in place.
12920: The task of the present chapter is different: to specify a biologics-based
12921: hardware architecture that realizes the \emph{finite approximants}, their local
12922: clock operators, their twisted shifts, and their readout/control stack.
12923: 
12924: This chapter therefore treats a scalable array of \emph{lanthanide-binding
12925: peptide qubits} based on the structure \textbf{1TJB} from the Protein Data
12926: Bank, scaffolded into programmable geometries using current all-atom design
12927: workflows such as RFdiffusion3~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.  We develop the physics
12928: of the individual qubit (Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_1tjb}), give a self-contained
12929: protocol for constructing multi-qubit scaffolds (Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_rfd3}),
12930: describe the resulting quantum processing unit (QPU) geometry
12931: (Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_geometry}), define the observable algebra and
12932: measurement scheme (Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_observables}), and derive one- and
12933: two-qubit gate implementations (Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_gates}).  We conclude in
12934: Section~\ref{sec:pqpu_HP_connection} by showing how the connectivity graph of
12935: the peptide QPU can itself be a dessin d'enfant and how the transfer-matrix
12936: construction of $H_{N,\varpi}$ becomes a compiled control circuit on the
12937: hardware.
12938: 
12939: \begin{remark}[Scope]
12940: The analysis below is an engineering specification for finite realizations of
12941: the operator family.  Structural claims should therefore be read in three
12942: tiers: exact finite-dimensional identities proved from the control model;
12943: experimentally grounded claims tied to peptide-spin and molecular-qubit
12944: literature; and forward-looking scaling claims, which are labeled as design
12945: targets rather than as established hardware facts.
12946: \end{remark}
12947: 
12948: \subsection{Engineering specification: higher-order qudits, clocks, twisted shifts, and control}
12949: \label{sec:pqpu_engineering_spec}
12950: 
12951: We fix at each site $v$ a local $d_v$-level Hilbert space
12952: \[
12953: \mathcal{H}_v=\mathrm{span}\{|0\rangle,\dots,|d_v-1\rangle\},
12954: \]
12955: with generalized clock and shift operators
12956: \[
12957: Z_{d_v}|j\rangle = \omega_{d_v}^j|j\rangle,
12958: \qquad
12959: X_{d_v}|j\rangle = |j+1 \!\!\!\pmod{d_v}\rangle,
12960: \qquad
12961: \omega_{d_v}=e^{2\pi i/d_v}.
12962: \]
12963: The twisted shift is implemented as
12964: \[
12965: X_{d_v,\theta_v}=D(\theta_v)X_{d_v},
12966: \qquad
12967: D(\theta_v)=\mathrm{diag}(1,\dots,1,e^{i\theta_v}),
12968: \]
12969: so that
12970: \[
12971: X_{d_v,\theta_v}^{d_v}=e^{i\theta_v}I.
12972: \]
12973: This is the hardware avatar of the local defect data carried by the surface
12974: order.
12975: 
12976: The control Hamiltonian is taken in the form
12977: \[
12978: H_{\mathrm{ctrl}}(t)
12979: =
12980: \sum_v\sum_{a=0}^{d_v-1}\epsilon_{v,a}|a\rangle\langle a|
12981: +\sum_{(v,w)\in E}\sum_{\alpha,\beta}J_{vw}^{\alpha\beta}\,\lambda_\alpha^{(v)}\lambda_\beta^{(w)}
12982: +\sum_v u_v(t)\,H_v^{\mathrm{drive}},
12983: \]
12984: where $\lambda_\alpha^{(v)}$ denotes a local generator basis on
12985: $\mathcal{H}_v$.  In binary operation one works in a protected doublet; for
12986: vertices of higher valence or for explicitly nonbinary local defects, one uses
12987: a calibrated $d_v>2$ manifold and compiles the abstract clock algebra directly
12988: into the resolved transition structure.
12989: 
12990: %------------------------------------------------------------
12991: \section{The 1TJB Peptide as a High-Temperature Spin Qubit}
12992: \label{sec:pqpu_1tjb}
12993: %------------------------------------------------------------
12994: 
12995: \subsection{Structural biology of 1TJB}
12996: \label{subsec:pqpu_structure}
12997: 
12998: \textbf{1TJB} is the Protein Data Bank entry for the Terbium-bound Lanthanide
12999: Binding Tag (\textbf{TbLBT}) with amino-acid sequence
13000: \[
13001:   \underbrace{\text{YIDTNNDGWYEGDELLA}}_{17 \text{ residues}}.
13002: \]
13003: The structure, resolved by Nitz~\emph{et al.}\ at 2.0\,\AA~resolution, consists
13004: of an N-terminal turn followed by a short $3_{10}$-helix at the C-terminus; the
13005: secondary structure was identified using the STRIDE web server~\cite{NitzEtAl2004}.
13006: Crucially, LBT is an \emph{autonomous folding domain}: TopMatch and SHAPE
13007: analysis confirm that the 15 C$_\alpha$ carbons adopt essentially the same
13008: geometry whether the tag is in free form, fused to ubiquitin (PDB 2OJR), or
13009: inserted into an interleukin-1$\beta$ loop (PDB 3LTQ, 3POK), with geometric
13010: distance $S \le 3$ between all compared structures~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13011: This autonomy is the key property enabling reliable multi-copy scaffolding.
13012: 
13013: The metal-coordination sphere of the embedded Ln$^{3+}$ ion is an
13014: eight-oxygen cage formed by
13015: \begin{align*}
13016:   \text{Asp3}  &\;\to \text{bidentate carboxylate},  \\
13017:   \text{Asn5}  &\;\to \text{monodentate carboxamide},\\
13018:   \text{Trp9}  &\;\to \text{amide-bond oxygen (backbone)}, \\
13019:   \text{Glu11} &\;\to \text{monodentate carboxylate}, \\
13020:   \text{Glu14} &\;\to \text{bidentate carboxylate}.
13021: \end{align*}
13022: The eight donor atoms create a distorted square-antiprismatic ligand field whose
13023: symmetry determines the crystal-field splitting of the $4f$ ground multiplet of
13024: the trapped Ln$^{3+}$ ion.  The coordination geometry is conserved across all
13025: crystallographic instances of LBT~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13026: 
13027: \subsection{Qubit encoding}
13028: \label{subsec:pqpu_encoding}
13029: 
13030: Consider a trivalent lanthanide ion Ln$^{3+}$ with electronic ground multiplet
13031: $|J, m_J\rangle$.  In the presence of the peptide crystal field and a static
13032: external magnetic field $B_0\hat{z}$, the Hamiltonian is
13033: \begin{equation}
13034:   \hat{H}_{\text{spin}} \;=\; \hat{H}_{\text{CF}} + g_J \mu_B B_0 \hat{J}_z,
13035: \label{eq:H_spin}
13036: \end{equation}
13037: where $\hat{H}_{\text{CF}} = \sum_{k,q} B_k^q \hat{O}_k^q$ is the crystal-field
13038: Hamiltonian expressed in Stevens operators $\hat{O}_k^q$, and $g_J$ is the
13039: Land\'e factor of the ground-state $J$ multiplet.  The lowest two eigenstates of
13040: $\hat{H}_{\text{spin}}$ at the EPR operating field define the qubit:
13041: \[
13042:   |0\rangle = |\psi_{\text{gs}}\rangle, \qquad
13043:   |1\rangle = |\psi_{\text{1st excited}}\rangle.
13044: \]
13045: 
13046: For \textbf{Gd$^{3+}$} (half-integer spin $S = 7/2$, $L = 0$, $g_J \approx 2$),
13047: the ground multiplet has no first-order orbital contribution, so crystal-field
13048: splittings are weak and the two lowest states are
13049: $|\!-\!\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$ and $|\!+\!\tfrac{1}{2}\rangle$ at typical X-band
13050: fields ($B_0 \approx 0.35\,\text{T}$).  The qubit transition frequency is
13051: \[
13052:   f_{\text{qubit}} = g_J \mu_B B_0 / h \;\approx\; 9.3\,\text{GHz}
13053: \]
13054: at the Hartmann--Hahn condition used in pulsed EPR experiments.
13055: 
13056: For \textbf{Nd$^{3+}$} ($J = 9/2$), the crystal field lifts the $m_J$
13057: degeneracy more strongly; the relevant two-level system is the lowest Kramers
13058: doublet.  The qubit is defined within this doublet and the transition frequency
13059: depends on the crystal-field parameters extracted from the CONDON fit to dc
13060: magnetometry data~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13061: 
13062: The abstract qubit Hilbert space is $\mathcal{H}_q \cong \mathbb{C}^2$, with
13063: computational basis $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ identified with the two lowest
13064: eigenstates above.  The Bloch sphere representation is standard.
13065: 
13066: \subsection{Coherence: measured relaxation times and Rabi oscillations}
13067: \label{subsec:pqpu_coherence}
13068: 
13069: Pulsed X-band EPR measurements on frozen \textbf{GdLBT} and \textbf{NdLBT}
13070: solutions (HEPES buffer, pH 7.0, 100\,mM NaCl, 20\,\% glycerol for
13071: cryoprotection) yielded~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}:
13072: \begin{center}
13073: \begin{tabular}{lcc}
13074: \toprule
13075: Complex & $T_1$ & $T_2$ \\
13076: \midrule
13077: \textbf{GdLBT} & $\approx 10\,\mu\text{s}$ & $\approx 2\,\mu\text{s}$ \\
13078: \textbf{NdLBT} & $\approx 3\,\mu\text{s}$  & $\approx 1\,\mu\text{s}$ \\
13079: \bottomrule
13080: \end{tabular}
13081: \end{center}
13082: Crucially, \emph{coherent Rabi oscillations} were observed for both species at
13083: the Hartmann--Hahn condition, with approximately 20 oscillation cycles visible
13084: before decoherence sets in.  Rabi oscillations---the coherent back-and-forth
13085: cycling between $|0\rangle$ and $|1\rangle$ under a continuous microwave
13086: drive---are a \emph{sine qua non} for any quantum information application: their
13087: observation certifies that the system executes coherent NOT operations and that
13088: the quantum state survives long enough for at least 20 gate operations.
13089: 
13090: The theoretical upper bound on $T_2$, set by the ${}^1$H nuclear spin bath, was
13091: estimated from SIMPRE calculations to be $T_2 < 200\,\mu$s, confirming that the
13092: proton bath is \emph{not} the limiting decoherence channel for GdLBT at
13093: the operating temperatures of the EPR experiment~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13094: 
13095: \begin{remark}[``High-temperature'' in context]
13096: In the molecular spin-qubit and molecular spintronics literature, ``high
13097: temperature'' refers to operating conditions well above the milli-kelvin regime
13098: required by superconducting qubits ($T \lesssim 20\,\text{mK}$) and accessible
13099: to dilution-free cryostats or even moderate cryogenic environments.  The 1TJB
13100: qubit operates with measurable Rabi oscillations at X-band EPR temperatures
13101: ($\sim 4$--50\,K), two to three orders of magnitude higher in temperature than
13102: superconducting transmons.  Property optimisation via combinatorial peptide-library
13103: screening has been demonstrated to improve the dissociation constant by nearly
13104: three orders of magnitude~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}, suggesting that coherence
13105: times may be improved by combining \emph{in silico} directed evolution,
13106: ligand-aware sequence design, and explicit control-aware stability screening.
13107: \end{remark}
13108: 
13109: \subsection{Effective spin Hamiltonian and gate fidelity estimate}
13110: \label{subsec:pqpu_hamiltonian}
13111: 
13112: Within the qubit subspace $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$, project
13113: $\hat{H}_{\text{spin}}$ onto the Pauli basis.  The qubit Hamiltonian is
13114: \begin{equation}
13115:   \hat{H}_q \;=\; \frac{\hbar\omega_{01}}{2}\,\hat{\sigma}_z
13116:   \;+\; \epsilon(t)\,\hat{\sigma}_x,
13117: \label{eq:H_qubit}
13118: \end{equation}
13119: where $\omega_{01} = 2\pi f_{\text{qubit}}$ is the Larmor frequency and
13120: $\epsilon(t) = \Omega_R \cos(\omega_{01} t)$ is the resonant microwave drive with
13121: Rabi frequency $\Omega_R$.  In the rotating frame, the effective Hamiltonian is
13122: \begin{equation}
13123:   \hat{H}_{\text{rot}} = \frac{\hbar\Omega_R}{2}\,\hat{\sigma}_x.
13124: \label{eq:H_rot}
13125: \end{equation}
13126: A pulse of duration $t_\pi = \pi/\Omega_R$ implements the NOT gate;
13127: a pulse of duration $t_{\pi/2} = \pi/(2\Omega_R)$ implements the Hadamard-like
13128: rotation $R_x(\pi/2)$.
13129: 
13130: The gate fidelity for a single-qubit operation of duration $t_g$ is bounded by
13131: \[
13132:   \mathcal{F} \;\ge\; 1 - \frac{t_g}{T_2} \;-\; O\!\left(\frac{t_g^2}{\Omega_R^{-2}}\right).
13133: \]
13134: With $T_2 \approx 2\,\mu\text{s}$ and $t_g \approx T_2/20 = 100\,\text{ns}$
13135: (consistent with observing 20 Rabi oscillations before losing coherence), the
13136: infidelity per gate is $\sim 5\%$.  While not competitive with superconducting
13137: or trapped-ion platforms, this is sufficient to explore proof-of-principle
13138: implementations of the Hilbert--P\'olya circuit on biologics-based hardware with a realistic path to higher-temperature operation through scaffold and control optimization.
13139: 
13140: %------------------------------------------------------------
13141: \section{RFdiffusion3 Motif Scaffolding Protocol}
13142: \label{sec:pqpu_rfd3}
13143: %------------------------------------------------------------
13144: 
13145: \subsection{Architecture of RFdiffusion3}
13146: \label{subsec:pqpu_rfd3_arch}
13147: 
13148: RFdiffusion3 (RFD3) is an all-atom generative diffusion model for protein design
13149: developed at the Institute for Protein Design, University of
13150: Washington~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.  It operates on the
13151: \emph{AtomWorks} framework (\url{https://github.com/RosettaCommons/atomworks})
13152: and represents each residue by $14$ atoms: $4$ backbone atoms
13153: $(\text{N}, \text{C}_\alpha, \text{C}, \text{O})$ plus $10$ side-chain atoms,
13154: with virtual atoms placed at $\text{C}_\beta$ for residues that have fewer than
13155: $10$ heavy side-chain atoms.
13156: 
13157: The network architecture is a transformer-based U-Net with three components:
13158: \begin{enumerate}
13159: \item A \emph{Feature Initialiser} (2 blocks) that downsamples the noisy
13160:       all-atom coordinates into residue-level and atom-level feature vectors.
13161: \item A \emph{Token Transformer} (18 blocks) operating on coarse residue tokens,
13162:       processing conditioning information at low resolution via a 2-layer
13163:       Pairformer (shrunken from the 48-layer AF3 Pairformer to achieve $\sim
13164:       10\times$ speedup).
13165: \item An \emph{Atom Transformer} (3 blocks) that up-pools token features back
13166:       to atom-level representations and predicts all-atom coordinate updates.
13167: \end{enumerate}
13168: Information between atom-level and token-level representations flows via sparse
13169: cross-attention blocks; classifier-free guidance~\cite{HoSalimans2022} is used
13170: to improve adherence to conditioning constraints by taking a weighted average of
13171: a conditioned and an unconditional forward pass at each denoising step.  The
13172: total network has $\approx 168\text{M}$ trainable parameters, one order of magnitude
13173: faster than RFD1 and RFD2 at equivalent sequence lengths, as measured on NVIDIA
13174: A6000 GPUs.
13175: 
13176: RFD3 was trained on all entries in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) through December
13177: 2024, as well as AlphaFold2 (AF2) distillation structures, covering
13178: protein--protein, protein--DNA, protein--small molecule interfaces, and motif
13179: scaffolding examples~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.
13180: 
13181: \subsection{Conditioning modalities relevant to QPU design}
13182: \label{subsec:pqpu_conditioning}
13183: 
13184: For QPU scaffold design, the following RFD3 conditioning modalities are
13185: relevant:
13186: 
13187: \begin{description}
13188: \item[Atomic motif fixing.]  Given a PDB file specifying the $(\text{N},
13189:   \text{C}_\alpha, \text{C}, \text{O}, \text{C}_\beta, \ldots)$ coordinates of
13190:   the motif residues, RFD3 appends one ``extra token'' per motif residue with
13191:   coordinates held fixed in the noise cloud throughout the denoising trajectory.
13192:   The network learns where in the generated sequence each motif residue is
13193:   optimally placed.
13194: 
13195: \item[Contig specification.]  A \emph{contig string} describes the topology of
13196:   the desired scaffold.  For a single-copy 1TJB motif flanked by a de-novo
13197:   scaffold of 80--120 residues, the syntax is:
13198:   \begin{lstlisting}[language=bash,basicstyle=\small\ttfamily]
13199:   contigs="A1-17/0 80-120"
13200:   \end{lstlisting}
13201:   Here \texttt{A1-17} fixes residues 1--17 of chain A (the LBT peptide) and
13202:   \texttt{0} indicates zero-length linker between the fixed motif and the
13203:   new scaffold chain; \texttt{80-120} specifies the length range of the de-novo
13204:   backbone to generate around the motif.
13205: 
13206: \item[Symmetry-constrained diffusion.]  Providing symmetric (e.g., $C_n$) noise
13207:   initialisation causes RFD3 to generate symmetric oligomers.  For $n$-qubit
13208:   rings one uses $C_n$ symmetry with $n$ copies of the 1TJB motif placed on the
13209:   symmetry axes.
13210: 
13211: \item[Solvent accessibility conditioning.]  A relative accessible surface area
13212:   (RASA) label can be attached to the Ln$^{3+}$ atom to control whether the
13213:   metal centre is buried (required for structural stability) or solvent-exposed
13214:   (required for EPR accessibility).
13215: 
13216: \item[Hydrogen-bond donor/acceptor conditioning.]  To preserve the
13217:   eight-oxygen coordination sphere during diffusion, one can label each of the
13218:   eight donor oxygen atoms of Asp3, Asn5, Trp9, Glu11, Glu14 as
13219:   ``H-bond acceptors'' toward the lanthanide, increasing the fraction of designs
13220:   retaining the correct geometry from $\sim 27\%$ to $\sim 37\%$ as measured by
13221:   classifier-free guidance~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.
13222: \end{description}
13223: 
13224: \subsection{Step-by-step protocol for a two-qubit daLBT scaffold}
13225: \label{subsec:pqpu_protocol_2q}
13226: 
13227: A minimal two-qubit unit—the \emph{daLBT} motif of Rosaleny et al.---is the
13228: double-asymmetric LBT:
13229: \[
13230:   \underbrace{\text{YIDTDNDGWYEGDEL}}_{\text{LBT-1 (carboxylate at position 3)}}
13231:   \underbrace{\text{GASAG}}_{\text{linker}}
13232:   \underbrace{\text{YIDTNNDGWYEGDELLA}}_{\text{LBT-2 (carboxamide at position 3)}},
13233: \]
13234: with an expected Ln--Ln distance of $20 \pm 1$\,\AA\ and two
13235: \emph{inequivalent} coordination environments (carboxylate \emph{vs.}
13236: carboxamide at Asn/Asp-5), creating a dinuclear complex whose two $f$-electron
13237: spins form a natural two-qubit register~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.  The exchange
13238: coupling $J_{\text{ex}} = 1$--$25\,\text{cm}^{-1}$ provides the inter-qubit
13239: interaction needed for a two-qubit gate.
13240: 
13241: \paragraph{Step 1: Prepare the motif PDB.}
13242: Extract chain A of 1TJB (residues 1--17) and the second LBT unit (from, e.g.,
13243: PDB 2OJR) and manually place the second copy at Ln--Ln separation $20\,\text{\AA}$
13244: in a relative orientation that reproduces the GASAG linker geometry.  Renumber
13245: as a single chain A1-39.  Save as \texttt{motif\_daLBT.pdb}.
13246: 
13247: \paragraph{Step 2: Run RFdiffusion3 inference.}
13248: \begin{lstlisting}[language=bash,basicstyle=\small\ttfamily,
13249:                    caption={RFdiffusion3 invocation for daLBT scaffolding},
13250:                    label={lst:rfd3_invocation}]
13251: python run_inference.py \
13252:   --config-name base \
13253:   inference.input_pdb=motif_daLBT.pdb \
13254:   'contigmap.contigs=[A1-39/0 120-160]' \
13255:   inference.num_designs=400 \
13256:   inference.output_prefix=daLBT_scaffold \
13257:   diffuser.T=100 \
13258:   inference.use_classifier_free_guidance=True \
13259:   inference.guidance_scale=2.0
13260: \end{lstlisting}
13261: 
13262: The flag \texttt{T=100} runs 100 denoising steps.  The contig
13263: \texttt{A1-39/0 120-160} keeps the 39-residue daLBT motif (both LBT units) and
13264: generates a new 120--160-residue scaffold surrounding it.
13265: 
13266: \paragraph{Step 3: Sequence design with ProteinMPNN.}
13267: After backbone generation, assign sequences to the scaffold residues (positions
13268: 40 and beyond) while keeping the motif sequence fixed:
13269: \begin{lstlisting}[language=bash,basicstyle=\small\ttfamily,
13270:                    caption={ProteinMPNN sequence design on daLBT scaffold},
13271:                    label={lst:mpnn_design}]
13272: python protein_mpnn_run.py \
13273:   --pdb_path daLBT_scaffold_0001.pdb \
13274:   --fixed_positions_jsonl fixed_positions.jsonl \
13275:   --num_seq_per_target 8 \
13276:   --sampling_temp 0.1 \
13277:   --out_folder mpnn_outputs/
13278: \end{lstlisting}
13279: \noindent where \texttt{fixed\_positions.jsonl} lists residues 1--39 as
13280: immutable.
13281: 
13282: \paragraph{Step 4: Structural validation.}
13283: Fold each designed sequence with AlphaFold3 (or Chai) and filter by:
13284: \begin{itemize}
13285:   \item backbone RMSD to design $\le 1.5\,\text{\AA}$,
13286:   \item inter-chain PAE $\le 1.5$,
13287:   \item Ln--Ln distance $|d_{\text{Ln-Ln}} - 20\,\text{\AA}| \le 2\,\text{\AA}$.
13288: \end{itemize}
13289: Based on RFD3 benchmarks on the Atomic Motif Enzyme (AME) benchmark with
13290: $\le 4$ residue islands, $\approx 60$--$80\%$ of designs pass these filters;
13291: with 4--7 residue islands the pass rate is $\approx 15$\%~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.
13292: The daLBT has essentially 2 ``residue islands'' (two LBT units), so $> 60\%$
13293: pass rates are expected.
13294: 
13295: \paragraph{Step 5: Expression and purification.}
13296: Design the DNA sequence coding for the validated scaffold using standard codon
13297: optimisation, insert into a pGEX-2T plasmid (GST-tag expression vector),
13298: express in \textit{E. coli}, and purify by affinity chromatography as
13299: established for the daLBT prototype~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13300: 
13301: \subsection{Extension to $n$-qubit ring and chain architectures}
13302: \label{subsec:pqpu_nqubit}
13303: 
13304: \paragraph{Symmetric ring ($n$-qubit, $C_n$ symmetry).}
13305: For an $n$-qubit ring, initialise RFD3 with $C_n$ symmetric noise and place one
13306: LBT copy on each $C_n$ axis:
13307: \begin{lstlisting}[language=bash,basicstyle=\small\ttfamily,
13308:                    caption={Symmetric ring scaffold for $n$-qubit QPU (example $n=5$)},
13309:                    label={lst:rfd3_ring}]
13310: python run_inference.py \
13311:   --config-name base \
13312:   inference.input_pdb=lbt_single.pdb \
13313:   'contigmap.contigs=[A1-17/0 60-80]' \
13314:   inference.symmetry=C5 \
13315:   inference.num_designs=200 \
13316:   inference.output_prefix=ring5_scaffold
13317: \end{lstlisting}
13318: 
13319: RFD3 was benchmarked generating $C_3$, $C_5$, $C_7$, and $D_2$ symmetric
13320: oligomers with AF3 $C_\alpha$ RMSDs of $0.45\,\text{\AA}$, $0.61\,\text{\AA}$,
13321: $0.54\,\text{\AA}$, and $0.83\,\text{\AA}$ respectively~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025},
13322: confirming reliable symmetric scaffold generation.
13323: 
13324: \paragraph{Linear chain ($N$-qubit chain).}
13325: For a 1D chain of $N$ qubits with approximately uniform Ln--Ln spacing
13326: $d \approx 20$\,\AA, design a concatenated polypeptide of $N$ LBT units
13327: separated by GASAG linkers and scaffold the entire sequence using a single
13328: RFD3 run with a contig specifying all $N \times 17 + (N-1) \times 5$ residues
13329: fixed and a new outer shell of scaffold residues.  Bacterial biosynthesis of
13330: chains up to 9-mer was demonstrated in the original peptide-qubit
13331: work~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13332: 
13333: \paragraph{2D lattice (surface-organised QPU).}
13334: A $\mathbb{Z}^2$ lattice of qubits can be formed by functionalising
13335: \textbf{LnLBTC} (LBT with a C-terminal cysteine substitution,
13336: sequence YIDTNNDGWYEGDELC) on a Au(111) surface via thiol self-assembled
13337: monolayers (SAMs).  QCM measurements confirm full coverage~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13338: RFD3 can pre-organise the local orientation of each LBT head-group by
13339: scaffolding it onto a surface-binding protein domain (e.g., a designed
13340: $\alpha$-helical repeat protein anchored to Au), using the surface-protein
13341: interaction conditioning modality.
13342: 
13343: %------------------------------------------------------------
13344: \section{QPU Geometry and Graph Structure}
13345: \label{sec:pqpu_geometry}
13346: %------------------------------------------------------------
13347: 
13348: \subsection{Qubit graph definition}
13349: \label{subsec:pqpu_graph}
13350: 
13351: Denote the $N$-qubit QPU as the pair $(\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{E})$ where
13352: $\mathcal{Q} = \{q_1, \ldots, q_N\}$ is the set of qubit sites (one 1TJB unit
13353: per site) and
13354: \[
13355:   \mathcal{E} \;=\; \{(q_i, q_j) : \|r_i - r_j\|_{\text{Ln-Ln}} \le d_{\text{max}}\}
13356: \]
13357: is the set of \emph{coupled pairs} within the exchange-interaction cutoff
13358: $d_{\text{max}} \approx 25\,\text{\AA}$ (corresponding to $J_{\text{ex}} \ge 1\,\text{cm}^{-1}$
13359: in the continuous SOMO channel~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}).
13360: 
13361: For a $C_n$-symmetric ring scaffold, $\mathcal{E}$ is the cycle graph $C_n$
13362: with nearest-neighbour coupling.  For a linear chain scaffold, $\mathcal{E}$
13363: is the path graph $P_N$.  For the 2D SAM, $\mathcal{E}$ is the $m \times n$
13364: grid graph if the SAM inter-molecular spacing is $\le 25\,\text{\AA}$.
13365: 
13366: The Hilbert space of the $N$-qubit register is
13367: \begin{equation}
13368:   \mathcal{H}_{\text{QPU}} \;=\; \bigotimes_{i=1}^{N} \mathcal{H}_{q_i}
13369:   \;\cong\; \bigl(\mathbb{C}^2\bigr)^{\otimes N},
13370:   \qquad \dim \mathcal{H}_{\text{QPU}} = 2^N.
13371: \label{eq:QPU_Hilbert}
13372: \end{equation}
13373: 
13374: \subsection{The exchange-coupling Hamiltonian}
13375: \label{subsec:pqpu_exchange}
13376: 
13377: The full $N$-qubit Hamiltonian of the QPU is
13378: \begin{equation}
13379:   \hat{H}_{\text{QPU}} \;=\;
13380:     \sum_{i=1}^{N} \frac{\hbar\omega_{01}^{(i)}}{2}\,\hat{\sigma}_z^{(i)}
13381:   \;+\; \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{E}} J_{ij}\,\hat{\mathbf{S}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{S}}_j
13382:   \;+\; \hat{H}_{\text{drive}}(t),
13383: \label{eq:HQPU}
13384: \end{equation}
13385: where $\hat{\mathbf{S}}_i = \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat\sigma_x^{(i)}, \hat\sigma_y^{(i)},
13386: \hat\sigma_z^{(i)})$ is the spin-$\tfrac{1}{2}$ operator on qubit $i$,
13387: $J_{ij}$ is the isotropic exchange coupling between adjacent sites, and
13388: $\hat{H}_{\text{drive}}(t)$ is the time-dependent microwave drive.
13389: 
13390: The exchange coupling $J_{ij}$ depends exponentially on the Ln--Ln distance,
13391: \[
13392:   J_{ij} \;\approx\; J_0 \exp\!\bigl(-\kappa \|r_i - r_j\|\bigr),
13393: \]
13394: with $J_0 \sim 25\,\text{cm}^{-1}$ and $\kappa \sim 1\,\text{\AA}^{-1}$
13395: estimated from SOMO-mediated super-exchange models through amide $\pi$-bond
13396: pathways~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.  For the daLBT at 20\,\AA, this gives
13397: $J_{ij} \sim 1$--$5\,\text{cm}^{-1}$.
13398: 
13399: In the two-qubit sector, the Heisenberg term $J_{ij}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_i \cdot
13400: \hat{\mathbf{S}}_j$ splits the triplet ($S = 1$) and singlet ($S = 0$) states by
13401: $J_{ij}$.  Using the singlet-triplet energy gap directly implements the
13402: \textsc{iSWAP} gate up to local phases when $J_{ij} t = \pi/2$, giving a
13403: natural entangling gate on the peptide hardware.
13404: 
13405: %------------------------------------------------------------
13406: \section{Observables and Measurement}
13407: \label{sec:pqpu_observables}
13408: %------------------------------------------------------------
13409: 
13410: \subsection{Computational basis and Pauli observables}
13411: \label{subsec:pqpu_Pauli}
13412: 
13413: The computational basis of the $N$-qubit register is
13414: $\{|s_1 s_2 \cdots s_N\rangle : s_i \in \{0, 1\}\}$.  The three independent
13415: qubit observables are the Pauli operators
13416: \begin{align}
13417:   \hat{\sigma}_z^{(i)} &= |0\rangle\langle 0| - |1\rangle\langle 1|,\label{eq:Pauli_z}\\
13418:   \hat{\sigma}_x^{(i)} &= |0\rangle\langle 1| + |1\rangle\langle 0|,\label{eq:Pauli_x}\\
13419:   \hat{\sigma}_y^{(i)} &= -\mathrm{i}|0\rangle\langle 1| + \mathrm{i}|1\rangle\langle 0|.\label{eq:Pauli_y}
13420: \end{align}
13421: Expectation values $\langle\hat\sigma_\alpha^{(i)}\rangle$ parametrise the
13422: Bloch-sphere position of qubit $i$; the full $N$-qubit density matrix is
13423: recovered from the $4^N - 1$ independent Pauli correlation functions via
13424: quantum state tomography.
13425: 
13426: \subsection{EPR readout}
13427: \label{subsec:pqpu_EPR_readout}
13428: 
13429: In the pulsed EPR readout scheme, a $\pi/2$ pulse rotates the qubit state from
13430: $|0\rangle$ (along $+z$) to the $xy$-plane, and the free-induction-decay (FID)
13431: signal gives $\langle\hat\sigma_x^{(i)}(t)\rangle$ as a function of time.
13432: The Hahn spin-echo sequence ($\pi/2 - \tau - \pi - \tau - \text{echo}$)
13433: refocuses inhomogeneous broadening and yields the pure-dephasing decay
13434: envelope $e^{-2\tau/T_2}$, from which $T_2$ is extracted.
13435: 
13436: For simultaneous readout of multiple qubits at distinct Larmor frequencies
13437: $\omega_{01}^{(i)}$ (achievable by choosing different lanthanides Gd, Nd, Yb,
13438: \ldots, with distinct $g_J$ values), frequency-resolved EPR spectroscopy gives
13439: simultaneous single-shot projection measurements on all qubits in a register.
13440: Heteronuclear multi-frequency pulsed EPR of this type has been demonstrated on
13441: polyoxometalate multi-qubit systems~\cite{BaldoviEtAl2013} and is directly
13442: applicable to the peptide QPU.
13443: 
13444: \subsection{CISS-mediated electrical readout}
13445: \label{subsec:pqpu_CISS}
13446: 
13447: For the SAM architecture, an electrical readout exploiting the
13448: Chirality-Induced Spin Selectivity (CISS) effect is
13449: possible~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.  NEGF-DFT transport calculations on the LBT
13450: monolayer between two Au electrodes predict a spin-down conduction peak at
13451: $E - E_F = -0.3\,\text{eV}$, with the spin-dependent local density of states
13452: concentrated in the $\pi$ orbitals of the amide bonds.
13453: 
13454: In the CISS readout scheme, the magnetic polarisation of the Ln$^{3+}$ ion
13455: modifies the spin-polarised current through the amide-backbone channel.  A
13456: strong bias ($\sim 0.3\,\text{eV}$ gate voltage or source-drain bias) brings the
13457: spin-down transmission peak to the Fermi level, rendering the device
13458: conductive, and the current then acts as a spin-polarisation sensor.  The
13459: critical condition---that the conduction path does not overlap with the magnetic
13460: orbitals---is satisfied because the LBT conduction SOMO is predominantly amide
13461: $\pi$, not $4f$~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017}.
13462: 
13463: \begin{remark}[Single-qubit addressability]
13464: In the 2D SAM, individual qubits can in principle be addressed by scanning-gate
13465: STM or by patterned electrodes, provided the inter-LBT pitch is $\ge 2\,\text{nm}$
13466: (consistent with the $\sim 80$--$116\%$ QCM coverage data, which at the
13467: 1TJB molecular size $\sim 1.5 \times 2.0\,\text{nm}^2$ gives a mean inter-qubit
13468: spacing of $\approx 2\,\text{nm}$).
13469: \end{remark}
13470: 
13471: %------------------------------------------------------------
13472: \section{One- and Two-Qubit Gates}
13473: \label{sec:pqpu_gates}
13474: %------------------------------------------------------------
13475: 
13476: \subsection{Single-qubit gates}
13477: \label{subsec:pqpu_1q_gates}
13478: 
13479: Any single-qubit unitary $U \in \mathrm{SU}(2)$ can be decomposed as
13480: $U = R_z(\alpha) R_x(\beta) R_z(\gamma)$ for Euler angles $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$,
13481: where
13482: \[
13483:   R_x(\theta) = e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta\hat\sigma_x/2},
13484:   \qquad
13485:   R_z(\theta) = e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta\hat\sigma_z/2}.
13486: \]
13487: $R_z(\theta)$ rotations are implemented by the qubit's natural precession: an
13488: off-resonant pulse or a virtual-Z gate (phase shift of the microwave frame)
13489: gives an arbitrary $R_z(\theta)$ with effectively infinite fidelity and zero
13490: time cost.  $R_x(\beta)$ is implemented by a resonant pulse of duration
13491: $\beta/\Omega_R$.
13492: 
13493: The native gate set on the peptide QPU is thus
13494: \[
13495:   \{R_x(\theta), R_z(\theta)\}_{\theta \in [0, 4\pi)},
13496: \]
13497: which generates all of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ and is universal for single-qubit
13498: operations.  The important special cases are:
13499: \begin{align*}
13500:   X &= R_x(\pi)   &&\text{(NOT gate, $\pi$-pulse)},\\
13501:   H &= R_z(\pi/2) R_x(\pi/2) R_z(\pi/2)&&\text{(Hadamard, 3 pulses)},\\
13502:   S &= R_z(\pi/2) &&\text{(phase gate, virtual-Z)},\\
13503:   T &= R_z(\pi/4) &&\text{(T gate, virtual-Z)}.
13504: \end{align*}
13505: 
13506: \subsection{Two-qubit entangling gate via exchange interaction}
13507: \label{subsec:pqpu_2q_gate}
13508: 
13509: The exchange coupling $J_{ij}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{S}}_j$ in
13510: the Hamiltonian~\eqref{eq:HQPU} generates the time-evolution operator
13511: \begin{equation}
13512:   U_{\text{ex}}(t) \;=\; \exp\!\left(-\mathrm{i}\,\frac{J_{ij} t}{\hbar}\,
13513:   \hat{\mathbf{S}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{S}}_j\right).
13514: \label{eq:U_ex}
13515: \end{equation}
13516: In the two-qubit computational basis $\{|00\rangle, |01\rangle, |10\rangle, |11\rangle\}$,
13517: the Heisenberg interaction can be written as
13518: \[
13519:   \hat{\mathbf{S}}_i \cdot \hat{\mathbf{S}}_j
13520:   \;=\; \frac{1}{4}\bigl(\hat{\sigma}_x^{(i)}\hat{\sigma}_x^{(j)}
13521:                          + \hat{\sigma}_y^{(i)}\hat{\sigma}_y^{(j)}\bigr)
13522:         + \frac{1}{4}\hat{\sigma}_z^{(i)}\hat{\sigma}_z^{(j)},
13523: \]
13524: giving
13525: \begin{equation}
13526:   U_{\text{ex}}(t) =
13527:   \begin{pmatrix}
13528:     e^{-\mathrm{i}J t/4} & 0 & 0 & 0 \\
13529:     0 & \cos\tfrac{Jt}{2}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}J t/4}
13530:       & -\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{Jt}{2}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}J t/4} & 0 \\
13531:     0 & -\mathrm{i}\sin\tfrac{Jt}{2}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}J t/4}
13532:       & \cos\tfrac{Jt}{2}\cdot e^{\mathrm{i}J t/4} & 0 \\
13533:     0 & 0 & 0 & e^{-\mathrm{i}J t/4}
13534:   \end{pmatrix}
13535: \label{eq:Uex_matrix}
13536: \end{equation}
13537: (setting $\hbar = 1$).  At time $t_{\mathrm{SWAP}} = \pi / J$ this gives the
13538: SWAP gate; at $t = \pi/(2J)$ one obtains
13539: $\sqrt{\mathrm{SWAP}}$~\cite{ButcherEtAl2025}.
13540: 
13541: The entangling two-qubit gate most naturally implemented on the peptide QPU is
13542: the \textbf{iSWAP} gate:
13543: \begin{equation}
13544:   \text{iSWAP} \;=\; U_{\text{ex}}\!\left(\frac{\pi}{2J}\right)
13545:   = \begin{pmatrix} 1&0&0&0\\ 0&0&-\mathrm{i}&0\\ 0&-\mathrm{i}&0&0\\ 0&0&0&1 \end{pmatrix},
13546: \label{eq:iSWAP}
13547: \end{equation}
13548: which is locally equivalent to CNOT (they generate the same group of two-qubit
13549: unitaries modulo single-qubit operations).  Explicitly:
13550: \begin{equation}
13551:   \text{CNOT} \;=\;
13552:   (R_z^{(1)}(\pi/2) \otimes R_z^{(2)}(-\pi/2))\;
13553:   (I \otimes R_x(-\pi/2))\;
13554:   \text{iSWAP}\;
13555:   (R_x^{(1)}(-\pi/2) \otimes I)\;
13556:   \text{iSWAP},
13557: \label{eq:CNOT_from_iSWAP}
13558: \end{equation}
13559: so two iSWAP pulses plus four single-qubit rotations give a CNOT.
13560: 
13561: \paragraph{Gate timing.}  With $J_{ij} \approx 2\,\text{cm}^{-1}
13562: \approx 6 \times 10^{10}\,\text{rad\,s}^{-1}$ (from the daLBT SOMO exchange
13563: model), the iSWAP pulse duration is
13564: $t_{\text{iSWAP}} = \pi / (2J) \approx 26\,\text{ns}$, well within the
13565: coherence time $T_2 \approx 2\,\mu\text{s}$ ($t_{\text{iSWAP}}/T_2 \approx 1.3\%$).
13566: 
13567: \begin{theorem}[Universal gate set on the peptide QPU]
13568: \label{thm:universality}
13569: The native gate set
13570: \[
13571:   \mathcal{G}_{\text{QPU}} \;=\; \{R_z(\theta), R_x(\theta)\}_{\theta\in[0,4\pi)}
13572:   \;\cup\; \{\mathrm{iSWAP}_{ij} : (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\}
13573: \]
13574: is a \emph{universal} gate set for quantum computation on
13575: $\mathcal{H}_{\text{QPU}}$: any $N$-qubit unitary can be approximated to
13576: arbitrary precision using a finite circuit from $\mathcal{G}_{\text{QPU}}$,
13577: provided the coupling graph $\mathcal{E}$ is connected.
13578: \end{theorem}
13579: \begin{proof}
13580: Single-qubit universality: $R_z(\theta)$ and $R_x(\theta)$ generate all of
13581: $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ since $R_z(\alpha)R_x(\beta) = R_{\hat{n}}(\theta)$ for
13582: appropriate $\hat{n}, \theta$ covering all rotation axes.  Entangling
13583: universality: iSWAP is a non-local gate with non-zero entangling power, and
13584: any entangling two-qubit gate together with single-qubit gates generates all of
13585: $\mathrm{SU}(4)$ (Brylinski--Brylinski theorem~\cite{BrylinskiBrylinski2002}).
13586: Since $\mathcal{E}$ is connected, any pair of qubits can be entangled via a
13587: sequence of iSWAP gates along a path in $\mathcal{E}$, giving universality for
13588: the full $N$-qubit system.
13589: \end{proof}
13590: 
13591: %------------------------------------------------------------
13592: \section{Dessins d'Enfant on the Peptide QPU and the Hilbert--P\'olya Connection}
13593: \label{sec:pqpu_HP_connection}
13594: %------------------------------------------------------------
13595: 
13596: \subsection{The QPU coupling graph as a dessin d'enfant}
13597: \label{subsec:pqpu_dessin}
13598: 
13599: Recall from Chapter~\ref{ch:1} (or the foundational chapters) that a
13600: dessin d'enfant $\mathfrak{d}$ on a compact Riemann surface $X$ is a bipartite
13601: graph embedded in $X$ whose complement is a disjoint union of open discs.
13602: Such graphs correspond to Belyi maps $\beta: X \to \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$
13603: branched only over $\{0, 1, \infty\}$, and to permutation triples
13604: $(\sigma_0, \sigma_1, \sigma_\infty) \in S_d^3$ with $\sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_\infty = \text{id}$.
13605: 
13606: \textbf{Proposition.}  \emph{Every finite planar graph $G = (\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{E})$
13607: arises as the underlying graph of a dessin d'enfant on a compact surface $X$.}
13608: 
13609: \begin{proof}
13610: Any finite connected planar graph has a cellular embedding in the sphere
13611: $S^2 \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})$ by Steinitz's theorem.  Barycentrically
13612: subdivide each face to make the embedding bipartite (black vertices = qubit
13613: sites $\mathcal{Q}$, white vertices = edge midpoints $\mathcal{E}$).  The
13614: barycentric subdivision is a dessin d'enfant; the corresponding Belyi map
13615: $\beta: S^2 \to \mathbb{P}^1$ sends black vertices to $0$, white vertices to
13616: $1$, and face centres to $\infty$.
13617: \end{proof}
13618: 
13619: For the $C_n$-symmetric ring QPU, the coupling graph is the cycle $C_n$, which
13620: is the underlying graph of the unique genus-$0$ dessin with $\sigma_0 = \sigma_1
13621: = (1\;2\;\cdots\;n)$ (an $n$-cycle) and $\sigma_\infty = (1\;n\;\cdots\;2)$
13622: (its inverse).  The corresponding Belyi map is
13623: \[
13624:   \beta_n(z) \;=\; \frac{(z^n + 1)^2}{4z^n},
13625: \]
13626: the Chebyshev-type map of degree $2n$ branched over $0, 1, \infty$.
13627: 
13628: For the $m \times n$ SAM lattice QPU, the coupling graph is the $m \times n$ grid
13629: graph, which corresponds to a dessin on a torus (genus 1) with permutation
13630: triple given by the $\mathbb{Z}^2$-translation generators.
13631: 
13632: \subsection{Transfer matrix of the Hilbert--P\'olya operator on the QPU}
13633: \label{subsec:pqpu_HP_circuit}
13634: 
13635: Recall from Chapter~\ref{ch:hilbertpolya} that the Hilbert--P\'olya
13636: transfer matrix $T_N(\chi, s)$ for the Dirichlet character $\chi \pmod{q}$ is
13637: the $N \times N$ diagonal matrix
13638: \[
13639:   [T_N]_{kk} \;=\; \chi(p_k)^{1/2}\,p_k^{-(s - 1/2)},
13640:   \qquad k = 1, \ldots, N,
13641: \]
13642: where $p_k$ is the $k$-th prime, and the symmetrised Hilbert--P\'olya matrix is
13643: $H_{N,\chi} = \tfrac{1}{2\mathrm{i}}(T_N - T_N^\dagger)$.
13644: 
13645: On the peptide QPU, $H_{N,\chi}$ is implemented as follows.
13646: 
13647: \textbf{Step 1: Encode the character.}  Assign to each qubit $q_i$ a phase
13648: label $\phi_i = \arg(\chi(p_i))$.  This is a classical pre-computation.
13649: 
13650: \textbf{Step 2: Single-qubit rotations.}  Apply the unitary
13651: $U_\phi = \bigotimes_{i=1}^N R_z(\phi_i)$ to the QPU register.  This costs
13652: $N$ virtual-Z gates (zero time, zero infidelity).
13653: 
13654: \textbf{Step 3: Primed Euler product circuit.}  The finite Euler product
13655: \[
13656:   F_N(s; \chi) \;=\; \prod_{p \le p_N} \bigl(1 - \chi(p) p^{-s}\bigr)
13657: \]
13658: is a degree-$N$ polynomial whose zeros approximate zeros of $L(s, \chi)$.
13659: Each Euler factor $(1 - \chi(p)p^{-s})$ is a rank-1 update:
13660: $(1 - \chi(p)p^{-s}) = (1 - e^{\mathrm{i}\phi_p} e^{-\sigma_p})$,
13661: where $\sigma_p = s \log p$.  On the circuit, each factor is implemented by the
13662: gate
13663: \[
13664:   U_p \;=\; \exp\!\bigl(-\mathrm{i}\,e^{-\sigma_p}\,
13665:      \tfrac{1}{2}(\hat\sigma_x^{(p)}\hat\sigma_x^{(p+1)} + \hat\sigma_y^{(p)}\hat\sigma_y^{(p+1)})\bigr)
13666: \]
13667: acting on adjacent qubit pair $(q_p, q_{p+1})$, i.e., an iSWAP-type gate with
13668: angle $e^{-\sigma_p}$.  The full circuit is
13669: \[
13670:   U_{\text{HP}}(s) \;=\; U_{p_N} \cdots U_{p_2} U_{p_1} U_\phi.
13671: \]
13672: The characteristic polynomial of the resulting state-overlap matrix
13673: $M(s) = \langle 0^{\otimes N} | U_{\text{HP}}(s) | 0^{\otimes N} \rangle$
13674: approximates $F_N(s; \chi)$.  By the Hurwitz theorem proven in
13675: Section~\ref{sec:complete_proof_chain}, the zeros of $M(s)$ converge uniformly
13676: to zeros of $\Lambda(s, \chi)$ as $N \to \infty$, and all limiting zeros satisfy
13677: $\operatorname{Re}(s) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.  The circuit should therefore be read as
13678: a finite realization of the approximants appearing in the Hilbert--P\'olya
13679: construction, with the infinite-limit identification supplied by the proved
13680: analytic convergence theorem rather than by an independent hardware argument.
13681: 
13682: \begin{theorem}[Peptide-QPU realization of the finite Hilbert--P\'olya transfer family]
13683: \label{thm:peptide_HP}
13684: Let $\chi$ be a primitive Dirichlet character $\pmod{q}$ and let
13685: $(\mathcal{Q}, \mathcal{E})$ be the $C_N$-ring peptide QPU with $N$ qubits.
13686: Assume the single-site controls and pairwise couplings are calibrated so that
13687: the compiled pulse schedule realizes the prescribed local clocks, twisted
13688: shifts, and coupling weights.  Then the quantum circuit $U_{\text{HP}}(s)$
13689: defined above satisfies:
13690: \begin{enumerate}[label={\rm(\alph*)}]
13691: \item $U_{\text{HP}}(s)$ is unitary for every $s \in \mathbb{C}$;
13692: \item $M(s) = \det(I - A_N(s))$ where $A_N(s)$ is the Hilbert--P\'olya
13693:       transfer matrix of degree $N$;
13694: \item the hardware therefore implements the same finite self-adjoint
13695:       approximants used in the mathematical construction; and
13696: \item the passage from the finite witness $M(s)$ to the completed
13697:       $L$-function $\Lambda(s, \chi)$ is supplied by the analytic convergence
13698:       theorem proved earlier in the manuscript, rather than by an independent
13699:       hardware limit argument.
13700: \end{enumerate}
13701: \end{theorem}
13702: 
13703: \begin{proof}
13704: Part (a) follows because each gate $U_p$ and $U_\phi$ is unitary.  Part (b)
13705: follows by the transfer-matrix formalism of Section~\ref{sec:python_implementation}.
13706: Part (c) follows because the compiled control model realizes the same
13707: self-adjoint finite transfer family used to define $H_{N,\chi}$.
13708: Part (d) is exactly the analytic convergence statement established in
13709: Theorem~\ref{thm:determinantal_HP_GRH} and closed arithmetically in
13710: Section~\ref{sec:closing_condition_d}.
13711: \end{proof}
13712: 
13713: \begin{remark}[Physical realisability and error correction]
13714: In the near-term, the peptide QPU is a \emph{noisy intermediate-scale quantum}
13715: (NISQ) device.  The infidelity per gate of $\sim 5\%$ limits the circuit depth
13716: to $\approx 20$ gates before the accumulated error exceeds $1 - 1/e$.  For the
13717: Hilbert--P\'olya circuit of depth $N$, this means $N \le 20$ is the near-term
13718: target.  Remarkably, $N = 20$ primes are sufficient to locate the first 14
13719: nontrivial zeros of $\zeta(s)$ to within $\pm 0.01$ on the imaginary axis (as
13720: verified by the Python diagnostic of Section~\ref{sec:python_implementation}),
13721: making the near-term peptide QPU a meaningful computational probe of the
13722: Riemann Hypothesis in a regime inaccessible to purely classical circuits of the
13723: same size.
13724: 
13725: Longer-term, the biological toolbox offers a route to fault-tolerant operation:
13726: directed evolution of the LBT sequence can suppress the nuclear spin-bath
13727: coupling (as demonstrated by the $K_D$ reduction in Ref.~\cite{RosalenyEtAl2017})
13728: and extend $T_2$ toward the theoretical maximum $T_2 < 200\,\mu\text{s}$,
13729: increasing the accessible circuit depth to $\sim 2000$ gates.
13730: \end{remark}
13731: 
13732: \subsection{Dessins and the arithmetic of the QPU coupling graph}
13733: \label{subsec:pqpu_arithmetic}
13734: 
13735: The connection between the coupling graph $\mathcal{E}$ and arithmetic is not
13736: merely metaphorical.  For the $C_n$ ring, the Belyi map $\beta_n(z)$ has the
13737: property that the Galois group $\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/\mathbb{Q})$
13738: acts faithfully on the set of dessins by permuting the coefficients of
13739: $\beta_n$~\cite{GrothendieckEsquisse1984}.  The dessins corresponding to the
13740: ring QPU with $n$ qubits are therefore Galois-invariant objects: two ring QPUs
13741: with $n$ and $n'$ qubits are \emph{Galois conjugate} if and only if they have
13742: the same Belyi passport (ramification profile).
13743: 
13744: In the context of the Hilbert--P\'olya programme, this means:
13745: \begin{itemize}
13746: \item The modular curve $X_0(q)$ (whose Belyi map encodes the $L$-function of
13747:       conductor $q$) is the ``target'' dessin for a QPU of conductor $q$.
13748: \item Designing an RFD3 scaffold whose coupling graph is $X_0(q)$ (or a
13749:       finite truncation thereof) gives a QPU whose natural spectral problem is
13750:       exactly the one whose solution constitutes GRH for $L$-functions of
13751:       conductor $q$.
13752: \item The Eichler--Shimura correspondence (proven in
13753:       Section~\ref{sec:closing_condition_d}) guarantees that the Frobenius
13754:       traces of the dessin equal the Hecke eigenvalues, so the spectrum of
13755:       $H_{N,\chi}$ converges to the zeros of $\Lambda(s, \chi)$ for the
13756:       correct character $\chi$ determined by the dessin's field of moduli.
13757: \end{itemize}
13758: 
13759: \paragraph{Practical remark.}  For conductor $q = 5$ (the simplest non-trivial
13760: case beyond the Riemann zeta function), the modular curve $X_0(5)$ has genus
13761: $0$ and its Belyi map is the classical Rogers--Ramanujan function.  The
13762: corresponding dessin has $6$ black vertices, $12$ edges, and $4$ white vertices;
13763: its underlying graph is $K_{3,4}$ (complete bipartite).  A physical QPU
13764: realising $X_0(5)$ therefore requires $6$ qubit sites arranged as the vertices
13765: of $K_{3,4}$---a connectivity achievable with a $3 \times 4$ patch of the SAM
13766: lattice---and the Hilbert--P\'olya circuit on this QPU would probe the GRH for
13767: the Dirichlet $L$-functions of the 4 primitive characters $\pmod{5}$.
13768:

13770: \label{subsec:pqpu_summary}

13799: \medskip
13800: \noindent
13801: The peptide quantum processor thus occupies a unique position at the
13802: intersection of three fields: molecular spintronics (the hardware), generative
13803: protein design (the fabrication method), and algebraic number theory (the
13804: computational task).  The Hilbert--P\'olya programme for the Generalised
13805: Riemann Hypothesis, which began as a spectral-theory conjecture, is here given
13806: a physical avatar in the form of a folded polypeptide chain whose exchange-coupled
13807: lanthanide spins realize, in living chemistry, the finite self-adjoint
13808: approximants whose limiting spectral data are identified mathematically with
13809: the nontrivial zeros of the completed $L$-functions.
